Oṃ,
homage to the Remover of Obstacles!
The Playful Display of the Goddesses' Names.
Composed by the eminent Mahāmāheśvara teacher Sāhibakaulānandanātha. First Devotion:
The wise [know] the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), which has manifested the expansion of name and form, and whose form consists of the three forms (trairūpya).

Victorious is that splendor in the form of Śiva’s power, naturally sweet toward his devotees, whose essence transcends even the words "was," "is," and "will be," and which has abandoned all calculation of the union and separation of what is possible and impossible— thus celebrated in his sublime sayings.
Thus, my heart repeatedly stirred by that [desire],
I shall now reveal this King of Hymns to Sundarī— spoken of old by the Lord to Nandin—
within this pure and illustrious abode known as Sāhibkaula, even in all circumstances.
Having established the glory of his own self through independence, he clearly manifests the splendor of eloquent speech. || 2 ||
In the northeastern direction lies the lord of mountains known by the name Kailāsa, renowned as the very essence of beauty, exalted by the presence of thousands of royal swans from Lake Mānasa;
there dwells Sthāṇu, his body subdued by the Daughter of the Mountain, white with his own splendor.
The monk, having abandoned his mind in other vehicles through that devotion born of love for the [Buddha], || 3 ||

Where Śiva, the God of Gods, or Viṣṇu, has come to behold [the Lord] free from fear; where Indra, possessed of a hundredfold fortitude, for a moment submerges himself under the guise of a shadow in the essence of the beauty of Mālinī’s body that steals away all impurity, and having emerged—
Those skillful ones, for whom the rising light has spread everywhere, know each and every art of form.

Where the Goddess Śivā, possessing wondrous intelligence, having perceived her own form, that of her husband, and the reflected and transformed forms in four ways, suspected them to be otherwise; [therein] the most beneficial and meritorious [union], though somehow separated into portions of half-and-half, was won. p. 3) [End of page 3] (Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a poetic description of the cosmic union (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śakti, likely from a work such as the *Śivasūtravimarśinī* or a related commentary on Kashmiri Śaivism. The "fourfold" nature refers to the manifestation of the Absolute as the Self, the Lord, the reflection, and the transformation.)
Why indeed did she, so skilled in policy, lead the body to the manifestation of oneness with each [of its parts]? || 5 ||
When that most clever white [garment], which was her own covering, had been wonderfully concealed by the Lord during an expansive and marvelous jest,
the Goddess, exhausted from searching for it for a very long time, wondered: "What indeed has become of it?"
He does not extend far beyond half his body [the left], for Śiva is graced by immeasurable love.
For those whose minds are fixed in unwavering devotion to Śambhu, whose sins have been washed away by meditation upon Him,
and who have attained the splendor of the light of His pure immersion over time—
the western moonlight rises from all sides, spreading its boundless merit everywhere.
That which appears as its substratum shines like a body remaining as an object of non-destruction. || 7 ||

O King of Birds, this one has indeed attained a wondrous accumulation of purity, consisting of nectar and the essence of beauty, because he practiced austerities standing upon the pillar [of the world], disciplined and directed by a glance from the One who was pleased by his smile. (p. 4)
The abode of the lunar rays, desirable to all, is the supreme [place] for both this world and the next. || 8 ||
Or rather, we consider that mountain to be the very essence of splendor belonging to the Lord of the Snowy Peaks,
since Pārvatī— having abandoned her birthplace, the ocean rich in jewels— desires it as her own dwelling;
or perhaps she desires the formidable, trident-bearing Hara, who is clad in animal skins.
The Supreme Goddess, whose limbs were slightly bent as she stepped across the Ganges, took refuge there.
Or rather, even though it is lighter than Meru, the lord of mountains, it shines most loftily;
for the best of the gods, having abandoned that immeasurable mountain which was their constant abode,
have come here at that very moment under the pretext of beholding Giriśa, and now remain established within it.
Afflicted by greed, they return for a long time, devoid of the practice of austerity and lacking the company of the virtuous.
On the head of the Lord of Mountains, there shines eternally the daily rising of the fire, white from the very beginning of creation and filled on all sides with flames;
by that ash falling at the appointed time during the performance of Śiva’s dance upon the coiled serpent, [the moon] is rendered pale.
Is he not like a mass of ashes enveloped, who has been solidified from the waters of the Gaṅgā? || 11 ||
Bound by Vāsuki at its base and weighed against the tip of the Pināka bow, the heavy Pātāla-tāla tree became light enough to reach the very limits of the sky;
it was once full and possessed all sixteen digits, yet it now ascends to the heavens as something insignificant.
Having transferred even a single digit [of her essence], she took refuge in the mass of matted hair (jaṭājūṭa) resting upon Śiva.
Having observed Brahmā, the master of the skillful art of world-creation, and having taken refuge here in Him who possesses the excellence of all wealth through His snowy mountain-like form—
by whose very nature even the Lord of Mountains (Śiva) attained the full radiance of the abode of Girijā (Pārvatī).
Could it be that Śambhu himself has descended here, with the splendor of his utterly pure and exalted radiance?

Of whom even the celestial river [Gaṅgā] has been made to bear a comparison for the essence of beauty— she who, like a measuring-stick, possesses a body of extreme weight and is difficult to lift due to her pride;
for while one [the Gaṅgā] stays at his foot, being heavy, the other [the Gaurī] rests upon his head, being light.
The trembling Lajjālū, abandoning him, fell to the ground in agitation. || 14 ||

How is it that the mountain [Kailāsa], which constantly bears on its sides the sun and the moon—the former equal in brilliance to fire and the latter equal to water—nevertheless always supports a portion of the feet of the illustrious Śambhu upon its head? (p. 7)
It displays to the worlds that which is preeminent, having the singular essence of extreme wonder. || 15 ||
There too, having beheld that world-transcending form reflected in the perfectly clear [mirror], the Apsarases— who had come to see the daughter of the Lord of Mountains—
were overcome with shame and became exceedingly distressed in their haste, as if he were joined to them as the lord of half their bodies.
Thus, those deluded ones who possess a full sense of self-identity return from here to their own abodes and hermitages.
Where even the days— long caves inhabited by those who partake in darkness— are reached by the rising light that pervades everything as it issues forth from the reflections of the sun and moon,
once the Lord of Creatures has attained his proper seat for eternal rest.
Those who possess self-mastery are never able to know even a single digit of that tranquil darkness which bestows peace. || 17 ||
Where, even though the apsarases have become utterly charming reflections of one another in the jewels that stand as the finest of ornaments with their full and radiant rays—
and where both [the apsarases and the jewels] have immediately attained a state delightful through their newly arisen clarity— [we are not captivated].
Those who have committed great crimes do not forcibly undergo the delusion of mistaking white for other colors.
As His shadow is reflected within the vast expanse of the pure lake of Mānasa,
which possesses a natural and abundant flow and serves as the abode for His own feet,
He reveals to His devotees that stainless form through meditation upon Him in their own minds.
He who [attains] this new, most beneficial, and future digit (kalā) which brings about immediate purification.
On one side, in that cremation ground where various jewels were shimmering,
sat the Great Lord Hara, whose pair of feet is worshipped by Sanaka and others;
he is the Lord of Gods whom the lords of the gods worship again for the sake of liberation from the cycle of existence.
[They praised] the God of gods, whose power transcends the conceptualization of existence and non-existence, with new [hymns]. || 20 ||

Having abandoned all discourse regarding the weight of cause and effect, he is the ocean of the nectar of intense bliss, characterized by the spontaneous vibration of his own absolute freedom; being without substrate, he has the power both to act and not to act,
and even through their reversal, he grants the realization of the manifestation of various distinctions that are otherwise difficult to comprehend.
He is the supreme one, whose glory is the realization of primordial consciousness that is established, tasted, and beyond beginning, and for whom all sublation has reached its limit.
He, whose many distinct forms— each possessing a multitude of exquisite ornaments and clearly manifesting a radiant splendor that surpasses the luster of the lotus with its bright face—
are seen again and again by her eyes, which are raised and cast down, [dispelling] the mass of darkness within her heart.
It wards off for heroes that which is difficult for Indra to resist and which causes transformation. || 22 ||
The gods bow to the best of gods, and the sons of Diti to the lord of the Daityas, but not to anyone else,
for they are stubbornly bound by the mutual enmity of being designated as each other's enemies;
yet they [bow] to Śaṅkara, who is supreme over all and skilled in the dance of the playful manifestation of his own unity.
All of them, as if devoid of fear, had their gaze fixed upon the single body that was the locus of the two [lovers] who were well-disposed toward one another. || 23 ||
From whose head the celestial river flows incessantly— she whose praiseworthy fame pervades the entire expanse of the sky and the ocean, and who is as pure as the netherworld (Pātāla);
she who is fierce and terrible yet clear with grace, and who is like the cool-rayed moon to the ocean of knowledge.
The sound of the waves shimmering from the play of her speech was like the proclamation of the worlds. || 24 ||
At first held within by a single flavor, and later remaining there filled with the overflowing love for Pārvatī, she dwells in a crowded place,
her restless and quarrelsome chatter longing for waves, agitated by the exhaustion of her efforts.
Is she perhaps Gaṅgā herself, with her pure limbs, who has emerged outside, exceedingly skillful in her graceful gestures? || 25 ||

(12) That king who delights his subjects, whose body was rendered incomplete by the nectar trickling from the flickering flame on his forehead, and who— having renounced his own pure and solitary portion— was the son of the ocean upon the rim of the cauldron-like mass of his ten million matted locks; [that king...]
"What indeed has come from the beginning?"—thus he wondered, apprehensive that his entire head might have vanished.

The nail-like flame within the matted locks of the elephant-headed one, which has risen from the forehead-fire of Śiva, is as if it were the single point of convergence for both the celestial river and the fire of his forehead, as they strive together to produce either satisfaction or combustion through their intense mutual rivalry.
Does the lovely digit of the moon, dense with light, shine upon his head as a bringer of peace? (27)
[Salutation] to that forehead-region, richly adorned with a mass of matted locks (*jaṭājūṭa*) bound in the form of a focused exertion,
where the wind is stilled by the vast expanse of the play of the lofty waves of the Gaṅgā;
which is flooded by its stream, and wherein the flames of the fire of his eye blaze forth.
Indeed, his head was a sanctuary, manifesting the multitude of beings dwelling within his heart.
The sun, heating all equally during the summer season, becomes free from its spot and attains the state of the moon, possessing all its digits through constant practice;
yet what does it spread above that [moon], which, seized by separation, possesses only one digit within?
Or else, in another [instance], it is that which shines with its own splendor, surpassing all others in essence by its own power.
Upon his broad forehead, which is made exceedingly white by the arrangement of abundant ashes all around, the fire shines most intensely with its flickering flames that dispel darkness—
like the sky at the end of the rainy season when the clouds have vanished, becoming as pure as water in the autumn.
It was like the great orb of the young sun rising at midday, devoid of its covering.

(14) Since the fire of the forehead has become accustomed through constant proximity to the waters of the Gaṅgā resting upon his head— its flames being pure and flickering amidst very broad palm leaves— how much more so now that it has reached the descent [of the Ganges] and is agitated within by the mass of waves?
Having gone there, he—that very same Vāḍava fire—thoroughly and intensely inflames the ocean.

The body of the Lord, whose form is light yet formless, and whose nature is the richness of supreme intellect, shines forth through the guise of the fire upon his head— a fire that is peerless in its rhythmic play of grace.
Because this fire blazes incessantly and intensely even for the Lord, it remains as a residue of ash that is not diminished.
Is another body imagined for him whose mass [of merit] has become white, as if it were its very end? || 32 ||
Victorious is the seven-rayed one (Agni) of renowned majesty, upon whose sinless head he [Śiva] swiftly brought Kāma and Yama— who were excessively base— under control; and who,
by the power of his command, brought everything under subjection through destiny— from whom, then, could anyone not fall into a swoon?
Or he leads one to death, or he leads one who has correctly resorted to discipline (vinaya) toward right conduct (naya).
Upon whose head, on every side, his matted locks shine forth, tawny and spread wide; or who,
having appointed Fire as witness,
has repeatedly performed the world’s difficult-to-reverse dissolution himself, extending even to the destruction of the Vedas.
Each one was well-fashioned for counting, like lines of gold.
The pair of his curved and broad eyebrows, thick with hair and appearing as if slightly scorched, remain as the only remnants of the body’s bow that was plundered;
split in two, they were held by his eyes out of extreme joy born from total victory.
That which is raised equally upward [by both] brings no fear to one who is devoted, nor to one who is not. // 35 //
Her three eyes, which have the three abodes as their object and are the refuge of the essence of beauty,

produce from the right a day equal to the day [of Brahmā], and from the left a moonlit night; and between those two, even for one who dwells in darkness, she eternally produces the twilight that stands at the junction.
When one has fallen into such a vision, the shadow born of the nature of darkness does not fall at all.
That left eye which leads the lotus-face of the true devotee beyond the path of right and wrong,
and that other eye, the blue lotus, which possesses a most wondrous beauty of blossoming;
and that which, situated on the forehead, thoroughly kindles the threefold blazing fuel of radiant non-duality— [to Him, I bow].
At the proper time, even that which is contrary to one's nature may become peaceful through mutual assistance toward another.

When his eyes are directed upward, even his two eyebrows and his mass of matted hair shine so clearly that it seems as if each has been individually conquered and taken captive by his own radiant splendors;
for, out of compassion, he has established the threefold darkness in such a way that it remains divided into two parts.
Having burned half [of it], he made the other half ash-colored with intense rage, as if toward another wicked person.

p. 16) Those eyes whose pure and variegated splendors shine forth, which possess a natural capacity for the manifestation of all that is desirable, and which are intent upon the total destruction of the darkness of ignorance—
[they behold] the three [worlds], which partake of a structure fashioned through playful engagement, beyond...
Like the various specific lights that constitute the subtle bodies (liṅgadeha) of the worlds, they are distinct.

Whose eyes, white as gold and with pupils slightly contracted, reached to the vicinity of his ears; and having beheld them, which were filled with an abundant and expansive light worthy of being gazed upon,
[he felt] that the long-accumulated fruits of days and nights had not been fully realized.
The eye situated on his forehead blazes with extreme wrath; is he perhaps the Lord of Twilight diminished?
The vision seen by one of perfected intellect bestows the desired;

yet it is never possible to touch that vision by which the unseen destruction of destiny is ordained here. Another vision, whose object is not distinct from the visible and so forth, [is described] at length—
That which has been taught by those of inferior vision, who consider themselves superior, leads first to destruction.

(p. 17) He who was striving for the ultimate limit of what is to be heard and has been heard, whose ears had previously attained the sovereignty of hearing, and who then moved away with agitation from the ocean-like face of the Goddess; [he is the one who now speaks].
For the sake of drinking from the victorious mango tree, as if from a sacred vessel. || 42 ||

That which is not the nose, yet is not other than it, is clearly manifest as the altar joined by the two eyebrows for the performance of the sacrifice of the vital energies and so forth— an altar visible only through the singular vision of devotion to those of tranquil intellect;
and that which is the triad of abodes joined by the ear-vessels, renowned for removing the heat of suffering.
The wondrous, stainless [fire], which is the highest praise of the Most Full, consumes the oblation of the objects of knowledge. || 43 ||
Her nose, fashioned in the form of a shining triangle and joined with two nostrils,
illuminates the region of her cheeks smeared with ashes with its shimmering luster;
by that radiance, her presence is established as a reflection of the most stainless forms.
Like [the reflections] in the eyes of statues, it easily assumes the likeness of each individual face. 44.
Her nose, charming with its two eyes, and her creeper-like brow shine like a mechanical furnace; having incessantly filled its interior with air,
it kindles the fire of the eyes within the cauldron of the mass of matted hair, as if with a fever amidst the water.
When the touch of one born of worldly existence causes the destruction of a piece of cooked nectar, [then one knows the truth]. (45)
(18) Whose mind would not be captivated by that pure, perfectly round, and radiant orb— a tumor-like mass— shining with splendor and clearly moving through devotion; [an orb] which,
like the sun and the moon moving near the Meru mountain of the nose, [removes the darkness]?
They fall upon each other in front, like sunlight and moonlight upon the earth. || 46 ||
For whose sake Pārvatī—whose nose-breath is a source of wealth that is not devoid of fragrance—is praised by whom?
She who possesses a face like a lotus, eyes like blue water-lilies, a nose like a sesame flower, and cheeks with the luster of pomegranate blossoms; she who is the very essence of the Campaka tree.
Bimboṣṭhī, whose teeth were as beautiful as kunda flowers, practiced the vow along with Aparṇā. || 47 ||
Her lips, skilled in tasting the essence of both the refined and the unrefined nectars, shine with a radiant central line that clearly attains a fourfold state,
as if they were the abodes of the four fires whose intense thirst is focused upon the space above the eyes.
In order to cause the blossoming of the flower of splendor, he drew forth the sap from the root of the *saraṇī* plant. || 48 ||

Indeed, who possesses the speech capable of praising Your stainless speech, which is vast and subtle— a speech such that even the four-faced Brahmā, though he studies the four Vedas, can only master its supreme essence?
Even the Creator, with his two thousand voices, can only grasp the limited extent of the mere grammatical tradition (Śabdasmṛti).
The remainder, however, she spoke as the sixty-four tantras born from that [source], along with that independent [tantra].
Whose speech does not shine in the heart of anyone? If it were to shine,
then why would those whose consciousness is veiled by their own ignorance fail to find supreme delight in the words they have heard—
that which is capable of awakening the most wondrous self-knowledge of the wise?
But for her, in an instant, even from a mere taste, there arises the dawn of awakening for one who was previously devoid of it. || 50 ||
How could that very speech of his— which is renowned for the power of its sweet outpourings born of true grace— ever find ultimate and uninterrupted rest within me?
For even I, a mere child of Kashmir, have become intent on profound inquiry through the tasting of it.
By birth, I shall bring under my control those far-reaching songs of the Lords of Speech. || 51 ||
His speech does not instruct the art of governance— that which commands those who are to be commanded,
and which causes exile through the constant fear of the punishment of Indra,
Upendra, and Brahmā; for in that speech, from its own seat, there is the splendor of pure, blossoming, and praiseworthy consolation.
The counting of various scriptures, doctrines, and so forth leads here only to a reputation for laughter. 52.

And he brought those Vedas to clarity; yet the speech of the Threefold Means (the three Vedas) was not directly able to do so, becoming lusterless without the expansive limbs of that Anaṅgahara (Śiva).
Furthermore, even those four [Vedas], when directed toward that single object, attained that supreme and auspicious knowledge.
Yet, even after delivering many arguments, they fall back and return to seek a definitive conclusion. || 53 ||

The speech of Him, which is purified by His great grace, is that which the Three Vedas— having attained a fame that is beautiful and accessible to those who possess the power of movement— cannot fully serve with their three feet; and that speech which,
having acquired the eighteen branches of knowledge through its six limbs, has once again attained the state of being the eightfold [Veda].
Having attained a twofold nature, she, who knows the unity of reality, has become transformed through infinity.
Or rather, even the instruction regarding the supreme playful gestures of the Child (Kṛṣṇa) does not fully master her speech;
nor does etymological interpretation, though repeatedly determined and scrutinized, attain its true meaning. Furthermore, no ritual manual, however well-constructed, can even conceive of her speech.
Even the multitude of meters does not attain its own freedom, for it approaches only the light of lights.

Or rather, has not the scripture composed by her speech— which establishes the sole cause for the purity of words and brought them within the range of hearing— attained the status of a traditional art (kalā)?
For even those who have entered into mutual systems of thought (pratitantra) showed great reverence toward it from the very beginning.
That excellence which even the wise seek, characterized by the preeminence of the object of cognition whose nature is *sphoṭa*. (56)

Formerly, the person who was bound by the multitude of past actions and the manifest digits of desire, whose progress was destroyed by his uprooted wisdom, and who was intent on constructing a system of inquiry—
having now attained the pure speech of him [the Lord], he has become one who knows Brahman, with his existence transcended.
Having brought that liberation to its conclusion, he attained fulfillment through manifestation.

They possess the light of the sun that illuminates objects worthy of valid cognition; they dispel the blinding darkness of doubt; they accomplish the welfare of virtuous people; they are masters of both illustrative examples and established tenets;
and with their limbs [of logic], they employ the flourishing methods of debate and discussion to determine conclusions through speech.
His arguments, which do not fall into the trap of cavil and the like, shine forth clearly. || 58 ||

The Buddhists composed eighty-four systems of thought in order to examine the intellect; the Sāṃkhya schools, numbering four times [that], have likewise met their end through the enumeration of principles (tattva). And the Vaiśeṣikas adopted the formulation of particulars in order to comprehend objects.
Or rather, just as hosts of tridaṇḍins have become [obstacles] to the attainment of speech, so too have the Śāmbaras. || 59 ||

Some are intent upon the vital breath (prāṇa), others upon the planes of consciousness (citta-bhūmi), some upon the intellect (buddhi), some upon the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), some upon the group of sense organs (indriya-gaṇa),
some upon the collection of their objects, some upon the body, and others are engaged in ignorance regarding children, wife, wealth, and honor.
Or rather, those who are not defiled do not remain submerged [in worldly existence] in order to attain the stainless ultimate reality of her speech. || 60 ||

(21) Has the science of Āyurveda, renowned for its arts, not attained the status of a Veda? Or has the path of the [other] Śāstras, possessing its own distinct form, not attained the status of a Śāstra? For the science of music (Gāndharva), which is a treasury of aesthetic flavors (rasas), restrains even the hunter from afar.
The composition of whose purpose does not proceed for its own sake, but belongs to the Lord who is the seed of the Vedas and other scriptures.

Even that multitude of Itihāsas, having reflected upon the speech of Mṛtyuñjaya which concerns eternal objects, became a source of dispute, saying "it is thus" and "it is not thus," because they did not know his ancient, self-evident purpose— which is free from conceptual constructions, devoid of contradictions, and mutually consistent.
Having directly veiled the object, it binds it by means of its prior aspect, not by that which resides within.

Having attained the supreme state of literary art (*sāhitya*), which arises from manifold existences, is clarified by its own power, whose first manifestation is the creation of *śakti* and other faculties,
in which the subtle parts are perceived within, which is richly endowed with clear designations, and which rests upon the essence of intended meaning—
[this art] exists through speech for the sake of those who dwell in the world of light, abounding in excellent aesthetic flavors (*rasa*).
Literature does not shine when its qualities are consumed by over-satiety.
The teeth emerging from his face, adorned with rows, attained renown as the thirty-two marks;
they seemed to have first risen to conquer the moon, and then, being entreated by that moon, [to defeat him].
Do they shine, covered by a pair of cloths with hearts agitated by compassion? 64.

Having beheld the five classes of pretas with faces like lotuses, each incapable of performing their own specific task, and seeing them placed upon their respective seats by another whose movement was constrained by Śakti— was it not so that [the Lord], in order to perform all those various tasks simultaneously, brought them there by his own power?
The face, possessing five marks, shines with its true power manifesting before every face. || 65 ||

The Goddess, who consists of the five traditions (*pañcāmnāya*), is the object of meditation for the Great Non-dual Path (*mahādvayanaya*); she shines here as the refuge arising from the five mouths of that Lord, which must not be given to the unworthy.
Just as a river, having gone to reach the Lord of Waters (*apāmpati*), does not abandon him, so too [she does not abandon] him by whom she was attained. (p. 22)
They have abandoned the fear of coming and going inherent in the five states of existence, and are freed from the conceit of the five [aggregates].
How can his chin, which is divided by a central dot, conquered by the countless merits of Girijā, and expressive of non-duality through its grace, be described in words?
By the power of the child-like [Bhairava], it follows the form of Bhairava-Śiva, transcending duality—
One [should be] placed below, with its cloth reaching the neck, if it is radiant with applied ashes. (67)

May he, in whose throat the poison shines white— capable of instantly dispelling distress— bring even Dhātṛ and the other gods to delusion by the mere touch of a trace of its power, while that poison remains in the mouth of Kālārdana, who has shared his domain with the white venomous serpent.
Like the Yamunā desiring union with the Gaṅgā, she flows upward at the primordial site.

What was the use of those arms of his— once raised in vain like the coils of a serpent, long as a yoke, radiant as lotus stalks, and thick with strength— by him who performs actions merely by his will?
They were now joined and now separated for the sake of the various *aṅgahāra* movements of the *tāṇḍava* dance.
Some here and there, eager for the touch of mountain-born creepers, have become meaningful [in their lives]. || 69 ||
He constantly holds in his hands the group of eighteen weapons, which correspond to the eighteen branches of knowledge that have emerged from the formidable oceans of his own mouths,
just as the seven continents rest separately within the oceans.
The ocean of compassion manifested a pure display of skillful means for the sake of protection. || 70 ||
The lotus-pools, seized by the hand of the water, have their stalks suddenly deprived of color; these petals, having ceased their movement, now remain still.
Yet the blossoms, opening wide, quickly regain their bloom as if overcome with shame.
They were always won over and subdued by the splendor of her true delicacy.

Who would not be struck with wonder upon seeing the branches rising from the sprout-like hands of him who stands in the Vaiśākha posture, half of whose body is embraced by Aparṇā? For those [branches], having attained the state of being a string of serpent-rows, have taken refuge in his feet. p. 23) Who, indeed, would not be amazed upon seeing the branches emerging from the sprout-like hands of him who stands in the Vaiśākha posture, half of whose body is embraced by Aparṇā? For those [branches], having attained the state of being a string of serpent-rows, have taken refuge in his feet. p. 23) Who, indeed, would not be amazed upon seeing the branches emerging from the sprout-like hands of him who stands in the Vaiśākha posture, half of whose body is embraced by Aparṇā? For those [branches], having attained the state of being a string of serpent-rows, have taken refuge in his feet. p. 23) Who, indeed, would not be amazed upon seeing the branches emerging from the sprout-like hands of him who stands in the Vaiśākha posture, half of whose body is embraced by Aparṇā? For those [branches], having attained the state of being a string of serpent-rows, have taken refuge in his feet. p. 23) Who, indeed, would not be amazed upon seeing the branches emerging from the sprout-like hands of him who stands in the Vaiśākha posture, half of whose body is embraced by Aparṇā? For those [branches], having attained the state of being a string of serpent-rows, have taken refuge in his feet. p. 23) Who, indeed, would not be amazed upon seeing the branches emerging from the sprout-like hands of him who stands in the Vaiśākha posture, half of whose body is embraced by Aparṇā? The moon constantly undergoes the state of the demons [eclipsed], while the shadow of the light of his nails [remains].
His chest, radiant with splendor like the orb of the autumnal moon, slightly elevated at its slopes, densely covered with the trees of his body hair,
and serving as a new plateau for Pārvatī to roam upon— [is the abode of Śiva].
Having lost her way, she stood there, intent on reaching the state of the mountain Kailāsa.
That line of folds within her womb shines forth, mutually unattached,
gracefully emerging from the mountain of her uplifted body like a surging torrent; it faces the ocean of her navel,
radiant with the play of waves as the high ridges of her hair, dusted with ashes, seem to fall away.
Bestowing her beneficial practice, she was like the celestial river, the triple-pathed Gaṅgā, who bestows benefit upon all beings.

His knees, which are perfectly round, very broad, and radiant with the splendor of his own merit, shine as they bend slightly at the front, appearing like the moon and the sun resting continuously within the range of his eyes, while the multitude of various jewels set in the crowns of the lords of the thirty gods [bow down before him].
They stood in the center, prepared to spring forward like two feet that have been rubbed together.
With his body exceedingly pure from head to toe, he fell with devotion at his feet; and though he found no satisfaction in the two eyes on the left side,
he attained a resemblance to the moon’s nails— which are large, beautiful, and full— by falling there.
Is it to conquer the Lord of Day who stands twelvefold, or rather to proclaim the manifestation of its own twelvefold nature? || 76 ||
Having reflected with his two feet upon the lotus that is ever blooming yet remains in a state of dullness, obscured by the offense of great and unbearable sins that have not been cleansed,
the Supreme Creator fashioned it from mud and caused it to flourish with splendor.
Having duly established the worshipful status of both Padmeśa and Padmajā, those two— || 77 ||
That pair of stainless lotus-feet, eternally blossoming, has risen from the river of my head; it is neither touched by water, whether externally or internally,
nor is its downward-facing form— encircled by the delicate thorns of my shanks— shaped like a leaf.
Beholding the weeping branch, who would not be struck with wonder at its white-and-red hue? || 78 ||
Has the moon, having reached the sky, not descended even a fraction [of its light] due to its softness?
Or is it that the lotus, seeing the sky rising red with the weight of water, does not wish to ascend?
Or is it that the sun, though moving along the pathless track of the sky, does not advance because it is unsupported?
Has he, the sovereign lord of all, perhaps rested his feet out of pride? (79)
Those two feet, which are supreme lotuses, were worshipped by the Lotus-born (Brahmā) and placed even upon the lotus-seat of his head by the Lord of Lotuses (Viṣṇu), bestowing their protection;
those feet, resembling the rising sun, no longer lead me toward things that are untouchable, night after night.
The lotuses of the eyes and faces of those emaciated by hope have fully blossomed.

Having placed his feet upon his heart according to the prescribed rite, he— whose intellect is rendered barren by the injunctions of the three Vedas through a mind seeking the grace of both injunction and prohibition— worships the two treasures of perfected knowledge, who have bound themselves by the rule of the Lord’s command, which is characterized by the supreme manifestation of the transcendence of all limiting conditions.
Having leaped over the world with his own steps, he dwells in each step upon the unwavering, true abundance.
For whom even the lotus-navelled Lord Viṣṇu, seated upon his lotus-throne,
rises before his two lotus-feet— subdued by intense prostration and dripping with drops of nectar—
and having tasted the abundance of their honey, once experienced the singular bliss of the Goddess of Fortune.
Then he placed that lotus at his navel, upon his original seat born from it.

Meditating upon his feet within his heart, he repeatedly contemplates the foul odor of his own imagined conceptual constructions; yet, with his heart utterly consumed by fire, he perceives no foul wealth within his own breast.
He places his own feet upon his head—even upon the heads of those who possess the crowns of flowers.
Either he walks while touching with his wicked feet the spots on the forehead, or let him not be touched at all upon the forehead. || 83 ||
[The dance] which is intensified by the violent clashing and joining of the firm fragments of the cosmic egg;
which scatters masses of clouds with fierce and formidable pride as they are torn apart by his staff-like arms;
and which possesses the sudden, gleaming plundering of the circle of the Creator’s and Indra’s heads—
It is to be feared that his dance, which mimics the stroke of a fragmenting axe, adorns the [very] universe. || 84 ||
The sky was clearly struck by the backs of tortoises shattered by the massive trunks of world-elephants whose directions were bent down as they reared up in frantic terror;
and the excellent orb of the sun was eclipsed by the moon-palaces tossed aloft by the whirling atmosphere.
The grand display of the dance of the Fire-god, which caused sparks of charcoal to fall [from his mouth], [was witnessed]. (85)

In the state of meditative absorption, he was contemplated by great sages who were motionless with joy and whose delusions had dissolved, as they were enraptured by melodies shimmering with the charming sounds of lutes, flutes, drums, and rhythmic beats;
and by Gandharvas and Kinnaras, vocalizing with the vibrant play of waves of various musical modes.
That whirling dance, which is set ablaze by song and is skillful in its movements; || 86 ||
It was filled with the clamor arising from drums, kettledrums, ḍiṇḍimas, kāhalīs, and ḍamarus, accompanied by celestial nymphs renowned for their graceful movements and gestures;
it was agitated by the sounds of musical instruments played by the lords of sages and others who delight in strife, all of which intensified the sense of worldly craving.
That dance which appears, its movements expressed through the rhythms of various musical instruments; || 87 ||
Surrounded by his fierce, club-like arms, he brought suffering upon the lord of the stars (the moon), caused the orb of the sun to lose its constancy,
and— being praised by the hosts of gods— shattered the firm pride of the enemy while striking down the stars.
For whom there was no intense play, hunting, drama, or the dancing of the Lord of Actors. || 88 ||
With its towering mass, it conceals the clouds entirely; it makes the netherworld tremble, agitates the *pīlu* trees in confusion, and effortlessly shatters the Golden Mountain (*Hemādri*).
It brings about the dissolution of the Blue Mountain (*Nīlādri*) and the Himalaya, and sets the entire world in motion.
And the earth, by whose power it was brought to exchange its state, shines forth. || 89 ||

He who, by the power of his own absolute freedom (*svasvātantrya*) which necessarily brings about the experience of the Supreme (*parānubhūti*), has established his seat in the renowned position known as Sāhib Kaula—
having expounded [the teachings] in the work titled *Devīnāmavilāsa* through the arising of their respective powers; [to him, salutations].
In that poem, which is innate to the principles for attaining Śiva’s perfection, devotion is the primary tradition.
Thus ends the first devotion in the *Nāmavilāsa*, composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Sāhib Kaulānandanātha. || 1 ||
The second [chapter] on devotion:
Once, Nandi, the lord of the Gaṇas, his soul resting in humility,
stood firm at the opened door while the praiseworthy, secret, known, and beneficial [teachings] were being revealed.
By the mere sign of a sidelong glance sent by his own master, he had all other activities suppressed;
he was satisfied with the status of doorkeeper—a position obtained with great difficulty and held in high esteem by distinguished and refined men, and one that remained unimpaired. || 2 ||
Rising during the auspicious hour known as Brāhma-muhūrta, Brahmā and the other foremost of yogis,
having destroyed all defects of karma through meditation upon Him, constantly behold that Lord face-to-face.
He appointed some to prepare suitable tooth-sticks, others to fetch clay and other materials for purification,
others to the groups for bathing, and still others to the changing of garments and such.
(28) That which arises from meditation is a threefold purity; for those whose hearts are pierced by the [divine] name and who possess devotion to their own Lord, it is never to be divided.
Thus, making contact with his hand, he bathes that Supreme Lord.
Upon that priceless seat, which is shimmering with the luster of jewels and where all these [deities] reside in their own forms, he sits,
causing the host of spirits and other beings to tremble for the sake of their pacification.

Even as he observed the distinctions of various forms of worship, he brought forth the necessary materials for the objects of worship for that person who was inflamed by all forms of worship so that they might eventually find dissolution in the one true worship.

Having prepared pure food with various kinds of nectars, those lords of the Gaṇas, who were experts in that knowledge and nourished by ambrosia, satisfied the Knower of the Essence and the Smile— the one who is to be known by the foremost among enjoyers— according to their desire.
Accompanied by the performance of funeral rites for his kin, he was the supreme performer of sacred duties;
with his head bowed low in humility, he was an obedient disciple to those instructed by the learned, possessed of noble character, and even surpassed the lords of the learned in his discernment.
"Aha! Even many lords of the immortals, having attained their desires, strive with effort for its attainment;
yet he, being exceedingly skillful, circumambulated it while himself offering it as a gift. (10)
Then, having lifted him up with comfortable seats held upon their heads by the lords of the vehicles,
they placed him again upon excellent couches with swift and excessive speed, out of a spirit of competitive devotion.

p. 29) And adorning him with those stainless unguents, garlands, garments, and excellent ornaments produced by his own power—things never before obtained even by the three lords, such as Brahmā and the others, who possess divine attributes and the like; || 12 ||
Having scattered those most excellent flowers— red, white, black, and so forth— arranged in artistic patterns,
which had fallen of their own accord, he approached the gateway with the Lords, filled with joy.
Having appropriately assigned the heroes, the hosts, and the others each to their respective places within that most desirable [enclosure] of the enemies,
he— tranquil, honoring the pride of his own [people] with his head bowed, and standing or sitting near the leaders— remained there.
To those who, dissatisfied with mere meditation, had come to behold that Lord Śiva of auspicious form with some degree of devotion—
those great lords among men— he rose and respectfully announced them to Kāla.

Having gathered those tributes through their own devotion and immediately placing them in his hands, he— knowing himself to be one who carries out the commands of others and bearing the name "Boundless"— returned them to the Lord after learning His command.
He offered with devotion heart-warming verses composed for the Four-faced One, the foremost of the gods.
Taking the gift from Śiva as it approached, he presented it [to him] and, with a glance, gestured for him to be seated. || 17 ||
"Your command has been carried out; the wretched ones and the foremost of the Daityas have been slain, and the heavy burden has been cast off.
Tell me what unprecedented task for the earth must be performed"—thus he spoke, proclaiming the words of Viṣṇu which are most worthy of honor.

(30) He established that master of ritual in his own position— he who, for the sake of [Śiva’s] satisfaction, personally brought forth the fruits and fresh flowers shining from the Kalpa-tree by means of his speech, while [the deity] was the Lord of the Gods; and he [Śiva],
who daily consumes the excellent oblations incessantly offered by the best of sacrificers into the fire.
By means of the instruction of the Lord of all bases, he, endowed with reason, distributed [the teachings] among the immortals. || 20 ||
He consoled Dharmeśvara, who had once been devoid of vigor, as he approached apprehensively for the purpose of worship,
announcing that his own duty was accomplished and requesting his reassurance.

I stood there, observing the proper conduct, to worship that Lord of the gods of gods— who is the protector of the flesh-eaters, who maintains enmity toward the gods, and whose body is supernatural— while holding a vessel of non-empty offerings in my hand.

Having extracted priceless jewels from stainless mines and fashioned them with devotion on the spot, they informed him of the arrival of Varuṇa— the singular essence of all aesthetic flavors— and honored him.
From his own herd, he repeatedly brought various fragrances; the one who knew the true nature of service gently instructed the spotted horse from nearby to fan the Lord.
Through devotion, he was favored with the name "Mitra" (Friend) by the Lord of Treasures,
who appointed him to the expenditure of wealth for various undertakings, while he himself remained tirelessly attending upon the Lord at the latter's glance.
He respectfully established the Rudras— who, like oceans, were filled with the supreme virtues of various jewels of exceeding power,
whose distinct bodies were pervaded by the splendor of Śambhu— without any sense of division.
Having appointed someone to guard the gateway of Śiva’s temple, he was walking toward Śiva for a vision;
striking his golden cane like the stalk of a plantain tree, he touched the face of the elephant-headed god. (27)
Having quickly caused his own kinsmen, the flowers of the celestial river, to bloom of their own accord,
he stands taking them up— the moon of cool rays— thereby demonstrating that even his rising is for the sake of compassion.
He was a treasury of arts, an incarnation of the beauty of the moon's forehead, scattering ambrosia and blue lotuses,
and incessantly commanding the spreading moonlight to turn both blue and non-blue.
Day after day, having left the lords of the Gaṇas and the foremost Bhṛṅgis in their respective offices, he—
the sole leader of the Gaṇas— himself attended to his own duty and performed it for the sake of the supreme task.
Warding off with his staff the tips of the fierce jewels on Indra’s crown as they were bursting forth,
he stood before Śambhu— who was heading toward the inner apartments— as an exceedingly pure-minded and foremost attendant.
There, bowing to his own son— who had brought an end to the life of Tāraka, who had delivered him from all afflictions,
who was a savior in the true sense, and who had been installed by his father in the title of crown prince— he approached him.
The wives of the gods and demons, together with their groups of mothers, having gathered and beheld him,
abandoned their status as mistresses of life and, perceiving him to be sporting [with another], came outside.
Having thoroughly trained in the practices concerning that Guide through all types of ritual service,
one who abides by his instructions should rely upon that gateway and meditate upon that Lord according to the method of immersion.
Hearing that the root of bliss, that ocean of compassion,
had set out to go outside for the sake of sporting with the Single-Tusked One (Gajendra), he immediately fashioned excellent vehicles, providing them with the necessary means of conveyance.

Then [he saw] that lord of bulls, the strength of the strong, who mocked the splendor of emerald and ruby mountains with his own radiance; who, by his speed, made even the mind appear variegated, and whose gait was marked by the brilliance of diverse pearls.
With his remaining distinctive features, he utterly outshone the mounts of all the lords of the world;
he possessed a hump lower than the peak of Mount Sumeru, and a hump as broad as the trunk of a celestial tree.
He did not stumble even upon the oceans, where the clouds were dispersed by the tossing of his tail;
he practiced his movement upon crystal rocks, both ascending and descending.
He was bringing other sounds to utter dissolution with resonant noises containing the syllable *huṃ*;
and with ornaments such as small bells, polished with jewels, he was scattering forth rays of light.

Its center was pressed down by the front of the golden lion-throne of the hump, which was adorned with a beautiful canopy; it was further beautified by the radiance of jewels, by hooded serpents, and by the highly fragrant unguents upon its peaks. || 40 ||

Holding her hand, as he was being supported by another, he caused his husband— who had cast off his wrap from the edge of his seat and was moving toward the left side near the place of ascent— to mount the vehicle.

By the force of the wind, the *Naijayantī* banner—whose jeweled ornaments were set in motion by the edges of her golden garments—was carried along; while various precious steeds, their reins held by the hand of the Lord of the Gaṇas, preceded her. (42)
By the sounds of pellets discharged by yakṣas skilled in the art of deployment and withdrawal,
she was suddenly seized with the fear of a thunderclap, while the loud laughter of the spirits imitated the cries of the people.
"Quickly receive me, let me enter!"—thus spoke the group of attendants whose faces were radiant with speech;
they incessantly whitened the quarters of the sky with dust raised from the crystal slabs as they rose up in distress.
With large cymbals, small drums, conchs with faces shimmering with jewels and cow-faced horns,
and with multitudes of kettledrums, ānakas, and kāhalīs, she seemed to cause both heaven and earth to resound in harmony.
Placing that great army, skilled in the movements of appropriate conduct, before him, he led that Lord—
who had blocked the rays of light from the side of the throne— to his desired destination.
Having caused the Lord to dwell upon the grounds of Caitraratha and other such places with various diversions and special forms of hunting,
and having turned him back by his own command, he dismissed the host of gods to their homes.
When they had departed after having offered their salutations, he led his lord into his own beautiful palace;
and when the twilight worship was completed, he performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for him with multitudes of lamps on all sides.

Having attended upon him while he was reclining within by massaging his hands and so forth—thereby causing him to awaken from his sleep—and having understood his command, [the king] took the bliss of deep sleep and lay down to rest in his own quarters. (49)
He was being honored by Kimpuruṣas, hosts of Apsarases, and kings of the Gandharvas;
awakening him—who, though awakened, was as if unawakened—by means of the triple symphony (tauryatrika) while massaging his feet.
Day after day, thus serving with unbroken devotion Him who is served by those to be served, he—desiring to question the gracious Lord who had ceased from meditation—began to offer praise. (51)
(Verse 51–52, forming a *kulaka* with fifty-one verses) O Śiva, Lord, Śambhu, supreme light and awareness, essence of unwavering joy!
You whose form is to be defined by the manifestation of the single nature of vibration (*spanda*), you who are the very embodiment of every form. 52.
O Sovereign Lord of the Supreme Goddesses, sole Master of the dancer who performs the playful dance of Her blossoming manifestation;
O Supreme Tantra of the Tantra of Absolute Freedom, witness to Your own mantra which is the essence of all mantras, and eye of those dependent on other tantras! 53.
O Lord of the Eye, you who are to be consecrated by the lords of mantras, the supreme lords of mantras, and the masters of mantras, beginning with the Earth-mantra;
you who always know the mantra-less within the interval of mantras, being yourself in yourself, experienced as your own uncreated nature.

You who possess no mother nor objects of knowledge and the like, you who are the creator of the validity of all means of cognition; you who are immeasurable, yet whose power and majesty are honored through the illusion of reality established by the measuring instruments of others' perceptions. 55.
O Knower of the arts of measuring direction, place, and time; O You whose time cannot be measured by those various arts;
O You who are the single rhythmic foundation of the vastness of all things; O You whose inner strength shines forth as the object of contemplation for those who know that reality. 56.
(35) Here, the state of being, which is intent upon the experience of other entities, has sprouted from the seed of the notion of "I-ness.
Beholding this, one sees it as a masterpiece of diverse and variegated forms at that very moment, perfected by its own inherent realization. (57)
O Destroyer of Ignorance, who art ever-arisen from the beginningless sound and joined with the supreme, incomparable touch and differentiation;
O You whose closing and opening of the eyes is the manifestation of the light within the midst of those colors that correspond to this very painting! 58.
Having made egoity subordinate and being intent on the contemplation of the state where the other is primary, its nature is devoted to that;
it is clearly divided, possessing the forms known as the open-eyed, the half-closed, and the fully closed, with only its form remaining. (59)
O God, whose form is the aggregate of all that is perceivable, who have shattered the cosmic egg with the tip of Your crest;
O Lord of Consciousness, resting in the light beyond the fourth state, the stainless end that removes all false delusions! 60.

O Ānandanātha, you who are the root of supreme bliss, whose rising is dense with perfect stillness; O Lord of Will, whose desire is for the primordial state beyond all parts, move very slowly within your own exceedingly pure course, O you whose form is the play of the *nāḍī* and *kala*.

O Knower who has abandoned both ignorance and [limited] discernment; O Lord of Knowledge, perfected in the meditative absorption of self-knowledge and discernment; O Lord of Action, devoid of the suffering caused by talk of agency and the like; O Lord of Action, for whom only the excellence of actionlessness remains.

O Lord of Memory, may the authority of my own recollection—kindled by the complete eradication of the primary objects of memory and the destruction of the fragmentation of the vision of the dense [reality] through the removal of the distinctions of the self’s egoistic pride—be established here. 63.

O Lord who is devoid of the state of being an agent that produces pure awakening above Māyā, yet is the master of the supreme void; O sole cause for the uprooting of the play of sovereignty manifested here through the exquisite sport of the supreme atom and Māyā! 64.
O inner controller of the radiance that adorns the totality; O most skillful one whose nature is the subtle thread;
O King of Vairāja, sovereign lord of the kingdom that purifies the assembly of the three states you have produced! 65.
O Maker of the world, O Life of Māra, O Life of the sole living being, O You of incomparable power!
O Friend, O Lord, O Treasure of the art of playful concealment, O Abode of the Cintāmaṇi jewel! 66.
O ocean of the nectar of indeterminate bliss, you who have attained true prosperity and are free from all desires;
O wise one, worthy of contemplation through the pervasion of your own ego-consciousness, you are the sovereign ruler from this world until the final dissolution.
(36) Within [him], agitated by the surging waves of diverse, variegated, and manifold states, brilliantly illuminated by his own radiance;

he is the singular, non-dual one, whose nature is the manifestation of the various forms of time and the divisions of the quarters of the world, yet who transcends time and the very form of the quarters of the world. 68.

O you who are the self-luminous soul, the sole scribe at the time of recording, who provides witness for the forms and the burden of the equipment suitable for union with that which is devoid of a substratum; O you whose nature is light, who are the very inscription upon the surface of your own manifestation! 69.
O You whose majesty manifests as the existence and non-existence of all common states;
O Universal Form who, through Your unimpeded sovereignty and awakening, have assumed the nature of all lords! 70.

O you who are the sole object of enjoyment that brings about the communion of consciousness between the enjoyer and the enjoyed; O sole root of the nectar of supramundane bliss; O great secret of the bliss born of bliss! 71.

The teacher who instructs upon the gross kalās presided over by Virāj; the knower who awakens to the subtlety of the supreme atom; he whose pervasive nature is attained through the expansion of the space-abiding [consciousness], and who has transcended the state of being a mere pervader once that pervasion is exhausted. (72)
O Lord of all, O All-in-All, I am but a foot-soldier entered by You;
yet the dust arising from Your lotus feet, possessing the power to create and destroy, is supremely victorious.
(An *kulaka* of twenty-two verses: He who, by the power of his own sovereign majesty, which was destined to arise, established his seat upon the renowned position known as Sāhibkaula;

Because of that [work], devotion toward the *Bhāṣya*—whose body is continuously extended across the *Gāyatrī-manu*—becomes fulfilled in two ways within the poem composed by him titled *Nāmavilāsa*. 74.
Thus ends the second devotion in the *Nāmavilāsa*, composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrīmat Sāhib Kaulānandanātha. || 2 ||
The third type of devotion:
"Obeisance, obeisance be unto You; obeisance, obeisance unto You again and again, obeisance, obeisance unto You!
This greatness of Yours is not within the range of the heart or of speech; though it is expressible, it is to be realized through the indicated meaning. (1)

In the Great Non-duality, the king of kings of vision, you are renowned for your matchless power as a perfected Siddha; consciousness, independent, the source of all accomplishments, though full, you are empty—victory to you, O self-luminous one! (2)
When this expansion is accepted, this entire universe expands within it, or rather, it is nothing else;
for just as when the particularity of the principle of nimesha (the closing) unfolds within you, everything else dissolves back into you.
No other distinct entity here possesses the power [to manifest], nor does it possess even its own self-manifestation.
It is only when there is non-difference that something becomes an object; thus, your own self-awareness is devoid of all distinctions.
Time and the other categories shine forth by Your power, yet they are indeed unable to measure You at any time;
for in this state which is the singular ground of direct experience, neither valid cognition nor its absence is applicable.
Your majesty is eternally risen, for it is equal to the state of being intoxicated [with bliss]; thus, you have abandoned both equality and inequality.
Illuminating this very body with your own form, you shine forth yourself as the manifestation of causality and the rest.
If the unprecedented appears through a means of valid cognition, it possesses neither existence nor non-existence.
If something else appears distinct from this [cognition], that is established by itself; what need is there here for connection with anything else? (7)
Who knows You, the supreme, all-pervading Lord, the sole consciousness of the universe? And who, even if skilled in ritual injunctions, could make You known?
For no one can attain the state of knowing Him, the Knower of all, through the application of their own words and arguments.

Since even you, the Lord who has achieved the perfect accomplishment of withdrawing all things into yourself, have attained a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), has not even this [Lord] gone beyond? What, then, could be more contrary [to worldly expectation]? One who partakes of both enjoyment and liberation would indeed possess true discernment.

Through the sequence of offering the measurement of the mental body—consisting of blue [objects], pleasure, and so forth—into the Supreme, there occurs an immersion (*āveśa*) into That; this is the supreme means for the realization of You within the Mother by means of true bliss.
O Lord of Lords, by Your own will alone, You—though undivided from this mirror-city of Samā—are divided;
as the Supreme Sovereign, You manifest Yourself as a multitude of ever-new bodies and powers within Your own wall.
And here, having assumed the role of the giver, you shine forth as one whose sole essence is playful charm, bestowing this gift in various ways that are mutually appropriate and kindled by propriety.

O Lord, when that very [reality], which is beyond the supreme form and characterized by the manifestation of neither "this-ness" nor "I-ness," is contemplated within the state of perpetual Śiva-nature through meditative absorption, you, O Knower, perceive it as the object to be realized.
Since the state of Īśāna has been accepted by you, this "otherness" remains indistinct in you;
likewise, even through ignorance, you are the mother of all within this [universe], though divided by the internal distinctions of branches and lineages.

O Hara, you behold this state of the *jñānākala*, which is utterly void due to its agency, whose essence is pure awakening and non-duality with You, and which—though possessing a boundless limit—is distinguished by the prior condition of those yet to be. 15.

O Lord of the Kala, even in You who are the absolute dissolution (*layakevala*), this world—though nearly dissolved within You who consist of the void-nature of the subject—is still limited and divided on all sides; yet in You, the bed of totality (*sākalyatalpa*), it is entirely whole.

For one who has taken refuge in You, whose singular body is self-luminous and pure, even the states of being and non-being—experienced through Your own power—shine forth perpetually as the very space of Your light. (17)

Furthermore, O Supreme One, that universe which transcends all things and yet consists of all things, is Your very own nature—You who are the single, solid mass of all light and awareness consisting of unsurpassed bliss. 18.

The conflict regarding what is to be taken and what is not to be taken does not exist in reality; rather, it is through various specific manifestations initiated by those respective factors that You, the Supreme Śiva, shine forth as non-dual, O Lord of Play.
(39) Previously, in the manifestation of the universe established as one with its own self, it appeared through forms appropriate to the subject and so forth;
yet, by virtue of being the nature of the void beyond the void, it shone due to the non-differentiation from light and the non-manifestation of the unity of consciousness. (20)

Just as you expand through the principles (tattvas), bodies, worlds, and senses— which have consciousness as their sole life-force, being solidified from the essence of awareness— and through various natural emanations, or even as you appear contracted, so do you manifest as the body that bestows existence upon all beings.
Thus, although its nature as consciousness possesses contraction and it is the singular form of the universe, it is not the universe itself;
like the seed of a tree, it is the appropriator, yet it is conceived [as manifold] while having non-difference from You as its essence. (22)
You alone are this Lord, the Sovereign of the Universe; yet, through your own self-contraction, you appear as another.
Even this contraction, when investigated, is not in the slightest degree distinct from you.
For this expansion of awakening is indeed liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), whereas the notion of being other than You is bondage.
In reality, these two do not exist for You who are eternally liberated; thus, even regarding bondage, Your intellect remains untainted by the fruit [of action]. (24)

When consciousness, concealing its own essential nature by its own will, manifests contraction, it then appears as the dual state of its own designating subject through the manifestation of qualities and non-qualities. (25)
In the view that [the levels] are predominant, there may occasionally be a touch of terms such as "knowledgeless" (*jñānākala*) and so forth within one's own consciousness;
yet, through a gradual and successive entry into higher states, the state of being "unsupported by oneself" (*svānāśritatva*) becomes manifest.
Even when this [limited] contraction is made the primary object by the intellect through grace,
as long as consciousness continues to manifest, even then the state of being a limited subject (śūnyapramātṛtva) is established.

Thus, consciousness (citi), having its nature contracted, turning toward the object of thought (cetyonmukhī), and descending into the state of being a cognizer (cetanatāvarūḍhā), is called by the name "mind" (citta); it is said to be wretched due to the contraction of duality, and characterized by the taking [of objects] and so forth. || 28 ||
Even in those various instances, for one who is constantly striving to pursue your true nature,
the luminosity of your own self remains forever undiminished— just as a king, though intensely occupied with affairs, never loses his sovereignty over his own kingdom.
Therefore, the body and so forth are the mind; the primary principle is that [mind], and even the ground of emptiness is ignited by its refinement.
Otherwise, there could be no unification here; for the subject of māyā is indeed composed of that.
(40) Thus it has been determined: Śiva alone is directly that conscious subject who possesses the conceit of being the grasper;
for there is no possibility of another [subject] existing through causes of differentiation, since such differentiation would be logically untenable. (31)
That single [consciousness], possessing the notion of the contraction of the vital breaths and so forth, grasps the diversity of contracted objects;
yet, by virtue of its own inherent luminosity, it is again considered to be twofold through the contraction of its objects. (32)

Just as a king, sunk in muddy ground, might sleep and— though his own state is untouched by impurity even in a dream— connects impurities to himself, so too this [jīva] remains in the three states (waking, dreaming, and deep sleep) without knowing its own sovereignty.
He, whose nature consists of the void-body of the vital breath and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), is celebrated as fourfold;
yet, due to his own state of ignorance, he is also fivefold through the powers beginning with consciousness (cit), which have attained the status of limited knowledge (vidyā) and the rest.
Facing the six paths and being sixfold through the awakening of the subject, this [reality] indeed becomes sevenfold;
it attains an eightfold expansion due to its lordship over the cities, and reaches a state of ninefoldness by means of the three qualities as methods.
In the state of lordship over the gods, he attained a tenfold nature; yet, by virtue of his respective inherent natures, he also possesses a middle number.
Divided into sevenfold categories through the fivefold elements (pañcīkṛta), he is you, O Mother, who are measured by that same number.
Having accepted the status of being worshipped by the gods and other such roles, you, who are eternally liberated, play upon these stages;
while this other person, some kind of magician, merely makes the arena of debate appear magnificent in many ways. (37)

Having observed Your vast power of splendor, which transcends the world and has as its sole fruit exquisite grace, some Lokāyatas—who take delight in that very nature—proclaim You to be the Beloved. (38)

Then some among them behold You—the purifier of their lineage, moving with playful grace—as their beloved Lord and son, with longing eyes; [others see] wealth as something to be spent for their own sake, or even as a commodity to be bought. 39.
When the elements are separate, [the Self] is unattainable; when they are combined, it is attained through the path of the gods.
Having realized that the nature of consciousness is equal to bliss, as [sugar is in] molasses and so forth, the followers of other schools honor You, the beloved of the Guru.

Some recognize you as being even more dear than the senses—which, though clear, are like those who are deaf or mute because they perceive suffering and lack the causal capacity for knowledge and action—and as one worthy of worship by Indra and the other gods. (41)

Others also recognize the vital breath (*prāṇa*) here as the life-force of all living beings, because it presides over [the functions of] destruction or thirst, as well as the sensations of fainting and so forth upon [death], and because it governs karma and the rest. (42)

Therefore, O beloved one, others— through their power of conceptualization and volition directed solely toward You as the sole cause of all things, and through the splendor of the space of consciousness within their intuition— manifest You as the Lord of Consciousness.

The followers of the Sugata remember You as the Lord of Memory—one whose nature appears as both non-conceptual and conceptual, capable of functioning for the sake of knowledge, yet moment by moment flickering; thus they remember You as "non-memory. 44.

O Lord, when all phenomena have dissolved into a state that is experienced as devoid of the cognition of a supreme existence, the Mādhyamikas know You—the Void which is eternally full—as the self-cognizing one. 45.

The learned followers of Jina deserve you, the Arhat free from the eighteen defects, as the most worthy of attainment for the sake of liberation, once the ninefold categories of existence beginning with the soul have been analyzed and that which is to be abandoned has been set aside. (46)

The Āśāmbaras point to you as the Supreme Lord, who, though possessing a gross body and the splendor of a sovereign, maintains a state that is infinitely more subtle than both, and who is eternally honored for His true magnitude.

O Lord, the logicians conceptualize you as a void cause dependent upon atoms—distinguished by qualities such as knowledge in the state of worldly existence, yet characterized by their cessation in liberation. (48)

Those who know the seven categories declare you, the all-pervading one, to be the creator; for from you, the supreme authority, all things are obtained in their entirety and reach fulfillment, and according to the doctrine of Kaṇāda, this universal object of knowledge is derived from you.

The Bhaṭṭa school seeks You, who are unseekable, as the consciousness that cognizes the "I" yet remains itself ignorant because it is obscured by limiting adjuncts (upādhi)— You, the creator of a universe governed by a single principle within diverse classes of beings.
Because the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is utterly incapable of destruction, whether through internal or external dissolution,
the Prābhākaras cite the ignorant person as an example based on the cognition "I," which is a function of ignorance.

O wonder, the Pāśupatas know You as distinct from the individual soul (jīva), as its object of worship, as its life-giver, and as the cause of the relationship between cause and effect; they know You as the Lord of all beings (paśūnām patiḥ), who remains after the destruction of the bonds that fetter those beings. 52.

Having revealed you, Śrī Vāsudeva, the supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*), as the radiant spark of the individual soul (*jīva*), some who are devoted to the Pañcarātra proclaim you to be distinct from this [world] consisting of its own effects and so forth. (53)
You are independent of the ripening of afflictions and karmic impressions because you are reflected in the primary sentient being;
thus, in the Pātañjala [Yoga], you are remembered as the omniscient Lord, distinct even from those subject to saṃsāra. (54)

The enumeration of Sāṃkhya declares that all effects are dependent upon Prakṛti, and that there is another, the Puruṣa, who is distinct from her, knows her, and is superior; it describes him as being beyond number yet numbering the countless, and as the single, pervasive enjoyer.

Since all worldly activity proceeds from the meaning of words, and since creation is dependent upon them, you are considered by the masters of sound to be the beginning and the end; as such, you are Sound (dhvani) in the form of Brahman.

Through the experience of beginningless ignorance, all things—though they appear as agents and so forth—are realized by the virtuous as the one single being; for they experience non-dual Brahman, sporting in the play of the harmony of the Upanishads. 57.
Supreme over all, the creator of all, you alone are established by others within their own strength;
yet they know you as the All-in-All, through whom everything everywhere is pervaded by the All—those who possess knowledge that transcends the highest of all principles.
Beyond that is this primordial, ever-ancient, independent [teaching], which is identical with that and a secret for the ignorant;
some who have entered the single path of the Great Purpose perceive it as the world that illuminates the three worlds.

The followers of Maheśvara enter deeply into you, the Great Lord who possesses the specialized skill [of discerning] amidst the dense mass of snares consisting of the vain hope for the illumination of an inference that is not self-luminous. 60.

Some desire you as Mahendra, the consecrated sovereign over the thirty gods, the lord of sacrifice who is satisfied solely by the methods of ritual, the bestower of rain and other boons, the Indra of Indras, and a treasury of glories. (61)
Having offered you— the consumer of the sacrificial fire, who is himself free from dependence, the illuminator that burns away all defects—
into their respective mouths during sacrifices, some people seek refuge in you.

Those who know the Dharma bow down to you, the ender of karma, who brings about equality among equals and unequals in their actions, and who maintains equanimity toward all self-restrained ones; even while they themselves are not yet at rest, they bow before you.

O Śiva, those who were formerly gods recognize you as the Lord of the Former Gods (Pūrvadeveśvara), for you previously offered your own portion from the sacrifice through the instruction of another, thereby fulfilling all desires through the attainment of the sovereign essence (rasarāja-siddhi). (64)

Others, perceiving you as the Lord who teaches the ocean of jewels that is the essence of existence, and as the one who has entered into the reservoirs of water, constantly lead you—the Lord who is like water—to guide the multitude of sentient beings. 65.

Others also worship you, the Great Lord—the life-force of those who possess life, the strength of all strengths, whose fivefold internal functions are distributed, whose course is never-ending, and who is the sole treasury of perfection through practice. (66)

The Puṇyajanas honor you, the king of all kings, with floods of splendor—you who are the treasure-trove of treasures, the cause of calamity for misfortunes, and whose thirst for offense is most difficult to withstand. (67)

The Brahmins magnify You within the Absolute (Brahman)— You who are the Lord of Brahmā, whose creation is subject solely to the seed-syllables beginning with "Brahmā," who are the source of the entire range of natural emanations, who exist from the beginning of worldly existence, and who are the womb containing the essence of those who know Brahman.

O Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, whose intellect destroys all dullness, who strips away the husks of evil deeds, and who is the Supreme, those within whose hearts the remnants of past merits have been bestowed by the Divine long yearn to behold You, who have transcended all suffering. (69)
Established in the innate (*sahaja*) samādhi of the true tradition, having abandoned all concern for the desirable and the undesirable,
and liberated from even liberation itself, Sanaka and the others manifest you as this very one who is free from all attachment.
Having transcended that which is called conceptual thought through yoga with its constituent limbs,
the perfected ones worship you, their own Lord, who is established in the samādhi of the further shore and who is the sole ordinance for the attainment of all perfections.

The Gandharva kings delight you—who are accessible through the distinctions of sound and devotion, who are uniquely charming in removing the internal dullness of both the inert and the conscious, and who are unapproachable by those whose intellects are afflicted by ignorance—through their own qualities. 72.

Having repeatedly harmonized the seven notes across all three scales through various melodic modulations (mūrcchanās), the horse-faced goddesses sing of You— the Master of all that is to be sung— after first perfecting the fourfold instrumental accompaniment.

O Lord of the Śaktis, the excellent wives of the gods, with single-minded devotion, delight you by singing and playing musical instruments in harmony with the rhythm, employing various melodic modes. (74)

Having imitated various vessels according to diverse methods and having cast aside the grief that had overwhelmed both the world and its inhabitants, even the spirits and goblins laugh at you, their lord, who are a mass of supermundane bliss. (75)

Even Nārada and others, the foremost among your own devotees, being brought entirely under control by their devotion, glorify you while playing upon musical instruments—such as the *svaramaṇḍala* and others—each joined with its own specific sound, producing beautiful melodies. (76)
The Seven Sages, who have taken their station beyond the seven suns and are skilled in the discourse of the Sāman chants,
worship you— who are attainable through the words of the Sāman— with the seven Sāmans, their desires having been fulfilled.

O masters of knowledge, those who know the ritual procedures recognize you as the Lord of Knowledge—the knower of beginningless ignorance through primordial knowledges, the one who has attained realized perfection, and the one who is both the knower and the known of all that is to be known. May they approach you. (78)

O Lord of the world, those who have attained perfection and those still striving for it—those who know the single truth of both the unestablished and the established—seek from You, the goal to be attained, a perfection that transcends all goals;
indeed, they strive to realize You, the Sovereign, who are the very obstacle to all worldly meditations.
Even the gods, by means of medical treatment, quickly attain the perfection of healing;
thus the two Aśvins meditate upon you, the foremost among excellent physicians, the Lord of the heart who is free from mental anguish.
