The All-gods (Viśvedevas) place you within their hearts— you who are the Lord of All, who shine forth in the consciousness of the universe, who are one and knowable everywhere by all, yet distinct from those who do not know you, even according to the sacred ordinance.

For those whose latent impressions have been purified by the absence of impressions, your dwelling is a state of non-dwelling within your own abode; even the Vasus, with their multitudes of riches, satisfy you—the cause of the sole Cause—for the sake of contentment.

O you who move through illusion, though you are the clever actor among the dramas of the *ceṭakas*, even the hosts of *guhyakas* empower you—the Lord, the secret of secrets—to manifest all around them. (83)
Out of devotion, the gods have made Mount Meru an offering at your side; yet even the demons, fearing the stain of enmity, abandon it and worship you, the most blessed Lord, along with the rākṣasas.

O Lord, those hosts of hosts, foremost among the countless whose wealth is skill, possessing excellent qualities through their diligent pursuit of service acquired by merit, always praise you, the king of the kings of the Gaṇas.
Having devoutly presented various and wonderful offerings upon crystal slabs inlaid with gems,
the preeminent celestial artisans, such as Tvaṣṭṛ and others, behold You as their own master craftsman through this mechanical device.
O Lord, having grasped the people through your power of sovereignty, you cause them to hold fast to both favor and restraint;
perceiving you alone as the Lord of Time, the planets always travel their paths free from obstruction.

The blossoming of trees and other plants occurs without seeds, and in the utterly empty forest of the sky, devoid of moon and sun, the form of the stars— exceedingly bright and acting as an aid to flowers— adorns you, their own lord.

Whether in some divine abode, in certain mineral waters, on a mountain, or by a tree—everywhere, even an ordinary person worships you, the beloved deity who grants refuge to the mind, as the universe of all universes. (89)

With their left sides embraced by women, the serpent kings, headed by Śeṣa, accompanied by double-tongued serpents, sing for the sake of praising Your virtues— You, the Lord of Śeṣa, who have made the remainder of all things remain as a remnant.

O Lord of Birds, even the flocks of birds—though endowed with beautiful forms, the speed of the wind, and various innate physical faculties, and being most skillful in the two modes of flight—fan you. (91)
In every forest, relying on a forest-dwelling lifestyle and inflamed by its own qualities such as musk,
the herd of deer— having cast aside pride— bows to you for the sake of favor, O Lord of the Five-Faced One.
And the elephant corps sings to you, who have performed your ablutions in the river Surāpagā and are being gratified with half the flesh of *sallakī* trees,
while they play the *burburaka* and other instruments upon their own female elephants.

Constantly performing their own rhythmic paces in accordance with the debate, these excellent steeds, through their various neighs, summon you—their incomparable master—for the sake of carrying you away. 94.
Adopting that mode of life belonging to Keshava, even the flocks of birds, following your lordship who remains in the waters with an irresistible course,
search here and there for the sake of satisfaction.

O Lord, the multitude bows to you, the Lord of Someśvara, who, while transforming even the Kālakūṭa poison into the state of the supreme Soma, bears the moon upon your crest and wears the Kali age as a necklace, and who are the great medicine for all things.

In these various stages, each renowned for its own specific master-and-possessed relationship, there exists this other, supreme one who abides in both the transcendent and the immanent— the playful sport of the sole player of play.
Indeed, those stages are manifested by the power of the *kalā* consisting of dependence on another and self-dependence;
they are differentiated by the varying degrees of the unfolding of self-concealment for the one who effects both differentiation and its dissolution. (98)
You have attained such pervasiveness through Your own will alone, even within the subtlest fraction of a fraction;
those whose vision is limited and who persist in their dogmatism do not realize that Your own word is most excellent and essential. 99.

Even on the plane of the body and so forth, those who know that their own consciousness—which extends even to the state of absolute nothingness—is essentially the reflective awareness that pervades each preceding level of subjectivity, do not require any further descent of the supreme power (para-śaktipāta). 100.
The restings of blue and other [objects], as well as pleasure and other [feelings], are bodies of inward-turned consciousness;
they are the means for Your manifestation and Your expansion, belonging to You alone, the Knower who perceives each of those. (101)
O Maheśa, whenever this [universe] appears as extroverted, it is at that very moment within its own essential nature;
for here, through the withdrawal of the external, even the internal state becomes a locus of peace by means of devotion to "this-ness."

This Fourth State (turyā) alone is the cause for the union [of all things] beginning with creation; emitting those various distinctions, it also withdraws them when it has attained its power. Though attenuated, it shines as the single ground of dual experience.

And when the conscious self, having submerged its all-pervading unity within differentiation, assumes a contracted state, then its powers manifest, yet [the self] does not appear as such [in its true nature]. (104)
Enveloped by impurity, this very Supreme Lord transmigrates at that time solely by His own will;
he becomes a pauper who conceives the pride of incompleteness and so forth, destitute of the fortune of the supreme power.
Nevertheless, like that [sun], His own fivefold activity shines forth unimpeded for the sake of defining Him;
for He is the sole cause of creation and so forth, appearing again and again as the manifestation of manifestations.
When the glory of the actions of others remains unknown, one's own state is characterized by delusion;
yet, through the unfolding of that very [glory], his own true nature as the Great Lord (Maheśvara) certainly becomes manifest. 107.

The inward-turned mind, having acquired the notion [of its own nature] and gradually established itself in the state of volition, repeatedly touches the true nature of consciousness and thereby attains its own supreme sovereignty. (108)

This fire of consciousness, even though concealed in the state of descent (avaroha) and pervading the entire range of the measurable, consumes all this by its very power; it is time, which is to be measured solely through one's own experience, according to each specific form.
Moreover, even when his own entire power— whether external, innate, or independent— is fully attained,
he directly makes this self-sovereign system (ātmatantra) range from Sadāśiva down to the level of the insentient.

Again and again, through the touch of the firm realization of the oneness of consciousness, he has attained the state of understanding; and even while the body and its primary functions are being perceived, he remains a wanderer who is utterly liberated.

(48) Even here, those well-known means, beginning with the abandonment of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which consist in the obstruction of the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and culminate in the expansion of the center (*madhya*) through the manifestation of light, are firmly established by reasoning. (112)
Through the blossoming of this middle state, the firm attainment of the station of the nectar-bliss of pure consciousness shall occur;
knowing the power of his own eleven digits, he cherishes each subtle portion of meditative absorption.
When there is oneness with consciousness, characterized by the thorough discernment of emergence within one possessed of the mental impressions of samādhi,
there shall arise the higher knowledge (abhijñā) of the ever-arisen splendor of perfect samādhi, again and again.
Then, through the repose in the self-reflection of the I-consciousness— which is filled with the singular, excellent essence of its own power—
the state of being the Lord of the wheel of one's own consciousness spontaneously manifests for the Self-Sovereign Anāśrita.
O Lord of the Great Lord, by the mere grace of a fragment of your glance, I have attained such self-permission; though I am but a servant’s servant, you yourself are that which I now take refuge in.
Therefore, that Dvāpara age has long established itself within my heart;
to ward it off, I ask whatever [I may]—that should be forgiven out of compassion, for indeed, the Lords are won over by devotion. (117)

Although I may cast aspersions upon this secret of reality while practicing the yoga of devotion to Śiva, nevertheless, O Lords, you must speak out of compassion for me, who has taken sole refuge at your feet. 118.
"I am a slave to slaves, yet I long for even a mere fragment of your singular grace. Having attained such a status, how could I not say this? Why do the Great Lords not show compassion? (119)

O Śaṅkara, O King of Kings, what other supreme deity exists even for you, whose praise is meditated upon by the conscious being who is himself unconscious? What else could there be that is higher than you, who abide as the Supreme? (120)
Thus questioned by Nandīśvara, the ocean of compassion and kinsman of the realized ones,
having set the welfare of all beings in his heart, spoke with a smile that was beyond description.

"O Nandika, it is well, it is well that you have asked this; for this is the wisdom of one who is a lord of the Gaṇas. It has arisen in your mind specifically regarding this matter, for the sake of bringing satisfaction both to yourself and to others. (122)
(49) Though I have been repeatedly urged by you, I have not yet spoken this even to Śivā’s son;
nevertheless, I shall tell it to you, who are the benefactor of all and whose love for me alone has increased. 123.

Having thus consoled him, the Supreme Lord— whose joy had arisen, who possesses infinite power, and whose face was smiling— remembering his supreme power and manifesting his state of individuality, spoke with the intention of being praised.
He who, through the power of his own absolute freedom (*svasvātantrya*) and supreme experience, necessarily brought forth the title "Sāhib Kaula" and established his seat within that renowned state—
the non-dual essence of the expansion of the consciousness of Lalitā, known as the *Devīnāmavilāsa*— [is this master].
There, devotion toward his brother, the king of poets, reached its third stage.
Thus ends the third devotion in the *Nāmavilāsa*, composed by the illustrious and preeminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Sāhib Kaulānandanātha. 3.
Now, the fourth verse: My supreme limb is beautiful with an innate erotic charm arising from its own excellence;
it is like a mountain peak, the incomparable crest-jewel of the lineage of the unbroken succession.
Victorious is that Great Goddess, who is to be propitiated by hosts of gods, asuras, excellent humans, and uragas, as well as by the Sādhyas; she is supreme and beginningless. || 1 ||
Then, attached to that innate Śiva-nature, this lord of ascetics becomes disciplined;
empowered by it, he is capable of restraining even Indra and the other gods.
Or, through compassionate grace, he becomes eternally liberated and devoted.
Even when embraced by her, his perception of external objects was extinguished. || 2 ||

In that essential nature which is the core of great non-duality, the sun that dispels the swelling darkness of the dense forest, which is formless yet possesses all forms, and which has quelled the multitude of calamities and afflictions— in that nature, which is the domain of fullness and free from the poison of separation from You— [I abide].
The supreme [consciousness] perceives that which is invisible as visible, having destroyed the power of the other.
She has attained the name "Paśyantī" (the Visionary), manifesting the state of supreme egoity;
she is Śivā, charming with the playful dalliance arising from the emergence of various states of being, her majesty praised by those whose intellects strive for the savor of eternal bliss.
She fashions here a new, auspicious creation that appears indistinguishable from existence itself.
Furthermore, she— having intensely embraced even that body which had been swallowed by the ego-sense (*svāhaṃtā*), thereby concealing the expansion of the state of the world as "this" (*idantā*)—
clearly proceeds toward the middle path, her course revealed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Having reached the opening of the sound, she bestows it upon those of clear intellect.
Resorting to the state known as Vaikharī for the experience of both even and uneven states, she is accessible through the three Vedas, delightful, and ever-inclined toward ever-new manifestations;
having made herself subordinate, she is graced by the perfect integration of the multitude of qualities.
Having manifested the state beyond attributes (nirguṇya), she who is within the midst [of all] reigns supreme. || 6 ||
Having dissolved itself into the station of Sadāśiva— the face of primordial nature (prakṛti) permeated by its own radiance—

and reaching the limit of the state of the individual soul (jīva), it shatters the fabrication of great delusion by devouring the jīva; thus, having dissolved itself into the hundred-petaled lotus in the station of Anāśrita, [it rests].
She satisfies those who have known and worshipped her with showers of streams of nectar.

That dissolution which does not occur for even a moment to the wise through various types of breath-control (prāṇāyāma) involving the pain of manifold restrictive bonds, nor through other limbs of yoga—
even that dissolution is forcibly attained through its manifestation.
On the great path, the vital breath generates incomparable supreme bliss.
"Is this flame entering the void, or has the void entered the place of the flame?"— this is a source of wonder for the wise.
Having dissolved the downward breath (apāna) on both sides within the cavity of the vital breath (prāṇa), [one perceives] that which possesses two peaks.
Therefore, this nectar-essence triumphs alone within the self. || 9 ||
Having placed the earth in water, water in the abode of fire, that [fire] in air, that [air] in space, that [space] in mind, and mind in the path of sound (nāda),
one should dissolve this [sound] into the point (bindu), and that which has reached dissolution into its own state.
Śivā, whose form is light, delights in solitude with her own husband.

Intoxicated by the taste of nectar and having shed the dense thicket of great delusion, she leads those various excellent lords— who have taken refuge at her feet through the sequence of her teachings—
to their respective domains.
The self again attains supreme satisfaction and dwells happily in its own state of tranquility.
This [power] has arisen from existence that is supreme manifestation, yet devoid of [ordinary] existence, or from non-existence that is incapable of becoming;
manifesting itself as something distinct from both being and non-being,
it reveals its quality of being a "quality" through its very differentiation, following the path of qualities.
The stainless one touches the untouchable; consciousness is devoid of calculation and beyond all reckoning.
In the manifestation of Śiva, she is Śakti; in the state of Paraśiva, she is Mahāvidyā through the principle of identity with Him; in the realm of Sadāśiva, she is Maheśānī;
in the state of Paśupati, she is Mahāmāyā and Māyā, possessing manifold creative powers (kalās).
This great and preeminent manifestation proclaims its own inherent power.
Unsurpassed, unconfused, and clear through the unity of the three-fold knowledge, she is the supreme reality, as if beyond all principles, blessed with supreme bliss;
desiring to emit her own stainless play of power through her sovereignty.
The method of manifestation is that which is to be known through its own reflection upon its own wall by itself. 14.
Exuding an intense outpouring of the flow of her own bliss, she thoroughly blended with him the emotions he had manifested at every step;
she herself was the primordial source of all requisites, and she herself was the very artifice of the great Śambara.
She herself falls into that very delusion regarding me, her own supreme self.
Having suddenly descended from her own station at every step of prosperity, she has become the embodiment of all conceptual constructions;
having fashioned according to her will the various systems of thought, she now displays her skill in the art of aesthetic wonder.
In this mastery of the arts, she is like a brand-new Cintāmaṇi jewel. || 16 ||
The supreme Speech, whose essence is the manifested ocean of the ultimate Word, transcends the range of the sun— that is, it lies beyond the reach of words—
yet it manifests for the attainment of the Veda of the world and for the sake of ordaining the conduct of the world.
She alone, the ordainer, is to be served by one who knows herself according to the rule; she indeed [is served] by that very rule.
By that power of Brahmā, the Creator fashions this creation; by the power of Viṣṇu, Indra’s younger brother, he protects it; and by the power of Rudra, Hara withdraws it;
and here, the Lord conceals it through the portion of the Great Power belonging to Īśāna.
Sadāśiva, while manifesting himself, bestows grace upon his own self which is free from all parts (kalās).
May that Umā Kaumārī, the daughter of the mountain king, who is some indescribable Śivā, grant the desired perfection to those whose intellects resemble mine, as well as wisdom;
and may she grant supreme peace in the shattering of the exhaustion born of delusion.
The supreme extraction of the essence, stainless, charming, auspicious, and pure.
Through its unfolding, the world arises at every step,
just as a multitude of trees with their various parts emerges from a single seed;
yet through its closing, it suddenly returns to dissolution, losing that stainless unity.
Like the essence within a peacock's egg, they are the supreme digits of the moon.
By her, those various forms were manifested out of compassion for her own people—
forms that initiate benefit and possess the equipment for the protection of the world;
seeing which, the Creator regards them as the sole objects of a brand-new creation.
He perceives his own labor, performed as if for the Creator, to be fruitless.
Among them, this certain one adorns my supreme crest— the half-body of the Conqueror of Gaṅgā’s crown, who bestows Śiva upon his devotees—
and it has taken refuge in the state of Mṛtyuñjaya, which is the supreme bliss of the Self.
And from a formless cognition, there arises something vast, clear, and possessed of great form.
Even I, though the Lord of Śakti, am not able to discern that peerless, pure, and absolute power of His through long acquaintance; nor am I myself capable,
even with my renowned mouths, of reaching the state of the Lord of Speech.
Having set forth in its entirety, it is free from all sound, yet it is the reckoner of time. || 23 ||
Therefore, knowing this, she alone is the supreme power capable of describing her here; she is also perfectly able to declare herself as "power.
When I undertake an endeavor, she constantly and boundlessly brings it to fulfillment.
For thus says the best of lords of the universe: "This is she, and I am he. (24)
Even though this secret of mine is known within your supreme heart, it must be guarded, guarded most strictly;
for my own true nature, which is the essence of existence, has fully manifested within you as the wealth of silver.
She belongs to someone whose object of expression is exceedingly pure devotion. || 25 ||

I shall speak of this entire [treatise], which possesses infinite ornaments, bears the virtues of others, is the best of true aesthetic flavors, abounds in manifestations, is the primary manifestation of power, has sound as its object, is of great measure, and is free from defects.
This form is patient, and it grants boons even to you through the worship of its feet.
Alas, as I contemplate her locks of hair and her ears,
blindness suddenly arises in my mind, obscuring the perception of both self and other; yet,
having always beheld the dark clouds [of her hair] scattering a multitude of bright rays [from her ears], [how can this be?]
The state of being the abode of the abodes of women has indeed been attained by the lotuses of their eyes. || 27 ||
Having perceived that very state of hers at the threshold of the Veda, I, who am established in the station of the Supreme Śiva, immediately spoke these words:
"Darkness existed," while reflecting upon certain supreme beings who are adept at extracting bliss.
Furthermore, with a whirling gait due to his radiance, he perceives all as full bliss and as the Eternal Reality. || 28 ||
From her tresses, too, I have attained a multiplicity that surpasses all,
as well as an extreme subtlety and a pervasive fullness on every side; likewise, she is forever a disciple of the most excellent teachers, even amidst their weightiest burdens.
Likewise, excrement may be black, variegated, or sometimes motionless and sometimes moving. (29)
My state as Mahākāleśa, my incomparable and immovable blackness,

has been brought about by the manifestation of devotion to Hari; for, seeing that what was worshipped by the venerable ones as highly beneficial within had become exceedingly beneficial externally, [the hair] emerged from the expanded and clear interior.
Is it not sufficient that the Creator, with his four faces, praises Him for the sake of attaining that very state? 30.
Her tresses, when disheveled, are capable of conveying nothing other than unity;
yet when gathered together and arranged in three rows, they are praised for attaining the status of Indra. Therefore, I am known as he who has reduced all branches to a single branch.
Whether taken together or separately, it is impossible to measure this innate power.
Seeing my loosened locks, alas, my mind— desirable yet deprived of its supreme goal, though it has attained a good state through its own firm resolves— runs toward bondage;
for it has itself, by its own hands, suddenly bound its natural braided tresses according to the prescribed rite.
And its liberation [is to be understood] even with respect to external objects, as if they were not external. || 32 ||
Worshipping the lords of hair (the gods) who are pure and radiant, I have become the one fallen upon their hair; I am the eternal destroyer of the infinite End-maker (Death).
Therefore, they are hairs, they are hairs, and I too am Maheśa, the supreme beyond the supreme.
In the sky of consciousness, which is luminous and possesses manifest glory, he is like a ray of the sun. || 33 ||
That essence which arises from the hair, that dust which arises even from the clear rays [of the sun],

and that darkness which arises from the splendors of Krishna— because it colors the path of our hearts despite their being well-known [to others], it is through devotion to Him that this [essence] comes forth.
Having assumed three forms through my strides, I, the performer of the threefold rites, have thus arisen. || 34 ||
Since these lords of hair have repeatedly entered my heart from their external state, each one individually from the mass of locks at every opening;
therefore, O Lord of Manifestation, if indeed this [heart] should attain even another [state], [it would be so].
I am not capable of determining what that respective state might be. || 35 ||
The mass of hair and darkness scattered across the sky of her head, the sun as an enemy entering her eyes, the parting of her hair fashioned like a swirling eddy,
and even the third eye, reddened by its own flame yet appearing as if smeared with vermilion— [all these she bears].
What is it appropriate to praise regarding her, that she possesses such a very firm staff? 36.
Having beheld the celestial Gaṅgā upon my head, has the divine Earth herself become the "Lord of the Ocean" (the mountain Śeṣa), as if with the intent to compete with me through her mass of tresses?
For these [tresses] shine forth within with clusters of flowers from the celestial trees.
Bound by the beauty of their waves, they truly bear a portion of the ocean's splendor.
This braid of hair shines like a beautiful female serpent upon my body; as if bound there, it seems to urge me on with great haste to seek out its own source.
Having ascended from another’s limb, it performs the playful dance of arranging hair upon my head.
Lallañjihvā, seeing this Vāsuki, turned her course away. || 38 ||
Though free from sin by his vow of carrying the clouds, the peacock feels fear at the offense of bearing her [the cloud’s] offspring; as if to balance himself on the tip of a hair,
he fans his own plumage before her, discerning and then realizing [her identity].
For the king of birds repeatedly censured what was done, saying, "This is pleasing. (39)

The rays of the eyelashes have cast out the king of darkness from the three worlds; they are fixed upon the three spokes of the head, which is fortified by its lofty brow-ridge; they have conquered the praiseworthy objects of the senses through their devotion; and they are appropriately arrayed by those lords of splendor.
Having seen him below, adorned with a crown of flowers, with their eyes fixed upon him.
When the three lords of the quarters each rose to their respective abodes, this darkness— which had made its dwelling within the three worlds— was driven out by Keśin;
though they blocked the doors, it immediately surged back forth.
Having seen that the world was once again enveloped here by those who were wandering about, [they remained]. || 41 ||
Having propitiated these children whose forms are like darkness, who have shed the water of sweat and are casting off their accustomed tears as if they were infants,
[he beheld] the lords of light, for whom the Sāman chants were composed by their own hands through sacred refinements.
Did she cast away her enemies along with these excellent, sensitive eyelashes?
(58) Considering that these good children had made a request with their feet placed [as a supplication] for the games they desired, Kṣamagati brought them near;
she even placed the sun and the moon in the midst of fire between them.
"Let it not wither even for a moment from the touch of excessive passion as it departs. || 43 ||
It is fitting that the Lord of the Gods has sent his own collection of flowers here for your hair under the guise of a garland;
yet, its exquisite length falls down to your feet as if to learn the art of such extreme prostration.
Is he withered by his own impotence, or is he as if humiliated by approaching her? 44.
The clouds, formidable with their swelling mass, have risen up as if to weigh these thick locks of hair with the rays of jewels from their crowns; yet,
though shimmering with brilliance and exceedingly restless, they cannot achieve a perfect likeness.
They abandon [their kin] while wailing, shedding copious tears and vapors, within their own realm.
Seeing this crown formed by the mass of matted locks entwined with the lord of serpents, and his tresses white at their ends due to the trailing braid following the contact with the moon,
what indeed could the lord of serpents, Rāhu, have done before Śivā? For she herself has held him [as her crest-ornament].
Having placed the fire in his stride and the sun and moon as his eyelashes. || 46 ||
The mass of hair, though remaining within, moves outward as if with difficulty for the sake of being weighed on a scale; emerging behind,
it is like a cluster of yak-tail whisks for the celestial women, intended to serve as fans to wipe away the offense of that [hair].
Or was it sent by the lords of the Bālas with the intention of performing the lustration rite (nīrājana)? || 47 ||
This celestial river, dangling with sky-jewels that have attained the state of pearls and possessing the three qualities (*triguṇa*), captivates my heart;
why then this attachment here to the daughter of the Sun (the Yamunā), whose mass of hair merely shines?
Is it for my inspection, or has the triple-pathed river come before me?
Under the guise of dangling ornaments, the planets— fearful of being swallowed by the sun and the moon— shine with various splendors as jeweled decorations upon the locks of hair belonging to Rāhu,
which are gracefully adorned by the heavy burden of his rising crest-locks.
Why have you come—to perform the lustration ceremony for the sake of honoring her? || 49 ||
Having fashioned the moon for his crown, has he perhaps left only the single digit of his body for the Sāman chant,
manifesting this forehead-slab from which issues forth a stream of nectar-drops of perspiration?
It brings about the complete consecration in the state of the Conqueror of Death. || 50 ||
Having made a request through the form of his crown, has the moon risen to acquire a delicate artistry or a certain curvature from the mass of heavy tresses?
Therefore, having attained a deeper blackness that brings internal joy, [he shines].
Under the guise of a blemish, it bears a quality not attained by others. || 51 ||

Since he, whose victory is renowned, has at the mere sight of me as his enemy— though my body is sustained by the moon upon her crown raining down nectar— seized the noose of her pure tresses and for even a moment binds the God of Love; [how can I survive?]
I cannot at all bear to go elsewhere, leaving him behind. || 52 ||
"O Mistress, shall I ever attain such exquisite beauty as that of these locks of hair?
Thus addressed by them with their ears and faces turned sideways, she, playing sportively, replied:
"What have you gained from the jewels of the flowers of the celestial trees?"
Or she is Sitā, Bhasā, or Vidyumukutā, who has taken up these [forms]. || 53 ||
Having been pleased by the constant gift of her body to all the gods, she fashioned from the remainder of her nectar-like form a moon with countless rays of jewels;
she who is the king of the twice-born, whose compassionate gaze is ever directed upward.
What indeed has she fashioned in order to utterly conquer the one who possesses a thousand rays?
Even before King Cikura, the peacock— renowned here on earth as the possessor of the most exquisite and tender plumage— became his beloved,
even though it was constantly adorned with shimmering eye-spots. Having praised him, [the king] remained ever devoted to that [peacock].
Somehow the peacock also managed to find that moon-spotted [snake].
O mind, which functions like a hundred shards, having entered these hairs along every path and being obstructed from emerging by the internal darkness on all sides,
you must search for this triad of my own luminous eyes.
The three [eyes] shine, joined and held by the frosty moon as a crown.
Having entered within, my mind— having abandoned its own state which possesses supreme bliss and provides extensive, beneficial rest—
spoke thus even though it was urged by me here to come forth externally.
Does he mock me with this moon of a crown resting upon the tip of his face? (57)
The moon situated in the middle of his crown, its luster shining through the three peaks,
with its crest-jewel rolling [therein], alas, bestows upon me the status of Mount Meru;
for the gods, though young, are renowned for their lack of decay.
Those who at the end shine forth, possessing the excellent qualities of those who are always well-disposed.
Adorned with a head-ornament set with pearls, it shines brilliantly, scattering its own moonlight amidst the darkness of her thick tresses;
it stands in mutual contrast to the radiance of the crown, the moon, and other luminous objects in front and behind.
In his own fortress, Kali-hara has established a boundary as if by his power. || 59 ||
This beautiful Ganges, adorned with reins inlaid with jewels, flowing through the three paths, and clearly manifesting her divine nature,
has attained the state of Śivā as she pervades the heart with her overflowing essence.
As if to demonstrate the oneness of aesthetic flavor (rasa) to me, she who is skilled in policy [has spoken].
Adorned with a necklace and shimmering with the luster of her blossoming hair, she plays like the celestial river Ganges leaping from my head and merging with the Yamunā;
for here, in the place of the braid, dwells this lord of the twice-born, possessing only pure melody.
Released from the lap of the Earth, he arose as a fragment of jewel. || 61 ||
I suspect this forehead— freed from the devouring of the rays of the planets— is the moon itself, which has manifested a great sun from its belly;
for [the goddess], her body emaciated by vows, has entered the mouth at Kurukṣetra with the intent to bathe.
For the lord of birds has alighted upon Sarasvatī, whose splendor is like a pearl.
Sometimes, through union with the moonlight on earth or sometimes with a beautiful woman in the darkness, the pure and radiant moon acquires a spot;
yet by both of these, it is rendered the site for the excellence of [her] tresses.
It is indeed not fitting that he should be renowned here as being equal to Prabhāta. || 63 ||

This ornament of the bridle has been fashioned by the Creator— who somehow managed to overcome the darkness appearing under the guise of her hair— after bypassing the difficult task of creating a crown for the moon, which already possesses its own innate form and position.
Or when the two creeper-like arms are thrown around, producing the pleasure of an embrace.
With a protruding forehead-protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) and an eye situated on the brow,
he always shines slightly outwardly with a reddish hue due to his internal radiance;
thus these masses of his hair appear very glossy and spread out like rows of lotuses.
The rising smoke, reaching the path of the clouds and stirred by the wind, [is seen]. || 65 ||
How strange it is that I do not perceive this fire, which is red like a *malika* flower and situated within my eyes, as being one from which cold rays have spread forth;
for upon merely beholding it, the wound of the fever born of love is instantly healed.
For that cause which arises within me, even though it takes the form of one devoid of a crown, [is manifest]. || 66 ||
This third lotus-eye of his, which remains perpetually unblinking here in the presence of the moon who dwells upon his crown,
is of the same nature as the eye born from the ocean of the Sage’s eyes.
By this very [method], one's own lineage, together with the lotus-born [Brahmā] and Ādi [Śiva], is established. || 67 ||
The sun and the moon revolve in turn, closing and opening their eyes, while on earth they simultaneously display the splendor of blooming lotuses and water-lilies even without looking.
This eye, however, though directed outward, is not external; it laughs at the beauty of both [the sun and the moon] alike.
Remaining there, watching with unblinking eyes, those two saw the supreme state of the slain.
This eye is a lotus upon the forehead, containing a blue water-lily within; even during the night, it remains in the vicinity of the moon’s rays,
yet its dark clusters of lashes are perpetually in full bloom.
Seeing the variegated [body] resting there, who would not be filled with wonder by those [limbs] resembling tender sprouts? (69)
Upon his broad forehead, these two— the moon and the sun— having cast down their respective domains, have made this beautiful eye appear as if blossomed with joy;
yet even so, he bears this small, curved crescent moon resting upon his crown.
Beholding him, [the moon] became as if red with indignation on the outside, while remaining white within.
Upon that forehead, which is a lake of the nectar of loveliness,
this certain red lotus-like eye has blossomed, producing wonder; leaving behind all other functions, it has spread across my eyelashes as its very form.
For it is like a bee that has come here from its dwelling in the form of a mental star. || 71 ||
What is this ruby emerging from the belly of the crystal stone, having burst forth as if from a mine wide with the swelling of clouds,
reaching these ever-radiant locks of hair that are like collyrium?
The eyelashes rested upon the pupils, which were raised upward and devoid of external impurities.
This eye, this eye, is a play of the multitude of [mental] fetters; it has arisen here for the sake of binding me within, or perhaps it is not made of a web.
That which is dependent within me, having destroyed the power of others, is the notion of a body— (p. 64) [this is the eye].
Even though he has endured this body, the Destroyer (Hara) will swiftly carry it away as well.

Has the white forehead grown so large that it must be entirely covered by the eye? Or does it appear reddened by the rising anger of a young woman’s obstruction? Therefore, young women are to be honored, for they are borne upon the head and possess far-reaching influence.
Indeed, this mark of the stars has its twinkling destroyed and is devoid of human deficiency. 74.
Therefore, out of fear, like thieves, even the *cakora* birds— though possessing wings and ever-fickle— abandon their beloved and flee to the lonely forest;
for, due to the agitation of the water, they must repeatedly lower their heads even when rising from the mud.
"I am not at all capable of attaining praise by means of this," he says. || 75 ||
The cakora bird is my mind; with its body as eyes, it is rendered utterly motionless by her thick eyelashes appearing like a mass of wings.
It has entered the interior of the moon in two ways—within her beautiful eyes and upon her head.
Drinking the moonlight, the impassioned one, having made his dwelling there, becomes exceedingly intoxicated.
Beholding me, the invincible wielder of the flower-arrowed weapon,
with my movements obstructed on all sides, this pair of ear-rings has assumed the form of a pair of curved swords as excellent weapons, by which they forcibly strike at me.
He made him, who was fearless in battle, subject to his own command. || 77 ||
Having slain many youths, this bow— bearing a heavy stain and exceedingly dark— is held with its string drawn back within the grip;
and having aimed these arrows simultaneously toward all sides, the multitude of eyelashes [of the slender-bodied one]...
While I am not yet bent by this very [suffering], he does not create that which would fulfill his purpose. || 78 ||
Having obtained from them a supreme blackness through its own instrumentality, has this pair of earthen banks become the joyful bow of Śunaḥśepa?
For, beholding the unshakable position of the clouds upon his head, it is as if they were his locks of hair.
Having taken refuge in the white [syllable] situated in the center, which is the single, most stable innate quality (sahaja-guṇa). || 79 ||
Beholding this cool-rayed one situated on her head or in her eyes,
she has attained a twofold position here within the pair of her eyebrows; otherwise,
how could these two moons have taken the form of a continuous line?
Having set forth in its entirety, it possesses a certain incomparable beauty that adorns its form.
Beholding the moon and the sun with their eyelashes raised, as if they had risen together here to conquer the fire situated upon her exceedingly broad forehead,
has she fashioned for him alone this fitting wreath of smoke-like creepers?
A double boundary wall, which causes strife and destruction, is for the purpose of demarcating the limit. || 81 ||
Seeing the pure-rayed Pālī of the three worlds, did the darkness simultaneously manifest its own pair of Pālīs?
Or is this Pālī truly mine, by virtue of being my protector?
And even though my enemy has turned his face away, I am not yet subject to death. (82)
Having fashioned this pair of eyebrows for me with a pair of pearls— curved like the crescent moon and equal in form— with a bright circle placed above them as a crest-jewel,
my beloved has, as it were, offered a sacrifice to the Sun using these two brows as the sacrificial ladles.
He fashioned crowns for his head and sapphire gems for his two other eyes.
Because this golden tilaka on her forehead is fashioned from jewels, it always bears the splendor of gold; thus,
at the edge of her blossoming face, the tilaka attains the luster of honey.
"That [lotus] was blossomed by her side-glances"—this statement of the poet has truth as its object. 84.
Seeing both the cold and the hot seasons arisen simultaneously and powerful,
has this *tilaka* flower on the forehead of the lady become a friend to fire?
It has surpassed the stars that possess a different luster, having risen with its own excellence.
Did he perhaps create a new, unprecedented mark by combining these two splendors? || 85 ||
She bears a forehead-mark of manifold rays, surpassing me who am endowed with three eyes; or rather,
she possesses a novel seal for the sake of victory, composed of portions belonging to the lords of the three lights.
Does Kandarpa, who makes even the beloved one tremble, bear the mark of the planets upon his body? (86)
When his two curved eyebrows meet simultaneously at their tips, do you become our refuge with your eyelashes, or rather, are you the "tilaka-eye" (the eye adorned with a forehead mark)?
For you are the very crest-jewel upon the tilaka of this entire threefold world.
Why does he not take hold of supreme fortune here on earth, standing above all? || 87 ||
Having beheld this forehead, which is like the ocean of milk and is the source of its progenitor,
the Kaustubha gem remains fixed there with steadfast love;
for were it not so, how could Lakṣmī have abandoned him here to seek another object?
The love between siblings has reached an exceedingly firm state. || 88 ||
With these two eyes of novel design and with his own four faces, Brahmā seems to search everywhere for a likeness;
for even now, the Creator remains awake night and day, seeking in vain to find a match.
Having consoled her further, he indeed slept again, his entire body exhausted.
These two eyes are a pair of golden honey-cups, scattering their own rays and manifesting an unprecedented state of intoxication both internally and externally;
they are as beautiful as blooming blue lotuses, and [the face] is like one whose half has been stolen away.
How else could I be so utterly reeling, were it not for the very thought of happiness? (90)
Are these two certain ponds, filled with the honey-like nectar of beauty, sprinkling him with streams in the form of your eyelashes?
Or are they your own limbs, ever-fresh and full of passion, moistening him again and again?
Since I too have attained these and have reached incomparable freedom from craving. || 91 ||
These two eyes, though possessing a most unbearable and beautiful radiance, indeed possess eyelashes that bear the quality of blackness;
for even when they are situated very close to them, [the lashes] quickly cast a shadow of apprehension.
They do not depart for even a moment, being exceedingly skillful in guarding their own stations.
These two eyes of yours are like dark gems within the waters of the ocean born of serpents,
set in a beautiful vessel; for the sake of consecrating the younger brother of Māra, why do you desire the tips of dūrvā grass from the outside with your rows of eyelashes?
The sectarian mark (tilaka) shines upon him, conveying the splendor of his royal parasol.
Neither the lotus nor even the blue water-lily is sufficient to attain the status of a comparison for these two eyes of the lovely-eyed one, which have now come together as a single object of vision,
joined with the dark-hued, beautiful lashes that resemble clusters of tender sprouts.
They went simultaneously for refuge to their own two kinsmen. || 94 ||
These fish, as if wretched because they have attained a state of dullness through their similarity to [the eyes], are submerged within, their swift movements stilled and their luster lost;
therefore, it is fitting that this Madana is known in the world as "he who has the fish as his mark."
Having attained the state of bodilessness, does he now seek companionship with Spring alone? || 95 ||
His two eyes are pure in their radiant smile, yet possess hands uplifted by compassion; they are filled with wrath toward the wicked, yet appear as if out of passion;
they are worthy of equal praise, possessing wondrous forms and supreme excellence.
To me, who bestows a flavor that is peaceful, full, and most beautiful. || 96 ||
These two eyes, out of a desire for the more stable play of the *khañjana* bird, seem to have set out to emulate its limping gait;
yet, though they follow the path, they do not proceed smoothly, but rather falter again and again.
Turning back and leaping up with eyes trembling from fear, she struck him with her ear.
On the new moon day, at the end of the sun’s course, the moon does not possess its full luster even when it has risen;
this fact is well known here. But if this is so when it is merely visible, how much more so when it has truly arisen with all its characteristic marks on that most excellent lunar day?
For by this vision, both the gods and the ancestors are fully satisfied.
Is it "amā" (non-measure) or is it "amā" (together)? What indeed becomes of it? Is it truly full?
For here within, these two moons—the cool and the white—are perfectly radiant with light;
and since their conjunction here has indeed become firmly established.
Then, the fire truly manifests the twilight within its own domain. || 99 ||
Having attained fame from this [world] as one born of the ocean,
it is indeed fitting that even at the end of the hot-rayed sun, he rises with beautiful luster, though his form is incomplete; yet, when full of all digits, he is always revealed by the sun.
Having abandoned enmity, may there be friendliness born from the dissolution of grasping, like the pure luster of the moon. || 100 ||
Since this best of the twice-born, having reached Tārā from here, remains joyful, pure in luster, and a leader among the twice-born even while standing at the end of the sun’s path,
therefore the Lord of Stars (the Moon) must indeed always [be surpassed] even by way of exchange.
Likewise, even Tārā herself follows him; such is this one who delights in virtue. || 101 ||
In some places white, in others dark;
in some places of a reddish hue, and in others with the luster of a blue lotus; in some places beautiful with yellow sprouts, and in some places shining with various rays of mixed light.
How can even the two eyes and their movements be determined? 102.
By means of which [vision], even a single, specific portion of merit is seen here;
by that, no other perceived object ever enters the range of what is conceptualized. For that vision, being solitary, experiences that stainless reality.
Toward whom all the great lords of vision direct their longing. || 103 ||
These two curved eyes of yours steal away crookedness through their stainless gaze;

when joined with pure colors, they surpass all calculation of color and the like; and when fixed in a steady stare, they further transcend the manifestation of worldly existence, having resorted to the path of supreme qualities.
In the path [of the heart], one should abandon duality and the expansion of mental fluctuations within the vast, radiant expanse of the heart.

These two views, having attained delight upon seeing [the truth], produce clarity through their quality of being "with ointment" (*sāñjana*), together with those born of their own kind who possess the word of ointment (*añjanapada*).
These two voices praise the Lord of the Best of Poets through their quality of being "suggestive" (*vyañjana*).
How can one's own boldness not be manifested through the medium of suggestion? || 105 ||
Seeing that the sun and the moon are always powerful here when their light is joined with the moonlight and sunlight respectively,
has the shadow of Alakā’s body perhaps manifested itself in order to pervade the entire rear portion [of the city], or have they risen to do so?
By this [power], they were forbidden from associating with one another through the subtle artifice of their connection.
Stationed upon the fortress of his head, the King of Darkness dispatched a pair of generals— the two ears— to seize the entrance;
yet they took on the role of curls to engage in combat face-to-face with the two lords of radiant luster.
If they had not resorted to this [method], how could these two have escaped with their lives? || 107 ||

Beholding me proceeding by three paths from my head, has the Yamunā—the beauty of my hair—become the triple-pathed Gaṅgā of heaven, as if through her two braids of matted locks? Or has she become like a serpent-vein? Is it fitting? Or rather, is she indeed a serpent-like braid?
Sprinkled with mercury, it produced a beautiful pair of hair-like serpents.
This is fitting: that the bees have established here, near the lord of the swan-birds, a formation beautiful in its symmetry;
for when the dense, excellent [swarm of] bees has approached, it eclipses the splendor of the lotuses.
Or like ears of water-moss, or hair, or the objects of the senses, even though they have emerged [from the depths]. || 109 ||
It is no wonder that the swan of your face— the lord of birds— found its dwelling in the lake of the nectar of your beauty, which is charming with the curls of your hair;
for it was there that he wandered, having fallen into the excellent well of your ears, while your lotus-like cheeks were shimmering.
Furthermore, what is it that has not been attained by both of these two similar classes? (110)
O Great Mistress, my mind, already wavering due to the net of impurities, is being shaken even further by Your exceedingly beautiful limbs; thus,
for each individual feature here, it becomes focused upon one part of Your body.
Having seen his prosperity, he once again set out toward another kingdom.
Has this ladder, consisting of the beautiful curls of hair, been fashioned by the Sun, who possesses rays, for the god Anaṅga to climb with ease?
For from these two conch-like breasts, joined with thick tresses, arise [the drops] born of sapphire.
Are the counting-sticks not crooked, like mother-of-pearl beads? (112)
Did the two earrings, possessing the luster of gems, assume the form of her eyes upon seeing those two ears which possess the radiance of the moon? Or rather,
did they do so to surpass the three-fold brilliance of her eyes, or perhaps to match their uneven number?
And her own cleverness has been displayed equally by this coiled [form]. || 113 ||
The pair of golden bells, fashioned from jasmine petals, split gems, and flowers, adorned with shimmering straps and cords, and possessing the form of earrings—
though heavy with the weight of another essence— could not be lifted up.
What is it here that, having overcome the Lord of Light (the Sun) with its brilliance, is perceived by these two ears? 114.

In its state of motion, [the horse] possesses the quality of being adorned with a bridle; yet, with its mane as thick as darkness, it obstructs this [bridle] with its rays that are as bright as excellent jewels. Having assumed the form of two earrings, it now strives to move upward with ease upon its shimmering back.
By remaining in contentment with the aesthetic flavor (rasa), one perceives the sun and the moon within the range of the eyes.
Is this nose, with its lofty beauty shining from two nostrils, perhaps the newly constructed inner apartment of Rati, the consort of Kāma?
For these two [nostrils] seem to have been fashioned to encircle from the outside the orb of the shimmering moon.
Or rather, let his two cheeks attain the splendor of a ruby surface from this [lip]. || 116 ||

Having observed that shadow on her cheek, which was as beautiful as Alakā, and seeing that the moonlight of her radiance had arisen at her side, why would there not be a distinct [shadow] in the region of her cheek?
Therefore, with the thought of filling it once more, she again made the middle part empty.
The position of Tārā was established by Girijā for the two lords who possess the luster of eyes. 117.
This nose is a quiver for the pair of arrows that are the two nostrils; it is the ornament of her own secret convention, exceedingly beautiful here on one side.
Her two hands are like lotus petals made of rubies, with the arrangement of leaf-designs—
Adorned with golden marks on their temples, they possess the quality of being excellent at seizing the cheeks of their rivals. || 118 ||
Does this nose, shining near the lord of swans [the forehead], produce a cluster of pearl-eggs within its lotus-like cheeks?
For here, the female swan [the lower lip] constantly displays her youthful charms while resting upon her own ornament.
Upon their birth, two swans appeared, adorned with jewels of twice-born ones and fashioned from earrings.
Seeing this pair of lords of serpents, heavy with weight and beautiful with wings made of gold,
these two [earrings] have somehow not entered into conflict, despite the brilliance of their shimmering earrings.
For this reason, even though he was confined within both abodes, he was not [confined] mutually.
Seeing Viṣṇu, who is exceedingly beautiful with his two-fold form,
did not Garuḍa assume a dual appearance consisting of earrings?
Moreover, the abode of Śrī has attained a twofold state here, residing within the region of his cheeks.
Even victorious Māra, having obtained his own various lineages fully manifested within me, [is defeated].
Seeing the multitude of feathered arrows drawn simultaneously by the two guards of the bow,
this nose-ornament, set with pure gems, seems to tremble here as if apprehensive of its own destruction.
It moves as if to enter those two openings, coiled and trembling.
(73) Does this nose-ornament move about in order to depart? No, for I shall not be separated from the beloved of the Lord [Śiva];
since from him alone has the boon of victory over death been proclaimed here.
Thus, he is attained by Śiva through other Lords, and his play is desired on all sides. || 123 ||

Are these two lips truly the reflections of the sun and moon, or rather are they the images reflected from those two luminous orbs? Within the fine, nectar-sweet, and radiant mouth, the rays of the teeth [shine].
From which the two cheeks emerge and rest here in a circular curve.
These two lips, red and protruding outward like excellent coral;
the teeth, like pearls, repeatedly scattering white rays within;
these two full [breasts], laughing as if multiplied by the trunk of an elephant or surpassed by it.
Your cleverness is indeed evident in the clear separation of the two bellies.
Her young sprout-like lower lip is not capable of being equaled by coral grown upon a tree; how then could it be compared to red coral, which consists of mere fragments?
Therefore, these two have been made to resemble each other by someone who has not grasped their true nature.
"Since it has departed from me, how can you two maintain this flavor here, or even one superior to it? (126)
We are lovely teeth, entirely suitable for assuming another color, and even by ourselves possess the pure radiance of pearls;
yet you two, though possessing other virtues, are constantly attached to passion (redness).
As if wishing to transfer their own full quality to the lips of the spring season. || 127 ||
(74) This [Goddess] is independent, yet by her own nature she is marked by being doubly dependent;
with her thirty-two teeth, she possesses a power that cannot be touched by ritual procedures (*vidhi*),
alas, through the slightest trace of dependence on the *siddhis* well-known [to others].
Nor is speech appropriate for even speech to proclaim misfortune. || 128 ||
Beholding Śrī pervading all her limbs with various forms, and seeing her herself shining upon the limbs of others while standing at the root of aesthetic flavor (rasa),
how else could this Speech (Vāṇī) describe the relationship between limb and limb?
One's own [nature], called Bhāratī, should lead people to the state arising from philosophical insight. || 129 ||
When this vision, fully blossomed in its threefold form, gazes upon the domain of the Right (Dakṣa) while possessing a radiant luster in the middle state of the Supreme Abode,
it scatters the stainless, far-reaching rays of the pervasive Fire.
Not being slain, yet being exhausted, she expands, being fondly cherished by the intoxicated one. 130.
This [nose-ornament], manifesting its own beautiful adornment upon the ear, brings about unity with the crest of the Vedas (*śrutiśiras*) through its own cleverness;
for it is the string of pearls that extends from both sides to the ears, eyes, and nose.
Or rather, the pervasive power of the abode has attained a state of beautiful limbs consisting of three parts.

Is this *sandhi*— which, through its secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), subsequent words (*upapada*), verbal roots (*kṛt*), and indeclinables (*avyaya*), is not merely rich in gender (*liṅga*) but possesses a clear path revealed by the *sūtras*,
and which, abiding in its own words, is endowed with qualities (*guṇin*) and supported by the primary words (*śruti*)— here extended into the state of grammar (*vyākaraṇatā*)?
Even the sound of his voice, though faintly resonating within, was sufficient to produce a sense of majesty.

O you of beautiful form, is not the Mīmāṃsā— characterized by words of praise— applicable here, since even the negation of the mass of light (tejas-rāśi) belonging to the Creator (Vidhi) results in his destruction?
For it brings about the rise of actions that yield non-corporeal bliss to the Enemy of Kāma (Śiva).
Stability, accompanied by the manifestation of expiation, is that state here. 133.
The rows of teeth, capable of reasoning and dwelling in duality through their sixteen parts,
do not release [the tongue] even when it is engaged in enjoyment, nor do they form speech-appropriate utterances; or rather, the two lips do not hold the tongue within the domain of both.
What need is there for a face that possesses excellence, when glory here has already attained its sixfold state? 134.
The two ears became her eyes, the nose became her lotus-face, and the other eye returned to its own natural state through its inherent beauty;
even the transformation produced by the specific arrangement of the two petals [of the face] was surpassed by her grace.
That very nature of critical inquiry did not reach its full limit here. || 135 ||
In her right eye, the Vaishnavi power of memory indeed flashes forth, discerning the various principles through thirty-two rays;
from Vishnu, Smara was born, and having come toward me, he has seized my life-breath.
With the ego-sense ceased, he perceives the mind through the full digit.
This one has departed through the seven gates, accompanied by the fire from the eye that shakes the crown; he is not unworthy, nor is his object here something new—
[he is like] the digit of the moon with its two-fold beauty and the arts of the true luminaries.
Even when mixed with those [qualities] and endowed with them, it does not partake of the state of a Tathāgata. || 137 ||

In the fullness of one's own nature, the vital breath carries [the consciousness] into the supreme state of the void within the region of the nose; from this point, the objective sphere of space also becomes manifest. Consequently, the Self as the object of that experience flashes forth, and its exquisite splendor is revealed.
One's own body is the goal extended here for all through the act of seeing. 138.
In her, my sonship shines forth, and likewise this wife and children; indeed, she is my everything— Pūrṇalalitā— who,
like a medicinal creeper from the Lord of Mountains, bestows the power of conquering death.
Once born, she indeed spread the path of the physician.
In this [land], the path of those with manifest weapons extends even to the realm of the limbs of the bodiless one; yet, in this very place, the ancient body of that [Purāṇa] does not shine forth.
Here, the extensive memory of the noble sages shines brightly.
Or who indeed knows this, other than the unshakable statement of the Itihāsa? 140.
Teaching the form of musical instruments through her various limbs, easily perceived by those of refined taste as she triumphs over various sounds with the words of *dhvani*,
she who always dances within the lotus-heart of mine with manifest movement— [to her I bow].
In this stage, this Gandharva-like state of mine flashes forth, reaching its ultimate limit.
Since her supreme purpose for my sake has been clearly proclaimed,
and since there is no other composition of meaning in her that is so manifest, why then do these sixty-four arts not always appear with the twofold luster of her teeth?
That which is celebrated here as skill in the arts is due to the *kalā* (aspect) that consists of all things.
Victorious is this manifestation of the supreme form of the ocean of literature, whose course is whirled by the nectar of the nine rasas— the beloved of the Lord of the World—
since Madana, having obtained his appropriate portion from that literature, is filled with joy.
It always proclaims its own meaningful and graceful name, "Smara" (the Mind-born), within me alone.
This speech, which is unable to be equaled by the lute (*vīṇā*) due to its multitude of qualities,
is here called the "lute" (*vipañcī*) because it is naturally liberated [from defects];
likewise, she who has a smoky luster and a very swift gait is like the female cuckoo.
This female cuckoo, abandoned by her own kind, has become a cuckoo for others.
Even a swan standing on the shore is capable of rivaling this swan with its deep-toned cries; yet how could it ever utter such a lament,
repeatedly seeking its beloved through words that are both timely and full of pathos?
And how might that peacock again attain the state of being desired by his beloved? 145.
The parrot, utterly devoid of passion, returns to its own elemental nature;
indeed, failing to attain her likeness, it merely cries out with its "kreṅ-kṛt" calls.
Likewise, the female osprey becomes an osprey by virtue of her form, but certainly not by her voice.
Or perhaps this sweet-voiced cuckoo has merely appeared here by chance. || 146 ||
Having seen her own chin— made triangular by the Three-Eyed Lord upon his forehead as a mark of Śiva— did she manifest an inner point (bindu) within it?
For her hair, acting as the door, revealed the state of being fivefold through the eyes, mouth, and other features.
They have attained the state of having eight petals, possessing double the number of petals due to their being encircled.
Since the two cheeks on the surface of her face have become manifest for the expansion of their own luster— the very light produced by her eyes— this chin exists here;
for what else could it be than the state of being the lower lip for the moonlight of her teeth?
He bestowed the names "Stayā" (the Stay) and "Bimba" (the Bimba) upon the two excellent lower lips, which surpassed the bimba fruit in beauty.
This entire moonlight spreads forth because from him [the moon] have arisen the teeth-born digits, doubled in number compared to the digits of the Lord of Herbs;
and that these [teeth], while playing here, pervade his face with their rays— this is indeed so.
The state of being a *kunda* flower belongs to the teeth; that [state] of being *sumanas* flowers belongs to the pair of eyes. (149)
The two cheeks are well-rounded, the face is exceedingly broad, the eyes are stainless, the nose is straight, and the teeth are always pure white;
the lips are deeply red, and the chin is not too prominent.
The pair of ears is curved on the inside and straight on the outside, as is appropriate. || 150 ||
Since even the moon cannot attain even a partial likeness to the beauty of its parts— the eyes and so forth— and since the lotus and other things are likewise unfit for comparison with this face,
it is therefore celebrated here as being more beautiful than all else.
By its very nature as a face, whose mouth does not bring delight through its words? 151.
Or was it that the lotus, though struck by thorns and withered at its edge, bloomed at the proper time without dullness and thus bestowed beauty upon the moon?
Or rather, did the Goddess Lakṣmī, overcome by her affection for her kin, take refuge there out of fear?
If even by a single fraction of its surface it might achieve a fitting comparison, how much more so [by the whole]? || 152 ||

Possessing an ever-present non-existent portion (the dark fortnight), eternally multicolored, perfectly beautiful with its own digits, and bearing that digit even through the lunar splendor of the twice-born (the moon)— revealing the luster of stars— his face alone is the true lotus-limb.
The moon is the friend of Śrī; no other moon is so appropriate. || 153 ||
Has the moon, rendered helpless by love, been made to abandon this digit and go to his waning, only to return here in full once more while searching for it?
For the moon of her face has himself attained that very digit which was attached to him.
He remains eternally full, free from all stain, and delights in that which is beyond [the senses]. || 154 ||
Is Fate weary of fashioning, month after month with the luster of its own face,
this moon which it repeatedly carves away?
Yet even so, it conceals this diminished orb in anger with its encircling halo.
Sometimes by difficult nights, or even by heat, darkness, or gloom.
Even when seized by others who are naturally sweet-spoken,
this moon of a face ascends to heaven for comparison;
yet those whose memory has failed do not recall even me, the lotus, when it has emerged from the mud.
Thinking that poets might perhaps seize it, why does this flickering [mind] dance about? 156.
Beholding his own empire like the moon, the enemy— his splendor eclipsed— performs the lustration ceremony (*nīrājanam*) out of delusion by means of his own digit;
yet even this [enemy] is one who knows virtues, for he compassionately bestows strength upon the weak.
Or has your gaze been fixed upon my left eye, O Moon? 157.

How many rays of moonlight have not been scattered from the mouth of the Moon— the bestower of nectar— by the flocks of birds under the pretext of his smile? Since that is well known here, how is it that even a single ray of moonlight, having somehow found a companion, has its luster destroyed [by the darkness]?
Even while knowing his harmful intent, she nevertheless appoints him as the lord of the moonlight.
O Emperor, having surpassed the faces of the sovereigns of the three worlds— the foremost of women— with the splendor of his queen’s face, this lord of the circle of vassals shines resplendent;
[his glory] flows from his ears through the scattering of jewels set within the petals [of her earrings].
The forehead mark shines as if accompanied by three moving parasols. || 159 ||

This pure, incomparable, and foremost of words shines forth, pervading the single ear with its many own parts and rays; it possesses manifold splendors and is the object of the great vision of the wise.
We bow down again and again to that which resembles the Supreme Brahman. 160.
This neck is clearly a staff fashioned from crystal, marked with an excellent depression at the nape, fashioned for the depositing of Māra’s weapons;
and this line extending to the ears has skin as smooth as a flattened bamboo joint.
If, here, the suspension [of the limbs] shines like a bowstring by means of the portion that has passed away. || 161 ||
Even if she were to obtain a thousandfold necklace for her neck,
O Varalā, how could she ever remain constantly devoted to her own neck? Nor would she abandon the livelihood she has always cherished, which has arisen from her own mind.
She may become exhausted or not, depending on her union with the Holder of the Lotus. || 162 ||
Full of longing, even this sweet-voiced cuckoo bears a multitude of notes rising from its throat, faltering at every step as if to hear her voice like that of its own offspring;
the flute, fallen from its bamboo stem, laments its own stainless lineage.
It is the manifestation of Pārvatī as she leads [him], and it is the conquest by the sound of her throat-voice. || 163 ||
As if to traverse these lines on her throat, the supreme song— possessing three movements, swelling with a multitude of notes through the divisions of the scales (*grāma*),
and consisting of pairs of the six notes at each step— reaches its seventh station.
Sloping toward the left, those limbs here dance about in the center.
This pair of arms is joined; it is even a supreme yoke that takes up a second pair of arms here for the protection of age after age;
it is joined to bear the burden of the chariot; therefore, my mind is a yoke.
The chariot was held by supports and fastenings, and it was excellent, yet not like a burden for the arms when one's desires are fulfilled. || 165 ||

Having gained a handhold on my head through the skill of his arms, Love has risen and established himself there; though Spring is present here with all his limbs, the fire of separation always dwells within my mouth, assuming a physical form.
Has he gone out from here, or has he merely taken his station at the forehead? (166)
By embracing with her two arms, she reveals her own pair of arms; resorting to the art of crookedness and consumption, she protects me.
If not for these, how could my purpose—both for myself and for others—be accomplished?
There would be illumination due to the extreme attenuation of the quarters, as the movement is directed toward a single point. || 167 ||
A multitude of serpents, having taken up residence upon her arms to attain the state of moving through the air, even as they moved toward me, attained a supreme state;
and that lord of serpents constantly adorns me here for the sake of Caṇḍī.
Why indeed should one not obtain from this a crest-jewel set with gems? 168.
Not having found this slender arm even within the hollows of lotus stalks,
she remains as if hidden outside within the petals of a water-born flower, having abandoned her heat; with a heart perpetually agitated by the suspicion of mud, she is unable to emerge.
Even by those separated from their lovers who long for the embrace of their arms, separation has been experienced.

Have twenty arrows been born from my arms to conquer each of these three worlds and me— arrows that are like branches granting vast power— or have they arisen from the Vedas, endowed with manifold virtues? For, having emerged from them...
Therefore, the location of the joints here is clearly manifest, distinguished by its elegant arrangement.
How could the moon, though it possesses a mass of risen rays, not look upon these [trees] again with its full white beams?
That these trees have risen from their branches like widows is indeed appropriate here.
How indeed has the principle known as the "moon with its branches" not been proclaimed? || 171 ||
Having obtained these four hands, how could he who has arisen with sixteen digits not become one with twenty digits through the form of his hands?
And how is it that there are not four digits for each of the four [faces]?
Having obtained these four here in their entirety and perpetually with excellent hands. || 172 ||
The coral branch, like a child, is unable to weigh these kings with its hand; it trembles in fear upon the forefinger as if making a rustling sound.
Covering its face with dust, it seeks to atone for the sin committed during the weighing against the one who moves in the water.
Even as her eyes wither away in their final maturation, she attempts to wipe away the lotus.
For a moment it blossoms by itself, for a moment it buds; its lotus-like hands are formed by the emerging branches of its leaf-like shape,
and it is held firmly by the lotus-stalk-like arms with their dense, soft thorns.
The lotus-hand is an indescribable abode of Lakṣmī, ever variegated with beauty. || 174 ||
For arms whose power is renowned for protecting the three worlds, it is fitting here that they possess a multitude of fine bracelets along with armlets as an ornament; therefore,
even finger-rings are appropriate in this matter of essential beauty.
Otherwise, how could the art of governance attain expansion through its hands? (175)
In some places, he has excellent arms numbering two, six, eight, ten, four, twelve, fourteen, eight, or eighteen in form;
and in other places, he holds a bow, an arrow, a boon-granting gesture, the gesture of fearlessness, a lotus, and a sword and a shield.
We bow to some who bear a goad, a sword, and even the letter 'Ka' and others. || 176 ||

Does this pair of breasts see each other’s embrace of the arms, or does it look upward at the sun that has come within the range of its vision— since otherwise, the lotus bud would not lose its exquisite beauty in the presence of the moon?
Then does even the moon partake of this, perhaps with the intention of using it as an ointment? (177)
Having crossed the Valī and Sindhu rivers— the belly and the wind-filled cavity of the navel—
Smara, as if bringing it under his own control, placed that incomparable, natural boundary of the Vrinda forest, which is the very essence of great beauty, within the fortress of the heart.
On the ground, one should smell [the offering] with the face turned downwards; on the chest, the breasts of the cow-faced goddess. || 178 ||
This is truly some king of lotuses in the form of her breasts, closed into buds, bearing a crown of sapphire-like nipples, endowed with a thousand petals,
possessing the expansive beauty of a shimmering disc, and having taken refuge in supreme splendor— thus it has arisen.
Even within that, how much less could a thread possibly fall? || 179 ||
Just as the fruit of the *śrīphala* tree here is well-known for its power to cure diseases through the perfection of speech, why should the fruit of the Goddess’s breasts not likewise be fruitful?
For it is by means of tasting the supreme nectar flowing from them [that such results are attained].
The supreme perfection of speech shines forth, manifesting here and there for the accomplished ones.
Having seen below the gently swaying palm leaf ear-ornament, which has blossomed into radiant star-like flowers, she—
by means of her two breasts acting as two palmyra fruits— is like a *tāla* tree with its pair of breasts upon her chest.
Even when reached near the vicinity of Lake Nābhi, it was not fruitful. || 181 ||
These two golden caskets, with their gem-set nipples shimmering upon them, were fashioned by someone intimately familiar with the land of Nāḍindhama;
they have completely captured the entire excellence of the great wealth of saltiness belonging to the Lord of Love.
To bestow [this] upon one who possesses the enthusiasm for playful charm and honors the fragrant mantras. || 182 ||
Having beheld this pair of *kokas*, which brings some indescribable fresh beauty, my friend is deeply delighted and has raised his face;
even upon encountering the moon, which is as if closed like a bud with apprehension, he attains great joy.
Then, that which has flowed through the internal channel does not depart from its presence.
Did the playful Smara, wishing to cross the ocean of her loveliness which is the essence of incomparable beauty, take up her pair of jar-like breasts?
Or did he take up the string of pearls from the whirlpool of the circle of light upon her chest?
He placed it within his hand, extended toward the edge for the purpose of departing.
O Pārvatī, this has been declared as excellent by the wise: that because her chest was smeared with the juices produced from various minerals, these two breasts have come into being;
therefore, she is the celestial river here.
Lolling from beneath her throat, there shines a wave of white pearl necklaces.
As if unable to weigh these two with their own trunks, the clever elephants, while the Goddess looks on,
serve her son with their trunks out of a longing for the nectar flowing from her breasts.
Those whose jewels are concealed shine by means of their own white, radiant gems. || 186 ||
Heramba touches his two frontal globes with his own hand;
does he strike them together here again in order to perceive their equality?
He even soils his two frontal globes with dust; therefore, [he seeks] the essence of the breasts.
Does he drink these two again, which are as beautiful as the celestial river, as if to make them so?
What benefit has been returned here by this [left side] to that friend who, out of kindness, performed a service for the one with nectar-like luster (the moon) as his right hand?
For these two breasts are like the two *kokila* birds, friends of the sun, situated at the edge of the moon.
The two extremely pure ones did not undergo any separation whatsoever, even though they were distressed.
Just as the lotus arose from the navel of Viṣṇu in the external realm,
why did this pair of lotus-bosoms not likewise arise from his chest? These two beautiful faces are surely situated within these very breasts.
Marked with golden signs, they two manifest the portion of Śiva belonging to Svāyambhuva.
This merit is indeed milk, the form of supreme nectar, a perfected elixir (rasāyana) of renowned power and stainless purity;
having tasted which, Skanda performed a most virtuous deed against the host of the gods.
That prince, adhering to the principles of conduct, is still capable of leading [the world] even today. || 190 ||
This milk, the elixir that restores the dead to life, has been obtained by the fortunate Vighnarāja through the ripening of his great merits;
otherwise, how could he have had his body transformed by the mouth of the Lord of Elephants?
Carrying a stream as if it were personified, they drank [the enemy] through the discharge of their arrows, as if death itself had departed.
If one should obtain this breast-milk through merits, some rare wise person here, unacquainted with the taste of a mother's breast, might drink it;
yet in this world, one would never again find such a thing to relish with a natural fondness for its flavor.
Even as a child, he becomes a knower of the state of Śiva; he too is a seer. || 192 ||
With its beautiful navel-lake, charming with the confluence of the river of the three folds,
and possessing a waist-shore that is exceedingly slender, has the moon arrived here, having made his own abode— Virinchi’s body— distressed by the exquisite beauty of her breasts?
Having manifested the supreme nectar of milk, he revealed the full state to behold. || 193 ||
(p. 86) "These two breasts of mine are clearly for the delight of the inner apartments;
yet, O maid-servant, they serve as a bond to my return, since this golden splendor has attained a beauty that surpasses even the cry of the swans."
Are those two golden bells on her breasts actually two *kokā* birds? || 194 ||
Having reached this divine necklace upon her jar-like breasts, Madana—

though he is the conqueror of the universe and possesses the status of the best of immortals— became utterly helpless; likewise, by means of the single-stringed pearl necklace held in her hand, he fell under the power of Time.
Then, even though bodiless, Madhumitra—possessing wonderful passion—suddenly rose up. || 195 ||
Having fashioned within himself four subcontinents and even a quartet of oceans— appearing here as if measured by the folds of his navel—
the enemy of Mura shines forth; on the back of this [body] is this mass of hairs, which is infinite.
