The one with a dark and beautiful body sleeps happily upon seeing the strength of his own son.
Is the pool of nectar her navel, and the mass of hair from the peaks of her breasts a female serpent, filled with exquisite beauty due to the influence of the cold-rayed moon?
Has she descended upon the earth marked by the lines of her wandering gait?
Why do these bracelets appear as if they have shriveled and drawn close together? || 197 ||
These three folds at the pit of her navel are like irrigation channels for the vines of hair; why else would she always shine with the sound of her breasts,
as if to water her own garden?
Spring, with its blossoming body of limbs and flowers, exists for the sake of amorous delight. || 198 ||
Beholding the Triveṇī, even the ocean does not permit this waist, filled with folds, to rise above its shore within its domain;
and though the fire of the submarine flame here is eager for an embrace, [it remains constrained].
Just as the submarine fire (Aurva) remains awake, its internal movement obstructing the powerful outward flow.
Is the collection of the four oceans not desired as the navel,
since their four shores simultaneously form the inner circle of that navel?
Therefore, it is as if one [fire] alone were unable to burn their external waters.
Alas! The fire from the mouth of the submarine mare blazes within the interior of the belly.
When asked, "Is there no one who can equal you? and "Tell me, what is this back of yours?", she immediately turned her face toward herself;
or rather, was she standing like a clear crystal slab from the king of mountains?
He laughs again and again at Vraja, which is shimmering with waves of exquisite beauty. || 201 ||
This subtle altar could not indeed contain him once he had entered its interior, for the elements were overwhelmed by his splendor, as if due to a shimmering envy;
yet the lizard remained there unconfined, because from this [altar] she was able to measure him from here and there.
When one advances against an opponent who has descended into the *godhā* position, it is called the *rasākrānta* (overpowering by the foreleg) movement; this is a symmetrical step (*samapada*).
Was the four-faced Brahmā born [only] because he was of such a nature that his intellect, though keen, was unable to properly discern something of the subtle beauty residing within her womb?
And even he, the thousand-eyed Indra, lord of the immortals, remained incessantly gazing with fixed eyes.
I am three-eyed, yet by my good fortunes, my feet are like those of the graceful lion. || 203 ||

Has her girdle, adorned with various radiant jewels, been made to act like a drum to clearly display her abdomen on all sides, while being joined together by clamorous and sweet-sounding jingles? Or is it that [the girdle] has become invisible due to the tumultuous noise?
Is this a swing for the pleasure of King Madana’s play? || 204 ||

p. 88) Even a lion, wandering about and having somehow found joy within himself, once attempted to measure his own belly with his intellect; yet, having failed to find even a single internal sound, he was unable to exchange his very name for that of the excellent poets.
Indeed, he was appointed to the position of lord of beasts in brief. || 205 ||
This middle region of the visible world is somehow not clearly defined on all sides;

therefore, it is celebrated here and elsewhere by the name "middle" and so forth, yet it is but a fraction [of the whole]. Let this [world] remain submerged, for it is merely the outermost limit of the Supreme. Thus [ends] the girdle.
Bound by its qualities, it is placed near the three folds [of the belly], or else it resounds with a roar.
Does this girdle, bound here with many jewels, tirelessly recite the thousand names of the Lord of the Gods?
Therefore, this line of hair does not appear to be there, as if it were hiding its face out of shame.
If one mutters this mantra, why would it not instantly bring about my subjugation?
Having seen this line of hair upon her waist— which is ever-shining and situated between the darkness of her pubic region— did he, out of envy for the beauty of her eyes,
perhaps create his own two orbs below that very spot?
For this [consciousness] is not able to manifest its expansion there. || 208 ||
Beholding both her reflection-places— the pupils of her eyes— which possess the luster of her gaze,
and the expanse of beautiful grace fashioned upon the courtyard of her cheeks by her beauty, [the onlookers wonder]:
"Is this the reflection residing in the orb of her head that shines forth, or is it something else that has followed after?"
Shining forth, it itself pervades both hips as if they were two beautiful mirrors. 209.

On the path that is without support, having remained perpetually awake above due to his vow, did the Sun obtain those two hips for his own chariot? Otherwise, how could the Sun have reached the mountain slopes by means of his two wheels? (p. 89)
She attained a long and stainless state that transcended all parts and possessed a rightward gaze.
On her hips, which are so exceedingly broad, no girdle has been fashioned;
for what need is there for mountain ridges on this terrain of the river of folds rising from her waist,
since these clouds of deep luster always dance together here?
With their heads and horns held high, they move with graceful gait and possess beautiful manes.
These two hips of the one desiring to conquer Madana strove to make this mountainous terrain their own, as if they were two drums;
for before them, the pair of eyes are like two fish-marks upon the temples of two elephants.
Then the two breasts, the thighs, and thereafter the pair of "cow-mouths" (the knees) are spread out. || 212 ||
Are her two hips not like two reservoirs within the lotus-stalks of the folds at the lake of her navel— reservoirs where the Sarasvatī’s water,
flowing toward her pair of feet, has its taste made indistinct as she drinks it again and again?
It has arisen from the two paths of the thighs with the flower-branches of the nails. || 213 ||
Did Kandarpa, having fashioned two incomparable hips from the three wheels, bestow one upon his father and assign the other to the netherworld?
Surely it was Viṣṇu himself who established the abode of heaven and earth, while Smara took his place here.
Smara is Viṣṇu; the various Śrutis also proclaim the truth of the identity of the son and the Self. 214.
"O thighs, abandon this pride of being like plantain stalks; why then has this tree-like state been attained by you, with your soles sunk deep in the exceedingly cold [snow]?
Hearing this from afar, even with only a fraction of its name compared to yours, [the plantain tree]...
But that other sovereignty over the Suras was like a mere illusion compared to his lordship over the Yakṣas. || 215 ||
Does he repeatedly move his thighs here with the thought that these [thighs] are the trunks of lordly elephants, in order to weigh them against his own trunk?
Therefore, from the very beginning, he has always been renowned as a "vāraṇa" (an elephant).
Then, by means of the coiling process, he makes that transgression completely purified once again. || 216 ||
The plantain tree was born as a superior alternative to the thighs because it cannot attain their symmetry;
alas, even this [plantain] sheds its mass of fresh leaves. The hips, too, are adorned with beautiful ridges, surpassing even the knees by means of their circular form.
Beholding her, he did not notice that she was not wearing a pair of gem-encrusted bracelets.
Is this [thigh] a ladder established for the ascent to the supreme state of the gods of the limbs of the shanks? Is it therefore renowned here as "jaṅghālaka"?
From that, this Kandarpa, the eternal lord of passion, is the conqueror of the universe.
Neither the shanks nor the staff [are used] in the practice of maintaining excessive sexual pleasure. || 218 ||
Does this ankle not manifest four faces? Does the Veda not correctly state its nature as if it were existent, even though it is non-existent,
since it bestows upon the foot even a lotus in the capacity of a seat?
Therefore, in this emergence of speech, the gait is like that of a female swan above and below. || 219 ||
These ankles, though firmly planted, produce a deep and resonant sound from their anklets that is both subtle and formidable with its swelling volume; yet,
even so, they are somehow not perceived as a mere mixture of sounds.
And thus, their cleverness as "Jaṅghālaka" poets is not celebrated here. || 220 ||
Śatadhṛti (Brahmā) first placed these two feet upon his own head;
Govinda (Viṣṇu) massages them with his palms;
and Giriśa (Śiva), ever beholding death, conquers it and worships them.
Sadāśiva, moreover, is solely devoted to his own eternally restricted power.

How can these two feet be compared to a lotus? For the lotus has a uniform gait, while these have uneven steps; the lotus is fixed deep within the mud, while these are stained by passion; and the lotus is fit for the hovering of winged bees, whereas these are struck down by the confusion of worldly wandering.
This very devotion, pervaded by qualities, is cultivated through a portion of friendliness.
This vehicle is a swan; since those two [other birds] are not capable of following it, they therefore constantly resort to this [vehicle], assuming the state of being swans.
Having attained proper discipline here, one becomes happy through that state of mind.
Having attained renown, he resorts to the stainless state arising from his [spiritual] faction. || 223 ||
That which remains stable throughout the day, yet is devoid of softness and distance; that which possesses wakefulness, yet is not oily;
and that which is not obstructed by the body—this, if it occurs within one's own branches, is the very essence here.
In the coral, the quality of being coral was not surpassed for the purpose of following its path. || 224 ||

Is this a lotus rich in gold that has risen from Lake Mānasa, which has followed it even with its petals to reach it, yet now has its feet submerged? Or have these two surpassed even its golden luster, generating a lake of longing within my mind?
The two feet, having the appearance of trembling leaves, do not possess the state of holding a water-pot. || 225 ||
(92) These two [feet] are not merely the heels; they have undertaken to emulate the rows of nails and teeth by rivaling the eyes and hands.
Having reached the state of being the "heels" (pārṣṇī), they possess twelve kinds of digits (kalā) corresponding to those [other limbs] reaching the eyes.
Both of them beheld [him] from below, their upward gaze obstructed.
Do these two feet not themselves bear the entire kingdom as a hundred rays of light, under the guise of the lustration ceremony (*abhinīrājana*) for the rows of the quarters?
Therefore, those lords of the directions have their kings slain and their hands bound.
In this world, those summoned by their own sovereign power do not fail to bow down at every step.
Since these two lords of the quarters have followed closely at their heels with their toes, they have established a tenfold stationing upon the tips of the branches; thus,
by their own presence, they cause the petals to expand even without being trodden upon.
Or rather, these two [eyes] of yours are not at all as intensely reddish-brown as those of a young partridge.
With the tips of their nails, they extend the commands of the lords of the ten directions,
each according to its own seal, in both administrative appointments and sacred recollections;
surpassing the gods and having conquered the Lord of Kamala, their feet—
The foolish have attained that state, yet they are even more devoid of mental composure. || 229 ||
Worshipping his feet with water for the feet, he worships that supreme state which is his own; furthermore, by means of fragrances, he brings to an end the fragrance born of worldly existence.
He becomes priceless through offerings of honor in this world, and through flowers, he becomes the very essence of the wise.
Honored for his naturally benevolent mind, he won over the hearts of all.

Remembering again and again, with no other thought in my mind, I worship Him directly; performing [acts of service] again and again, I offer Him praise; being His Lord, I carry out His essential purpose again and again; and time and again I bow at the feet of the Master.
That balance which was taken by me for the sake of the class of fortunate beings, using only a single incomparable fraction of its parts— (231) p. 93)
Indeed, even for the sake of removing the fame [of someone] desired by some, there is no lack of compassion in this matter. 232.
Having somehow gathered her own limbs together from one side, she contemplates how to fashion another form that is inconceivable yet appropriate;
and having joined this [new form] with my own excellent features and those of others—
Through these verses, she attained joy and made herself fulfilled. || 233 ||
In some places dark, in others white, in some places with a reddish hue, elsewhere green, in some places yellow, and in other places possessing many natural colors;
in some places of gentle form, and in others most terrible— [I bow to] her of radiant splendor.
We constantly revere a certain Great Power (Mahāśakti) who is ever devoted [to Him]. || 234 ||
He who, by means of the power of the experience of supreme freedom inherent in himself, inevitably brought forth the renowned title "Sāhib Kaula" and established his seat—
[he] who [is like] a cluster of blisses possessing the excellence of the primordial state of Being-Consciousness (saccit).
When his creative play arose at the gateway of that [creation], devotion reached its fourth stage.
Thus ends the fourth devotion in the *Nāmavilāsa*, composed by the illustrious and preeminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Sāhibakaula. || 4 ||
This is the fifth hymn of devotion:
having attained her grace through devotion, I praise that Great Goddess repeatedly with my own divine forms, following those names numbered in the thousands. (1)
The Sarasvatī, whose domain is the world of Brahmā, effortlessly composes various philosophical systems;
she does so with the desire for her own vision to be seen, [a vision] which possesses the unity of the seer and the seen.
She alone, on the earth of Viṣṇu, is the supreme Vaiṣṇavī, adorned with garments and ornaments of various jewels;
known as Indirā by those who have realized the play of the Self, she deludes the foremost of the immortals and their enemies. || 3 ||
The celestial maiden, the protector of Indra and the other gods, is eternal and ancient;
she, the biḍālikā who causes fear to the bull-like Daityas, attained the status of Lakṣmī through Upendra.

Alas, even in the city of Uṣarbudha, some people worship that [image], whose form is practiced upon by the world’s pillars, as "Tajjanā," the cause for the satisfaction of the mouth of Devanātha, taking it to be their own taste. || 5 ||
Even Dharmarāja, honoring this [city] with self-restraints and disciplines, keeps it under control;
he, who has cast aside all fear and is free from every cause for dread, is not overcome by misconduct despite his great power.
The host of Rākṣasas, apprehensive of enmity from all the gods, constantly serves with worship the Sovereign of the three worlds, the protector of herself, who possesses noble grace.

(95) Though he is the leader of the blind and is himself subject to dullness, the Lord of Beings, known for his true essence, adorns Śivā—the Mistress of Flavors—with incomparable heaps of jewels, ever-new and refined. 8.
The one whose movement is ever-arising, riding upon his own lion-vehicle, drives that vital energy—the constant witness to the life of living beings—by means of his pure-scented vehicle. 9.

Even the Lord of Yakṣas, the sovereign of treasures, though he has attained the rank of King of Kings, propitiates the auspicious Śivā— who assumes forms subject to others— by offering inexhaustible wealth.

She is propitiated by those who have attained fulfillment through the various Nigamas, Āgamas, and Agamas— by those who are capable of subduing Death and Desire, even through the formidable sounds of the Tripura-Bhairava.
Constantly remembering that maiden who was the mother of Kumāra, does this six-faced one, assuming his own form as Kumāra and leading the host of the God of Gods, not indeed act like a child? (12)
Even the host of former gods, remembering her state as an object of no distinction,
made Kauśika— who revealed his desirable form— fall from his position, yet not Kauśika [the sage].

Ah! The yogins headed by Sanaka, whose minds regarding the world and its people have ceased to wander, behold that Samādhi within their own meditations as if it were right before them, even though they have transcended all ordinary states of concentration.

I bow to the Mistress of Mercury (Raseśvarī), by whose knowledge mortals here are capable of attaining even a portion of immortality through such acts as reviving the dead; she who has cast away the very conception of the Kali age. 15.
Having everywhere established their consciousness upon the feet of the beloved of the Lord of the Universe,
those who are honored by the entire world attained the state of being worshipped by all, bringing satisfaction to the universe, even as they became gods named Viśva.
Even the Vasus, though they themselves dwell in this place which is perfumed by Vāsava and by Vasu, and which is further perfumed by the luster of the jewels adorning their crests,
perfume the hearts of those who dwell here with their own garments, even though those hearts are otherwise devoid of fragrance.
(96) Having been brought into the midst of the village, she is sung of by celestial minstrels who have fainted with emotion and are singing in harmony,
using names that celebrate her most famous exploits and honoring her at every step.

They know her through that primordial supreme knowledge which is heart-pleasing, innate, irreproachable, and immediately manifest as the prose and verse of consciousness; thus, they are free from the experience of dullness and possess that [knowledge]. (19)

Following the instrumental music, and following the song as well— surpassing all with its unrestrained ocean of melody— the celestial dancers, having attained their proper gait, delight her by performing in the three tempos (layas).
He gratifies the beloved of Supreme Śambhu, who transcends all notions of the goal and its attainment;
he brings about the realization of the host of goals within his heart for the sake of the knowledge of the non-dual.

Skilled in acquainting himself with the host of Siddhas, he strives in his meditations to approach this Vidā, who accomplishes success, failure, and even that which transcends both, for the sake of the assembly of Siddhas.

The Sovereign Lady, resplendent with the King of Aesthetics (rasa), is incessantly gratified by the Apsarases—who are the very embodiments of aesthetic flavor—through their graceful dances and jests, and who are skilled in the expression of amorous gestures and emotions. 23.
Secret even from the secret domain, honored by the contemplation of its concealed nature through its specific attributes,
even the Guhyakas hide it within the deep cavernous hollow of the cave of the heart.

Like those who apply the Yakṣakardama ointment, the Yakṣas always protect this Kālī—the dark one who devours all time—within their hearts through constant remembrance, she who is the protector of all. 25.

He meditates here upon this Goddess, the sovereign power of the Lord of beings, who is the manifestation of the elements, who is both existence and non-existence, who pierces through the past, the future, and the present, and who is the splendor of the leader of all creatures.

The hosts of demons, though wandering about, somehow manage to worship her who is meditated upon within their own minds— she who threatens the world-demon of ignorance with awakening, and who fulfills the requests of those who supplicate her.

Though she is devoid of qualities, she is adorned by multitudes of qualities; though she transcends the lordship of the hosts of secondary attributes, the Gaṇas always enumerate her by names that are joined with the fame established by those intent on secondary attributes. (28)

Constantly contemplating her as the eternal one upon the path of the beautiful-browed goddess, though he himself was free from worldly flow, yet beholding this world as devoid of permanence, did not that Dhruva attain the state of the eternal? (29)

Even the seven sages, who have attained their desired abodes and whose desires are subdued by the pure and unyielding Sāma hymns, delight in union with her, who bestows her own desires upon those who seek them.
In both the restraint and the grace of the worlds, the planets— having assumed their ordained positions—
cause those whose bodies are the conscious self (cidātman) to grasp ever-new [truths] on the path of debate.
Śanaiścara slowly and gradually afflicts her with his gaze, which is impaired by subtle defects yet beautifully adorned,
and which perceives both this world and the world beyond.
The Teacher, who humbles the leaders of the gods by surpassing the ancient deities through his scriptures,
and who manifests great reverence toward his own teachers, praises that Guru who is the teacher of the three worlds.
May Maṅgala, whose auspiciousness has flowed forth, be worshipped here first among all auspicious things;
he worships her who is the source of all rising auspiciousness, she who is the auspiciousness of all auspiciousness, free from inauspiciousness, and the embodiment of all auspiciousness.
And Bhāskara, illuminating his own world, shines upon this auspicious goddess who has illuminated the entire triple world;
he worships her fervently with heaps of jewels shining upon his crown at her feet. 35.

The poet alone, whose intellect is devoted to supreme power and who possesses the singular artistry of poetic skill, effortlessly composes that [work] which displays mastery in donning the mantle of the Vedic path.
Being gentle by nature as well as in his qualities, he never perceives things like the planets [as being merely] auspicious or inauspicious;
for that reason, that wise man is truly "Budha" (the Wise), and as such, he fully devotes himself to the most gentle sovereignty of the Lord.
The moon, ceaselessly spreading its nectar-filled moonlight along every path, personally worships the Lord of noble grace with these very blossomed blue lotuses. (38)
Threatening both the sun of fierce rays and the moon of cool beams, and having discarded all other lords by his surpassing majesty,
even this celestial luminary, though fainting at its tail, causes that [celestial body] to appear as if it were pervaded by light here on earth.
The sage born from a jar (Agastya), who is exceedingly self-controlled, dwells steadily in the southern direction;
with a mind that is most subtle and capable of subduing the anger of Dakṣa, he constantly remembers the gift of awakening (bodha-dakṣiṇā).

The inhabitants of the atmosphere bow to that [cow] named Surabhi—the foremost of the world of Surabhi—by whom even those devoid of merit are made fragrant by her excellent qualities, which are abodes for the accumulation of meritorious deeds. (41)
Even the sky-dwellers, though possessing the speed of the wind, fan her— who surpasses their own inherent nature—
with the multitude of their wings as excellent whisks, imitating the conduct of the lords of the sky-dwellers.

And on earth, those wise men who pride themselves on their being and whose splendor is worthy of honor bow to her—who bestows various forms of joy—as each bows to his own chosen deity here and there. (43)

And those on the surface of the earth who know her to be the Sustainer of the World praise the Mistress of Men— the one whose domain is the remainder of Śeṣa— with various epithets, their eyes fixed in an unblinking gaze.

Thus, living beings whose devotion is intensely focused upon this Supreme Goddess worship her here with recitations, fire-oblations, and libations—beneficial rites extensively prescribed in many tantras. (45)

Having mastered this King of Hymns, which is distinct from all worldly characteristics, she—having clearly and swiftly composed it according to the lineage of the gurus—entered into me, having indeed attained great joy. (46)

From that time forth, I have attained a station superior even to that of the Lord—a state that is unsurpassed, patient, and impartial—by virtue of which, alas, I am now capable of creating, destroying, or otherwise altering this entire universe. (47)

Such am I: minute among those more minute, yet great; the teacher even of the most venerable elders; lighter than the lightest of breaths, yet the most stable among the most massive; the granter of all desired objects. (48)

(99) Adorned with mastery and sovereignty, skilled in bestowing the state that is to be attained, and perceiving everything as my own portion, this Bhava is the source of both existence and non-existence. 49.
Possessing the dharma of the waves of bliss of non-dual consciousness, and having a majesty free from waves, by means of this independent power which has blossomed and turned toward me,
I have fashioned this entire world of moving and unmoving beings.

Having manifested the bindu and having united it with the seed-syllable (bīja), these two [again] become, by means of the line (rekhā) known as the three cavities (puṭa), the letters, words, and sentences. 51.
Referring to that collection, I, Sudarśana, have well-remembered and composed those various philosophical systems (*darśanas*);
because they consist of the vision of that which is devoid of any visible object, they have been fashioned by me as the "Creation of Sound" (*śabdasarga*).
The Supreme Power first opened her eyes; from that [state] arose Sadāśiva through his own wisdom.
He attained the state of Īśvara with a threefold radiance, performing the three-fold task as manifested by his own power.

Though enveloped by Māyā—consisting of necessity (niyati), time (kāla), and attachment (rāga), and joined with its various powers (kalās)—as if by coverings (kañcukas), he has attained his supreme human nature through the qualities (guṇas) and through Vidyā. || 54 ||

This one is indeed renowned by the name "Jīva," performing internal activities through the mind, intellect, heart, and ego, as well as external activities through the ten sense organs characterized by sound and the other [objects]. (55)
From his qualities arose the manifestation of the five elements for the sake of cosmic power, and from them the world;
even the mines, with the earth as their crown, shine there separately by the will of the Lord.
That [creation] is fourteenfold, encompassed by fourteen distinct groups of worlds; thus the creation of objects, though illuminated, shines forth as a multitude of beings through my power. (57)
Relying upon her, I have thus fashioned this entire universe, so exceedingly profound;
I know her to be the auspicious cause of all, and I worship and chant while meditating upon her. (58)
(100) O Nandikeśvara, I praise this very Power, both supreme and non-supreme, who is the locus of my grace, by means of this hymn composed of a thousand names as requested. 59.
Having thus spoken and ceased, the lord Maheśvara, the teacher of all that moves and is stationary, remained silent;
then Nandikeśvara, the master of speech, bowed his head with palms joined in reverence and spoke again.
O God of gods, Supreme Lord, Śaṅkara, Protector of the world, Blessed One, homage be to you!
Be gracious toward me, who have reached the state of being your servant’s servant and who take refuge in you alone. 61.
I have never been honored by Brahmā, nor by Nṛhari, nor by Śiva, nor by anyone else at any time or in any place;
yet, thinking "my devotion and love are directed solely toward You," I venture to take refuge in You—thus do I begin this bold act.

May this be forgiven, and let this hymn, difficult even for the lords of the immortals to obtain, be uttered. Until today, I have not been worthy of it; nor does a prayer that has never before been fruitless deserve to be in vain.

Although my mind indeed desires to hear the wonderful secret, even though it is something that ought not to be told, it must nevertheless be spoken by those who take refuge in compassion out of their mercy for me. (64)
If they say that wealth is not a secret, then where indeed shall I go? Alas!
For as long as one is born, one should propitiate Śiva, for propitiation is the means to achieve supreme perfection.

Even if there is a rule that it is not fit to be played by the great lords who are the best of teachers, one should nevertheless practice it, for even that is the truth; otherwise, how could there be a definitive conclusion?
Having displayed such unsurpassed compassion and considering even my status as a servant,
as well as Your own lordship, O Lord, You ought to speak in praise of the powerful Master.
"Beholding this terrible form of yours, alas, this question is repeatedly asked regarding the supreme realm:
that such a thing is being done is indeed improper, for for the highest, victory is death on the field. (68)
Even before the constant remembrance of the Lord, my mind was yearning for that place;
but today, having heard of his great majesty, it blossoms forth even more intensely on every side.

(101) If that which has not even been heard by Kumāra, Gaṇeśa, and others, nor by the best of gods, is indeed proclaimed to me, then my devotion shall attain renown, and your compassion will be manifest. 70.
Not only do you show compassion toward me, but also toward your devotees;
for who would not praise this wonderful new king, considering that he has emerged from your own mouth? 71.
For even this all-pervading mind is experienced as having arisen here to attain renown;
since it has not been otherwise until today, why then is it not asked about today? (72)
Thus let all this be discerned, and let the unsurpassed Navarāja be proclaimed;
for even that which ought not to be given is bestowed by those whose wealth is compassion—how much more so upon one who serves at his feet? (73)
Thus, the Lord of Lords was delighted by his words, which were full of humility and established in right policy;
having discerned his fitness for the true scriptures, He said: "What is not easily obtained from one who has taken refuge in the True One?"
O Nandikeśvara, in the past you were the gatekeeper and beheld [Śiva] in secret;
that fruit has now ripened for you, namely, that your intellect is intent upon a specific matter.
Other people were not capable of requesting this excellent and most steadfast hymn of praise;
nor has it been requested by anyone else, even by me, who am well-acquainted with the conventions of the occasion.
But you alone, having no other refuge and having abandoned all mental constructs, have become a vessel for me through your ever-increasing devotion throughout your births; this has been heard by me.

Long ago, I was greatly gratified by your asceticism and your abundant merit accumulated over divine years; for the fruit of that is now in your hands, since you have constantly stood at my door, even in secret.
For what other supreme deity strives for that state which is eternally established in you? O Śivā, who does not exert themselves for their own sake? Whose mental discipline attains perfection? (79)
This fruit of your abiding in that state has indeed become manifest, since you have engaged in inquiry;
for even here, at some auspicious moment, there is a regard for my speech as if from one whose mind is reeling.

(102) It is true that you, my beloved, are constant in every way; for, having been questioned by me, you have praised the Supreme Lord—who is most excellent—even though he is your own supreme secret, treating him as if he were something external. 81.
Until today, you have been non-existent in the external world, having authority for me only in private;
but today, having heard the words of one of great majesty, you are, oh, some indescribable being even within my innermost self! 82.

Since this hymn has been expounded by me with extreme clarity, how could it not attain renown? For who would not praise that which is called "the True" (Sat), which is the very meter employed here and which bestows benefit upon all? 83.
O Nandikeśvara, listen thus to this wonderful king of hymns as it has arisen;
having heard it, you must propagate it among those seeking my grace in such a way that they may truly understand me as I have been understood by you.
This king of hymns, unsurpassed and ever higher, which grants all desires through its thousand names—
this must be remembered, this must be recited, this must be read aloud, and this must be offered in sacrifice.
Through meditation, recitation, chanting, fire-offerings, and libations, that multitude of accomplishments is not far for him—
even for one who has entered the supreme path of Durgā-yoga, where even the attainment of supernatural powers remains uncertain.
When even an ordinary person, whose mind is intent on departure and who disregards all other conversation, regards his own Lord as the foremost,
how insignificant indeed must this entire mass of enjoyments appear to him?

But that which, having departed from here, never returns and is no longer present here, consisting of which that very opening of liberation—abounding in great joy—would become dependent on the power of meditation and the like; [that is the Self]. (88)
Having performed the threefold purification and the installation, and having uttered the supreme *jīva-ghoṣa*,
one who is mindful and adorned by the unity of the *nyāsa* should recite this with conviction at the three times of day, or in the morning.
This hymn has reached the ears through the Vedas; it is the very form to be remembered by the Smṛtis, the primary object of all perspectives, and the singular light of all lights.
It is the ultimate goal of all literatures and the supreme extraction of the primordial power.
Who would not bow down again and again to that which is the very essence of all that is essential? 90.

p. 103) He who establishes his seat in the renowned position known as Sāhib Kaula—a state that necessarily arises through the power of experiencing the supreme autonomy of one's own self—in that poetic work of his, which is composed and gathered from the playful manifestations preceded by Śiva and Śakti; [in that work...]
The fifth stage of devotion, named Vilāsa, marked by the sign of power (śakti), has been attained. || 91 ||
Thus ends the fifth devotion in the *Nāmavilāsa*, composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Sāhib Kaulānandanātha. || 5 ||

The sixth [element] is devotion toward this Lord of Praise; the sage is "I," the cause for the reflection upon the ego-sense (ahaṃtā); the meter is Anuṣṭubh; that which is called the narrative is the non-narrative; and the deity is the primordial Śakti.

When various accomplishments are to be achieved, the application [of the mantra] is established as fourfold: in the state of manhood, or in the acts of recollection, muttering, burnt offerings, study, and libations. || 1 ||

Those names of the Goddess of gods which Śambhu previously and clearly set forth by way of enumeration—Sāhib Kaula, brought entirely under the sway of devotion, has composed them in verses that reveal their meaning. (2)
In this [work], the one named Viṣṇumāyā and Siddhasarasvatī are also described; here, by way of synonym and also in the genitive case, she is designated as Taruṇī. (3)
In various places, other names and forms concealed by different appellations have been described; these are not to be censured, as they were intended merely for the purpose of illustration.
Though devoid of appearance from the very beginning, he who causes the manifestation of "I" and joins his own being— as if it were something stained— with various marks of self-doubt,
is that same wondrous one who, through wisdom, again turns back toward himself.
He remembers one thing immediately; and this very Self of Consciousness is victorious! || 5 ||

(105) That which, though beyond thought, appears as the very nature of the manifestation of the conceptualization of objects of thought; which, though one alone, is heard of under various names in manifold systems;
which is all-pervasive in the process of birth and so forth, stainless, and independent of any other self—she is the Supreme (Parā).
May this very consciousness, possessing the splendor of indivisible bliss, shine forth by its own radiance.
It awakens the self-nature that is supremely peerless and infinite,
and it immediately effects the removal of the anxiety of death;
it relishes the king of essences (rasarāja), which is completely full in every respect.
Such is my thought, and this is indeed the play of those named Śakti.

He is the erotic hero (śṛṅgārī) when smiling within his own mind; compassionate toward his devotees in the ways of the world; the heroic (vīra) in the destruction of egoism; the furious (raudra) in the wandering of the mental activities;
the cause of fear in the impure, intent on loathing; and the marvelous (adbhuta) in the play of universal unity.
Victorious is Sāhib Kaula Raseśvara, radiant with the nature of peace. || 8 ||

I bow to that Supreme Mistress of Knowledge, who possesses the realization of the unobscured state of being, who is sought after by the wise for her manifold desires, and who is a fresh row of aesthetic flavors.
The Great Vidyā. || 1 ||
That Supreme One, whose nature is consciousness and whose internal power has manifested, desiring "May I become many," subsequently expands this world— which is equal to herself— diverse,
beginning with the pure path (śuddhādhvan), and providing rest for the intellect through its non-duality.
May the Great Vidyā, which is beginningless and bestows pure bliss, grant [that] state. || 10 ||
The Mother of the World. || 2 ||

Having manifested the world— which is beyond all description— from her own luminous nature through the invocation of that which possesses a fixed form, she who is pure and repeatedly brings forth this manifold universe has, in an instant, brought me here as one who praises her.
May the Blessed Mother protect the world from the heavy downfall of the universe.
Mahālakṣmī. || 3 ||
May she, by whose taking refuge as a monk even the Lord of the Daityas becomes the husband of a husband,
eternally bring about total destitution for him who dwells in my heart.
May that Mahālakṣmī, who brings forth lovely fruits, deliver us from the flood of misfortune.
Beloved of Śiva. || 4 ||
When he realizes that day and night are but a fleeting moment and that this very world is full of calamities, he gives his abundant wealth to others and,
being himself fully content, dwells in the utterly empty cremation ground and rejoices supremely in Śiva.
When meditated upon as beloved, may she grant the glory of innate, natural devotion. || 13 ||
The illusory power of Viṣṇu. || 5 ||

Alas, having manifested through the power of his own innate and independent nature which expands everywhere, even he— Viṣṇu himself, who is the Self by whom this world has taken its course— maintains delusion, consisting of the pervasive and measured confusion of the subject-object duality.
May that Māyā of Viṣṇu, who is the supreme delight, protect me from calamity.
Auspicious. || 6 ||

From that light which is free from sorrow, which is easily accessible through the descent of compassion for others despite being difficult to contemplate, and which belongs to those of celebrated and expansive super-mundane intellect— [a light] which brings about auspiciousness even within existence, a state that is inherently difficult to beautify and characterized by the power of delusion.
May that auspicious one, who has dispelled the impurities of the Kali age, bestow well-being. || 15 ||
Peaceful. || 7 ||
When the horse of the mind, utterly difficult to pacify and ever-conquered,
relies upon him, those virtuous ones abandon this delusion;
for by his own compassion, he brings the wicked one— who has given rise to every impurity— to cessation.
He has bestowed upon himself a constant, immeasurable, and equal state of tranquil stability.
It is established. || 8 ||
The conscious self (cidātman) brings about accomplishment through the unity of manifestation;

it is not unestablished in itself. How, then, could that which is inert (jaḍa)—wherein [consciousness] is entirely bound by conceptual constructions (vikalpa), yet remains somehow unbound—ever achieve such a state?
May she, who is renowned and perfected, bestow unsurpassed, complete success. || 17 ||
Siddhasarasvatī || 9 ||
That which is the alms of instruction from the mouth of the Guru, and even the scripture [obtained] without [formal] discipleship,
that flood of bliss (Ānandalaharī) has been eternally proclaimed here by the perfected ones (Siddhas) who know it.
May Mother Sarasvatī, who is made most delicious by those who know the essence of flavors, grant me aesthetic delight.
Forgiveness. 10.

When there is suffering from an object of perception, it does not always arise from wicked people who are like serpents; and for those whose minds are struck by delusion, rivalry remains firmly bound.
But for the virtuous, the light of perfect awakening shines clearly within the sky of their hearts.
May that patience, which encompasses the assembly of living beings, protect me according to my desire.
Radiance. || 11 ||
Though bodiless, the God of Love—

desiring union with the weak-bodied Rati, whose great weapons were countered by flowers, and who was devoted to her— reduced even Śiva, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, to agitation by means of his sixfold stratagems during the season of flowers.
May that splendor bestow its own radiance, which is the object of the world's infatuation. || 20 ||
Radiance || 12 ||
When even from a slight glimmer of light, at every step, a living being suddenly utters "Alas! Alas! regardless of the circumstances;
and by which [darkness], when released, nothing whatsoever possesses beauty—this is appropriate.
May that radiance, out of curiosity, illuminate some peerless beauty.
Moonlight. || 13 ||
May that [Buddha] be our protection— he who, even as a mere moon, gladdens the entire world when risen, and from whom people, casting off the heat of calamity, take refuge in cool bliss;
he who possesses a form transcending all forms.
O Bhava, may your full moonlight prevail in the battle against darkness that causes miserable rebirths.
Pārvatī || 14 ||
Having been insulted by Dakṣa in his presence at an inappropriate time,
she descended with a cry of distress into the dwelling of the best of mountains; there,
she brought that lineage to infinite renown through her excellent conduct.
May she bestow her compassion upon Pārvatī, making the attainment of good fortune fruitful. || 23 ||
Sarvamaṅgalā || 15 ||

May that Bhavānī, who is all-auspicious (Sarvamaṅgalā), be victorious—she through whose meditation, arising from radiant splendor, there comes the supreme blessing for attaining the state of the virtuous everywhere. 24.
Hiṅgulā || 16 ||
Seated upon the six mountain ranges, she is inaccessible to the wicked yet desirable to those who know the singular essence of auspicious power and wealth;
with her beautiful limbs, she has indeed rendered her own station free from attachment— such is she, it is said.
May that young girl, who is most intent on the destruction of Time, protect me. || 25 ||
And Caṇḍikā. || 17 ||

At that moment of battle, the slaughter of the enemies of the gods was as if strewn with blossoming flowers— the shimmering stars— scattered from the sky as it was shattered by the staff-like arms of the dancing [demons], while the hosts of excellent gods were distressed by the serpents. And she...
And Caṇḍikā, the fierce one, shall lead [us] from misfortune to fortune, and from difficult paths to secure paths.
The Tamed One. || 18 ||

Overcome by compassion, he becomes self-controlled; from the utterly repulsive enjoyment of worldly existence— which consists of the essence of others' deceptive guiles and is exceedingly difficult to abandon— may he extend his mind toward the supreme abode.
Having attained perfect rest, she has destroyed the veil of artificial joy through self-mastery. || 27 ||
Padmā || 19 ||
She who, through the ripening of her own merits, created the stainless lotus;
who, out of fear of the ascetic, does not resort to its primordial instability;
she who is the world’s indicator, the one to be praised, whose beauty is supreme tranquility—she is born from the heart-lotus.
May that lotus-foot of Padmā, praised by the mouth of the Lotus-born (Brahmā), grant [our] success. || 28 ||
Lakṣmī. || 20 ||
May that ever-new [speech], which people consider to be the ripening of the multitude of virtues even when conversing with men who possess faults— provided they are bowed in humility—
constantly create a pure and blissful prosperity.
Supreme prosperity, with a languid gait as her heavy breasts are adorned by pearl necklaces. || 29 ||
Beloved of Hari. || 21 ||
Even though they performed ritual acts, those who have not conquered their minds and attained the beneficial have indeed not been beheld by the compassionate side-long glances of the beloved of Hari.
Tripurā || 22 ||
When, meditating on Śivā as Tripurā, I am reeling with bliss, I realize the state of being Tripureśvara; that [state] is not distinct from intoxication.
Nandinī || 23 ||
Or she laughs, gladdened by the beautiful Indirā obtained through her compassion, like Purandara;
she who increases the unity proclaimed as "Nandinī" in heaven, whose abode was not built with many hardships.
Nandā || 24 ||

With his heart sprinkled by the nectar of devotion to Nandā, he has severed the cycle of rebirth; such a person does not perceive even the vast joy found in dwelling in the Nandana garden as being great. || 33 ||
Sunandā || 25 ||
"Distressed by this body, which begins with youth and perishes in an instant, I have become a being free from fever, having greeted you as 'O Sunanda' (O Good Joy). (34)
Worshipped by the gods. || 26 ||

Having taken away the *surā* (liquor) and having conquered the *asuras*, you who resound with the melody of the five-stringed lute (*vipañcī*) and bring joy to the gods— you are indeed that one who is worshipped by the gods.
The science of sacrifice. || 27 ||

Meditating upon that knowledge of sacrifice, a certain person, possessing the merit of great skill, offers the oblations of the senses into the fire of consciousness through the sacrifice of the vital breaths and other such rites. (36)
Mahāmāyā || 28 ||
Even though she is one, presiding over [the universe] as a witness through the play of her threefold sovereignty, she fashions creation and the other cosmic processes; she is celebrated as Mahāmāyā.
The Mother of the Vedas. || 29 ||
Victorious is she, the Mother of the Vedas, who, being praised by Nirveda, was pleased and bestowed upon Brahmā the Veda whose source is the syllable Oṃ.
Nectar. || 30 ||
O wise ones, let that nectar—the taste of the realization of the Supreme Brahman—be tasted by you with devotion, for the gods consider even an obstacle to be such a taste. (39)
p. 112) Fortitude || 31 ||
Even due to delusion, exhaustion, or passion, the intellect of the wise does not abandon its own inherent quality;
how then can steadfastness be attained by the fickle? (40)
By her, some indescribable affection—which has attained supreme renown—was joined with the lotus, the sun, and others, even though their relationship as kin was never possible. (41)
Fame || 33 ||
And that which has been made known by those who have proclaimed it cannot be denied individually;
for where is that manifestation, established by its own inherent nature, not evident? (42)
It is well-known. || 34 ||
Though they manifest individually in the various directions and other realms for their own divine play, may they— famous here by their singular own form— grant us spiritual perfection.
Mṛḍānī || 35 ||
Since even he who is fierce and terrible has attained supreme renown everywhere by her name as "Mṛḍa," that is surely due to the weight of his association with Mṛḍānī.
Vindhyavāsinī || 36 ||
Mounted upon an elephant, you who are beautiful with the bliss of your own unfailing sovereignty, O dweller of the Vindhya mountains, sever that which is unyielding and most difficult to bind! 45.
The perfected vidyā. || 37 ||

Victorious is that Supreme Goddess, who, though devoid of internal color and external grasping, is the cause of the manifestation of the universe's manifold variety, even as she is the perfected Vidyā. 46.
The Great Power (Mahāśakti). || 38 ||
How could this—which is without foundation, without material cause, and unreal—be made to appear as if it were real, were it not for Paśupati, who is endowed with great power? (47)
The Earth || 39 ||
Even among seeds, that which does not unite even a single seed with another within itself—oh, it is you who are celebrated in the world as this Earth! (48)
Served by Nārada. || 40 ||
Having become renowned for truthfulness as the cause of the Kali age,
you are that very daughter of Brahmā who was served with devotion by Nārada.
The beloved of Puruhūta. || 41 ||
By whom can the compassion of the beloved of Indra be described, since out of love for her devotees, Viṣṇu even assumed the state of Upendra? (50)
The beloved. || 42 ||

May that auspicious Goddess, whom no person can look upon with a mind directed elsewhere even for a moment, grant the destruction of all evil deeds and remain forever as a beloved to the virtuous whose hearts are ever tranquil in every way. (51)
The passionate woman. || 43 ||

This night-like woman spreads a darkness that obscures the perception of the Supreme Self, as if by her very appearance; yet, when she is perceived by the wise, the terrible fault of Death is here pacified. 52.
The lotus-eyed one. || 44 ||
"Is she defiled by a particular outburst of anger, or is she overcome by the intoxication of her own good fortune?
May that lotus-eyed woman protect you, as she was thus observed by Hara within his own eyes, filled with doubt.
p. 114) Prahlādinī || 45 ||

For the wise, even sovereignty must be renounced, and the fitness for divine service—though it may seem obstructed—is indeed Yoga; since without devotion to Him, a person suffers as if from disease, may this [devotion], which brings joy, delight the heart. 54.
The Great Mother. 46.
O venerable one, whose greatness is renowned throughout the three worlds as that of the three gods born from her own portions and qualities—who would not revere her as the Great Mother? (55)
Durgā || 47 ||

May that Durgā be the bestower of victory upon me among her devotees— she who, though possessing but a single power, led the young swan-like [Śiva] to the difficult-to-attain union with Yama, whose name has transcended its literal meaning.
The destroyer of miserable rebirths. || 48 ||
Your intellect is equal to forbearance and possesses growth, by which it never fails to attain success;
you are that very Durgatināśinī (Destroyer of Misfortune), who, merely when meditated upon, removes that misfortune in an instant.
Jvālāmukhī || 49 ||
Whether she has arisen from above, from all sides, or indeed from below— her form being impossible to determine—
may Jvālāmukhī, who blazes forth incessantly, grant us the most excellent prosperity.
Of noble lineage. || 50 ||

May she who, when merely recited, bestows her own state free from anxiety—which cannot be attained even by performing penance for infinite eons—and who possesses the hue of molten gold, grant prosperity to the composer of this hymn; may she be of noble lineage. 59.
Light. || 51 ||

"Is the sky itself ablaze, or has the pure flame attained the state of a lotus?"—thus do the astonished gaze upon her with wonder. May she, who is light in every respect, be for our prosperity here. (60)
She who smiles with white water-lilies. || 52 ||
Hara was once filled with doubt as to whether that full moon upon his head was indeed the moon;
because of her smile, he placed his hand there—you, who possess the smile of a white water-lily, are she.
Difficult to traverse. || 53 ||
Even without water and such, this place is difficult to traverse; it is most difficult to pass for the multitudes of the foremost of the wicked.
O Durgā, you who are hard to attain, remove the suffering of coming and going in this world of miserable existence born of evil deeds. 62.
It is difficult to obtain. || 54 ||

O Pārvatī, you who are all-encompassing, present everywhere, the source of all, and always to be contemplated by everyone; yet, possessing a form never before seen and having destroyed all prior states of being—how is it, wondrously, that you are difficult to attain? 63.
Knowledge. || 55 ||
Seeing him, how could they all not become like cakora birds with gaping mouths?
For his primordial, gracious knowledge is indeed one whose mind is greedy to taste the nectar of his speech. 64.
The path to heaven. || 56 ||
May she who, with a mental state agitated by greed, abandons this human body so difficult to obtain in order to attain heaven—may she become our refuge. 65.
A resident of the city. || 57 ||

In ancient times, for the sake of protecting the cities, she divided herself into as many distinct forms as there were cities; because she was the supreme presiding deity (adhidaivata) of each, she became renowned as Puravāsinī.
She whose form is beyond description, who is perfected through the nature of all letters, who possesses a golden complexion, who has assumed many colors;
she whose praises are dear to all, who is the supreme primordial sound, Aparṇā, who holds a leaf in her hand—she is victorious!
The illusion of Śambara. || 59 ||
May that indescribable, absolute Śāmbarī Māyā of Śiva be victorious—she who spreads a web of illusions within non-duality, and therein [creates] duality as well. 68.

How can those ignorant of the world ever know that wine which, when merely thought of, spreads here for the wise a mind that is unattached, beautiful with intense bliss, and transcendent of the mundane?
It is possible for those afflicted by grief to resort to it fully. || 69 ||
She smiles gently. || 61 ||
"May this devotee not fall from his meditation because of my loud laughter"—knowing this with such compassion, that goddess smiled gently. (70)
Kulavāgīśvarī || 62 ||
Because she quickly uplifts the lineage of devotees who are distressed by wandering here and there,
she is known as Kulavāgīśvarī.
Eternal. || 63 ||
For it is well-established that an effect indeed conforms to the qualities of its cause;
yet this [notion] is not true, since even though she is eternal, she extends this [world] which is impermanent. (p. 117)
His majesty is the singular abode of all wonders; his luster is like that of the moon.
Nityaklinnā || 64 ||
A seed, when moistened by the flood of water from clouds, eventually attains the state of blossoming through its own sprouts and so forth;
but how does this [consciousness], which is eternal, suddenly emerge as something eternal?
If the Blessed Lady, the sole mother of the world, were not moistened [with compassion]. || 73 ||
She has a slender waist. || 65 ||
O Goddess Śivā, if you had always been the destroyer of saṃsāra, then how could you, whose hopes were fulfilled by the virtuous, have been renowned as "Kṛśodarī" (the slender-waisted one)? || 74 ||
Kāmeśvarī || 66 ||

O Goddess, how is it that you, the Mistress of Desire, do not in an instant make that very person free from desire within, once that devotee has been sprinkled by you with a shower of the nectar-stream of the realization of the Supreme Self? 75.

The goddess, whose natural splendor rivals ten million suns and moons, once appeared with all her limbs turned blue; was she perhaps distressed by the blue-throated Lord, or did her body simply take on that hue? (76)
Bhīruṇḍā. || 68 ||

Beholding from afar her fierce staff, even the Daityas within the cosmic egg were unable to remain due to fear; may that Bhīruṇḍā, radiant with cruel stars and holding a severed head in her hand, protect us.
Vahnivāsinī || 69 ||
May she who dwells in fire— being praised by her devotees with devotion as she directly partakes of the oblation offered with love— make our minds free from latent desires.
Lambodarī || 70 ||
That which is reflected from within, like an image in a mirror, does not abandon its dwelling place;
may she, renowned as Lambodarī, be the support for us in this abyss of saṃsāra. (79)
Mahākālī || 71 ||
Seeing Giriśa, whose body is stainless, deluded and afflicted by passion, thinking it was night while his eyes were closed, the celestial river—
her foam appearing like laughter— becomes as if smiling at the suffering born of your glance.
May Mahākālī, out of compassion, remove the darkness of those who worship her. || 80 ||
Vidyāvidyeśvarī || 72 ||
Since knowledge and ignorance have never been equal anywhere at any time, does that one Sovereign Lady of Knowledge and Ignorance not cause wonder? (81)
The Sovereign of Men. || 73 ||
Having realized that among men and women there is no destruction, and that the state of being is omnipresent and independent,
may the Sovereign Lady, who always bestows happiness, manifest that path of the Self everywhere.
Truth || 74 ||

Since it is through superimposition upon her that the unreal cycle of existence appears as if real, who would not consider themselves to have accomplished their life's purpose by joyfully meditating upon her as the Reality? (83)
The increaser of all good fortune. || 75 ||
Having obtained good fortune through devotion to her, Kāma removes this very desire;
she alone is that Goddess who increases all prosperity. (84)
Saṃkarṣaṇī || 76 ||

Who among the wise would not obtain supreme joy in the hereafter from Saṃkarṣiṇī, who draws the bird of the mind intoxicated by passion far away through her wickedness, and who rains down a supreme stream consisting of the nectar of immortality within the hearts of the virtuous?
Thus, by studying this [work], which destroys committed sins and uproots delusion, [one attains the goal]. || 85 ||
Nārasiṃhī || 77 ||
Hari, out of compassion for that Supreme Goddess— who is such that what has been, never was, nor will ever be anywhere, even now— manifested her form;
having slain the chief of the Daityas, he made his own devotee fulfill the weight of his complete vow.
And that auspicious Nārasiṃhī utterly conquers even Prahlāda. 86.
Vaiṣṇavī. || 78 ||
How could he, though beautiful in the form of a dwarf, attain the state of Viṣṇu, unless that Vaiṣṇavī power, both supreme and non-supreme, were indeed pleased? 87.
Mahodarī || 79 ||
If it is true that the goddess Mahodarī is always to be served by the gods, then why does she display this wonderful and diverse spectacle outside? (88)
Kātyāyanī || 80 ||
Sovereignty and the Lord have clearly manifested in manifold ways;
may that Kātyāyanī, who is the eternal goal attained by reaching whom alone, remain forever eternal. 89.
Campā || 81 ||
May they eternally destroy the trembling born of the excess of delusion within worldly existence, and may they reveal the well-composed *campū* to the virtuous. (90)
She brings about all forms of prosperity. || 82 ||
Since she reveals that all other forms of prosperity are trivial, she alone, when meditated upon, is therefore proclaimed as the bringer of all success. (91)
Nārāyaṇī || 83 ||

That girl, who dwelt alone at Badaryāśrama and was exceedingly frail, became renowned throughout the three worlds through her devotion as "Nārāyaṇī"—she who is indeed difficult to measure because she cried out, "Nārāyaṇa! || 92 ||
The great sleep. || 84 ||
No one is able to abandon those conceptual constructions that are as treacherous as evil states of being; yet they surely reach a state of quiescence for even a moment,
by relying upon which there is a constant disregard for both artificial and natural joys.
May Mahānidrā dispel calamity and the state of difficult passage. || 93 ||
Yoganidrā || 85 ||

O Yogic Sleep, just as one who has fallen asleep immediately recovers from the fainting fit caused by the blow of opposing states, so too, having regained your own clarity, bestow upon me the heart-pleasing accomplishment in my own yoga. 94.
Prabhāvatī || 86 ||

May that light, which is without beginning and stands before the host of stars, which does not enter into conjunction with them even during the day, and which is not surpassed by anything else— may she, possessing such splendor, grant her own radiance.
The Perfection of Wisdom || 87 ||
She who, through the play of her own manifestation, renders even the senses as firm as mountains—
capable of both knowing and acting— even the lords such as Hari, Hara, and Brahmā, though they are omniscient,
fall silent in an instant when deprived of her grace.
May the Perfection of Wisdom be for the sake of the complete accomplishment of wisdom for the virtuous. 96.
Wisdom. || 88 ||
He, whose conduct is irresistible, sports with kings who are renowned for their magnanimity and valor and are handsome in form;
he, the possessor of merit, treats them like a ball, while this virtuous woman, his wisdom, maintains her steady composure within him.
Tārā || 89 ||
Even though they remained awake throughout the nights without any support,
they somehow attained a semblance of equality with her name alone.
May Tārā, who protects from fear, be my refuge in times of danger. 98.
Madhumatī || 90 ||
"Does this Soma flow from above, or from all sides, or perhaps from below?"— thus they cried;
yet it could not be discerned even by those best of heroes.
May she who protects me from misfortune be full of sweetness for me. || 99 ||
Madhu || 91 ||

May that sweet speech of the devotee be victorious here—it which, as soon as it is heard, triumphs over the honey-like sweetness [of other things] and renders the mind motionless and bound by sorrow, even for the wise, like a moth. 100.
She who takes the nectar from the ocean of milk. || 92 ||

May those who consume the nectar from the milk ocean, whose form is Viṣṇu, and who are the cause of the destruction of old age and death and the removal of the wicked delusion of the Asuras, be my protection. 101.
Kālikā || 93 ||
Even the five [faces] beginning with Brahmā are seemingly unable to behold it, for they flow only from below toward that great lion-throne enriched by Mahākāla;
and even a devotee of that [throne], having abandoned all blackness, attains a wondrous identity with it.
May that Kālikā, through meditation alone, grant immeasurable strength eternally.
She who has a lion as her vehicle. || 94 ||
Having once beheld her own husband, who was fickle and fearful of falling, taking refuge with a bull,
she— whose nature is beyond names— was overcome with compassion.
How much more so, O lady riding upon a lion, have you become on this path? || 103 ||
Oṃkārā || 95 ||

From whatever measures [of sound] this fourfold Veda arises—the sole cause of knowledge and action for the sake of that which is difficult to cross—may this *Oṃkāra*, which eternally resonates within here, grant the sovereignty of the yogis. 104.
The form of the earth. || 96 ||
In the *mūlādhāra* resides the Supreme Goddess, whose form is the Earth;
I worship her, the Sovereign of the Gods of gods, the independent Mother of Mantras. (105)
Volition || 97 ||
Although the wise, due to the power of obscurations, always remain intent on various doctrines and do not know their own independence regarding that which constitutes their very self,
nevertheless, that [nature] which is ever-present is never at all concealed by them.
May that consciousness, which is the awareness of its own nature, remove all duality.
Having the appearance of one who is angry. || 98 ||
Although she is always of a gentle nature, I know that she herself has assumed an angry appearance toward those wicked ones who cause distress to her devotees. (107)
She who bears the half-moon drop. || 99 ||
Aha! Even though this [ocean] is born from but a single portion, it is renowned for its vastness; by what wise person could she, who bears half a drop, ever be measured? 108.
The stream. || 100 ||
May this stream of power (dhārā-śakti), which is itself supportless yet the support of all,
become the cause for the extraction of the essence from this shoreless and boundless saṃsāra.
Śrī Kṛṣṇakaula, whose glory consists in the experience of his own self as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, begot a son, Sāhibkaula,
whose mother was the virtuous Buddhi-prabuddhi;
in that [son's] poem titled *Kuladevatā*, there is this hymn to the venerable Śārikā.
In the measurement for the extraction of the mantra, one's own innate nature attained the state of aesthetic flavor (rasa) through devotion. || 110 ||
Thus ends the sixth devotion in the *Nāmavilāsa*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Sāhib Kaulānandanātha. 6.
The seventh devotion is Viśvamātā. || 101 ||
May the Mother of the Universe—who creates the world without depending on the depositing of any other seed, and who shines by herself—shine forth in the hearts of the virtuous. (1)
Kalāvatī. || 102 ||
Measuring the triple goddess with her own part,
and the three worlds along with their constituent parts by means of that part; and all the divisions of space and time therein—
The course of time has been grasped by us, who possess all arts. || 2 ||
Padmāvatī || 103 ||

May that Padmāvatī, whose further shore could not be reached even by the Lord of the Lotus (Viṣṇu), the Lotus-born (Brahmā), the Sun (the friend of the lotus), or the bees who gather the pollen of her lotuses— may she abide within my heart-lotus.
Well-dressed. || 104 ||

Worshipped here and in the hereafter with garments of the quarters, yellow robes, and the like, she is without a vessel; O she who is well-clad, take away from my body and clothing the sense of selfhood.
Awakened. || 105 ||

May that awakened consciousness, which—having been awakened by the instruction of the true guru—reveals in an instant its own state within both the insentient and the sentient, and which possesses a unique nature therein, grant us our desire. (5)
Sarasvatī || 106 ||
Having first become steam, she then attains the state of the seed-syllable and the drop;
immediately assuming the union of lines, she is described as taking on the nature of the phonemes.
She who resorts to this state "this-ness" leads her own body to expansion.
May Sarasvatī, who is to be tasted in three ways, bestow her entire essence upon us.
Kuṇḍāsana || 107 ||
Having conquered the three abodes and established her residence therein, she shines forth as the cause for the longing to behold her;
manifesting everything everywhere, she is thus renowned as Kuṇḍāsanā.
The sustainer of the world. || 108 ||
May she, the sustainer of the world, be for our prosperity— she from whom all things manifest and in whom they abide for a moment, even though they are transitory by nature, as if for a long time.
The Mother of the Buddha. || 109 ||

When one who has relied upon the Buddha with a mind free from afflictions and with all desires stilled is not resorted to by the ignoble, he attains his own natural state which is non-dependent; may that Mother of the Buddhas shine within our hearts. (9)
Jineśvarī || 110 ||
May that Queen of Jinas— who, while honoring her seat as being like a blade of grass and wearing the deerskin,
attained omniscience which is the cause of ending all calamities— dispel our suffering.
The Mother of the Jinas. || 111 ||
How can her play be described, she who, though the mother of the Jina and skilled in statecraft, removed the fear born of the Jina’s birth? (11)
O Lords of Jinas! || 112 ||
With a peaceful mind and a heart full of compassion, wearing saffron robes, she is ever devoted to the glory of the Lords of Jinas; free from enmity, she wanders at her own will.
Śāradā || 113 ||
When a virtuous person has attained perfection, conquered the afflictions,
and mastered renowned sciences, may he cast off the limiting adjuncts acquired through the state of the body and so forth, and grant [liberation].
That Śāradā took up residence at the soles of his feet. || 13 ||
She whose vehicle is a swan. || 114 ||

May this Goddess, whose vehicle is a swan, protect you on your path— she by whose compassion even the unborn Brahmā, though his movement is like that of a young swan, becomes the leader of the gods such as Airāvata, the king of elephants.
The royal fortune. || 115 ||
May that royal fortune, which bestows a good kingdom, be [attained] by those who have never meditated upon greed, yet who, upon seeing her, become helplessly infatuated.
The Vaṣaṭ-call. || 116 ||
May that Vaṣaṭkāra, by meditating upon whom and by offering oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rite, people who are ever-supported attain supreme perfection—may she be mine. (16)
The moon. || 117 ||
When immortality is doubtful to attain through difficult rites such as the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), it may be achieved in an instant by meditating upon the Maker of Nectar (the Moon).
Consisting of nectar. || 118 ||
She who destroys delusion, who brings about the full realization of one's own true self, who is of the nature of nectar, and who sustains the universe—may she be victorious everywhere. 18.
The Science of Politics. || 119 ||
How could there be universal existence for a single mortal being when you, O auspicious one, are not pleased as the policy of governance? (19)
The triad. || 120 ||
He who, through the knowledge of the meaning of that well-heard and esteemed [scripture], attained proficiency even in what ought not to be done as well as in what ought to be done;
and by whose true instruction the fainting caused by the venom of the serpent of treacherous objects—
May this triple Veda, whose mistress is Speech, grant destruction [of sins] and take away all evil.
The livelihood. || 121 ||
May that news, by whose grace the subject heard appears as if seen and reaches one’s ears—even though it is far away from even a single location—remove my pain. 21.
The science of government. || 122 ||

Shattering the ignorance of the entire assembly of scholars, adorning her husband’s conduct in every respect from all sides, and mocking the one who carries out his commands and wields the rod of punishment; (p. 128) [she is] Bhaṇḍayantī.
The policy of punishment is auspicious when it strikes fear into those who deserve it. || 22 ||
Possessing action. || 123 ||
Even Śiva, having attained the state of a living being, becomes subject to merit and demerit in an instant;
for by taking refuge in her, he becomes capable of bestowing fearlessness.
May she who is full of action bestow what is dear upon us. || 23 ||
True existence. || 124 ||

May she who, without grasping, manifests existence as a manifold splendor of her own bliss, and who brings about the welfare of all beings through her very nature—may that true being be for your prosperity. (24)
The Savior. || 125 ||

How can one cross this most treacherous ocean of saṃsāra— where the jewel of secret knowledge is hidden, where the crocodile of delusion dwells, which is difficult to traverse due to the serpents of passion, whose shifting waters are the drink of craving, and which is teeming with the turtles of persistent greed— without the aid of another?
O Tāriṇī, if you do not rescue me out of compassion for yourself, I am wretched indeed. 25.
Truly, even though my speech is bound by its own nature and cannot awaken that Abode when it is separated from superimposition,
may that faith which is ever-giving always be mine.
A good rebirth. || 127 ||
Even those situated in the unreal cycle of existence never resort to an unreal understanding;
since the virtuous, honoring you who are real, proclaim that you are the "True Goal," therefore you are she.
The true ultimate refuge. || 128 ||
The servants of other gods fall, even if they are self-controlled, for they lack your power;
but those who are always absorbed in you never fall, since you are sung of as the supreme refuge of the virtuous.
The Sindhu. || 129 ||
The moon in the ocean of Dharma, a drop at the boundary of karma, the cause for kindling the ocean of Brahma’s sovereignty,
and a kinsman to the salt waters through its effortless light.
May the Sindhu river be a source of joy amidst the fuels of evil deeds. || 29 ||
Mandākinī || 130 ||
As she moves, she instantly renders the bird of the mind intoxicated with pride lame;
yet, as she stumbles here, she strikes down the very impulse of that stumbling and its restless agitation.
And when she is seen in her entirety, she is like a river of pure waves that carries away everything in due course.
May that Mandākinī, who is worshipped by the gods, remove our dullness.
The Gaṅgā || 131 ||
That bud-like crest-ornament of the Lord’s head, which grants all desires when meditated upon,
yet causes one to abandon old age when held in the hand of the aged son;
that which, though standing upon the sole of Kṛṣṇa’s foot, removes the blackness of even the wise when beheld— [that very lotus I worship].
That Gaṅgā also makes people stainless, wonderful, and situated above all.
Yamunā || 132 ||
Even those who observe the restraints and observances (yama and niyama) are terrified by Yama; yet that very [state] which, upon seeing it,
instantly becomes free from the fear of Yama through its own power— [that state is the Supreme Reality].
May the Yamunā, the subduer of Maya, bestow the state of Yama.
Sarasvatī || 133 ||

May that Sarasvatī— who protects the forest by extinguishing it, who is the fire that burns away the forest of ignorance through her gift [of knowledge], and who, though born from water, bestows the essence of enjoyment— be present.
Godāvarī || 134 ||
May the Godāvarī, who instantly becomes a recipient of cows upon her banks for one who gives them, dispel our dullness with the cattle of awakening. (34)
Vipāśā || 135 ||

Although the domain of the Holder of the Noose (Varuṇa) is there, it effects the destruction of the bonds of worldly existence; therefore, for that reason, she is celebrated as Vipāśā, "the one who releases from bonds. (35)
The Kāverī || 136 ||

May that Mother protect [us] from the beginning— she who, having smelled the ever-flowing stream of Māyā which carries not even a drop from the mass of water consisting of rows of most tremulous waves as it reaches the shore,
yet at times bears a shadow-form moving with continuous gait.
The Kāverī, flowing down the slope, attains the power to destroy moments through its arrival with joy at the lower depths.
The Śatadrukā || 137 ||

When the mind, for a moment, attains the manifestation of a single fluidity through her light, how could that Goddess not be celebrated here as the Śatadrukā (the Hundred-streamed) by hundreds of virtuous ones? 37.
The Sarayū river. || 138 ||
May the Sarayū, born from Lake Mānasa and witness to the various noble destinies of the people of Ayodhyā, remove the mental agitation born of the mind.
Candrabhāgā || 139 ||
Oh, how wonderful! By the mere proximity of this river, birds attain the state of trees and trees attain the state of birds;
indeed, the Candrabhāgā is possessed of the essence of nectar.
May he endow you with great fortune. || 39 ||
Kauśikī || 140 ||
Having attained the imperial sovereignty of yoga through the enjoyment of stainless waters and other such means,
the sun of the Kuśika lineage rendered the lords of the gods, headed by Brahmā,
distracted by their preoccupation with the undertaking of the nine worlds.
May Kauśikī, the well-luminous one, bestow a treasury of excellence.
The Gaṇḍakī || 141 ||

Since the description of Devakī and others, whose bellies contain each of Viṣṇu’s individual incarnations, would indeed be endless, how could that Gaṇḍakī—whose belly contains not just one Viṣṇu—possibly be described fully? She is eternally pure. (142)
Though she always feeds upon the states of existence and non-existence, she remains ever pure;
may she, who is beautiful yet impure by nature, become pure through her own formative causes.
Narmadā || 143 ||
Born from the moon, conquering the moon, filled with water, beloved by the Lord of the Moon, moving with equal gentleness—
may that infinite one always strengthen us on every side.
That Narmadā is skillfulness in playful jests. || 43 ||
Karmanāśā || 144 ||
That for the attainment of which even those sages performed endless penance may be attained by one who performs ritual action through the mere sight of Him— without delay.
This, indeed, is the state of actionlessness resulting from the destruction of karma.
The Carmaṇvatī. || 145 ||
May the Carmaṇvatī river, which is considered by the virtuous to be a protective armor against the wounds of weapons, always be for you a remover of the fear of skin-diseases. 45.
Devikā || 146 ||
Become the refuge that cuts off untimely death!
You are the supreme goddess, greater than Brahmā and the others, renowned among the gods as Devikā.
Vetravatī || 147 ||
"How can a single king be invincible to all if there are no gatekeepers?
If they were to carry triple staffs, the river Vetravatī would become auspicious. (47)
The Vitastā || 148 ||

This Vitastā, the soil of Kaśmīra and the abode of the fame of the immortal Takṣaka, brings happiness even through meditation upon her wondrous life-giving power, reviving those whose lives are scorched by the heat of suffering. 48.
The Bestower of Boons. || 149 ||

She who grants boons to true devotees, she who grants boons to those who are not devotees, and she who is wondrous in granting boons—why is the Mistress of Boons (Vareśvarī) sung as "Varadā" by those of excellent intellect? 49.
Naravāhanā || 150 ||
May she who carries men, who is carried by men within the heart,
and who is praised as the vehicle of men— Naravāhanā— be for our prosperity.
Being existent. || 151 ||
Though she has entered into an unreal body, she never abandons her true nature;
may that Satī among you grant us a hundredfold a mind established solely in the final determination of truth.
Devoted to her husband. || 152 ||
"You are devoted to your husband; speak, for there is a certainty [in this]. O Sovereign of all, I am unable to say everything.
You possess the vow of devotion to your husband—is it that you alone are the constant vow of your husband, whose heart is ever attached to you? (52)
Virtuous woman. || 153 ||
This certain wonderful woman is considered virtuous, for she brings even the wicked to a state of goodness by slaying them through her unrighteous actions— such as the Asuras.
One with beautiful eyes. || 154 ||
Since he was always in the forefront of this goddess Sadāśvacakṣus,
all [beings], having attained supreme vision through him, were made to possess true sight.
Kuṇḍavāsinī || 155 ||
She who dwells in the sacrificial fires, the moon, and the sun, yet also resides in the hearts of the virtuous—
she is Kuṇḍavāsinī, who bestows both heat and peace.
The one-eyed one. || 156 ||
Even they have attained lordship, possessing eighteen thousand three eyes;
may she who is the source of their grace grant you the single eye that is the eye of oneness.
The thousand-eyed one. || 157 ||
When the Victorious One (Viṣṇu) felt ashamed because of his thousand-eyed state, she too became thousand-eyed; for is she not affectionate toward her devotees? (57)
She of the beautiful hips. || 158 ||
