O Hara, when Rambhā beheld his hips, she abandoned the pride born of her own softness and thereafter attained heat, becoming cold; thus she became "Suśroṇī" (the one with beautiful hips) and dwelt in your womb. 58.
Bhagamālinī || 159 ||
She who is the abode of sovereignty, virtue, and fame, and the ordainer of the glory of dispassion and liberation—
for the devotee and for the evil-minded man who seeks to barter them— (p. 135).
May she, who wears a garland of fortune, destroy our misfortune for us. 59.
The army. || 160 ||
All those who have propitiated that Lord with the four limbs stand at His gate:
masters of supernatural powers (siddhi), masters of speech (bhāratī), masters of intellect (mati), masters of knowledge (jñāna), masters of honor (māna), and masters of wealth (dhana). || 60 ||
O Goddess, wherever and whenever this series is present, at that very time and in that very place, that entire creation partakes in the nature of being a creation.
The banner. || 162 ||
May this banner of the Goddess, which consists of many colors and is borne by a fourfold army, be for your prosperity as it moves at the forefront. 62.
Well-arrayed. || 163 ||
When the army is not properly arrayed according to strategic principles, even if it is contented, all its other components will fall into inferiority in the presence of the enemy. (63)
Desirous of battle. || 164 ||
How could they abandon this human body, so difficult to obtain, for the sake of a momentary fame, were it not for you who cause such fainting and desire battle? (64)
The army with its banners. || 165 ||
Falling with its fear dispelled, it obstructs the flight and luster of the descending sun;
standing there, it conceals the great mountains.
May that army, bearing its banners, remain steadfast for the sake of our welfare.
The commencement of compassion. || 166 ||

Since even Hara attained the singular manifestation of the state of becoming (bhava) by taking refuge in her, it is true that she alone, through the initiation of her compassion, is the one who sustains the three worlds. 66.
She who is fond of the lute and the fifth note. || 167 ||
Even those whose heads were turned upward upon hearing [the sound], and even those who were turned sideways, were deceived;
for how could this be if the Goddess, who is fond of the fifth note of the lute, were not present? 67.
She is beloved by the supreme and non-supreme creative powers. || 168 ||
Since her constituent parts cannot be definitively characterized as either superior or inferior, may she, who is adorned with both superior and inferior parts, always stand before me. (68)
The triple power. || 169 ||
Likewise, those whose minds are deeply attached do not become partakers of liberation, nor partakers of devotion, nor even partakers of worldly enjoyment, despite being radiant.
In which, indeed, the Triple Power is well-pleased. || 69 ||
The bestower of liberation. || 170 ||
For everything is composed of you;
indeed, there is never any bondage for you. Who else could there be? I do not know of anyone who possesses distinctness from you.
O Sovereign! Alas, you are the bestower of liberation to him! || 70 ||
Aindrī || 171 ||
May the consort of Indra, who wonderfully nourishes other people— that is, her devotees— by the offering of water,
yet brings about the removal of that very state of being water by ascending upon the lordly elephant, grant us prosperity.
Māheśvarī || 172 ||
Though he acts like a madman, dwells upon corpses, is naked, and is a friend to ghosts and goblins, yet he is the trident-bearing Supreme Lord; such is the grace born from serving Māheśvarī.
Brāhmī || 173 ||

May the Goddess Brāhmī, who has entered the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), who instructs her devotees in the knowledge of Brahman, and who is the sole witness to the creation of Brahmā, be ever present. 73.
Kaumārī || 174 ||
May Kaumārī, who sports through the cycle of existence by means of the stages beginning with childhood, and who captivates even the young, be the remover of the fear of Māra. 74.
Kulavāsinī || 175 ||
Free from pride regarding high or low birth, devoted to the path of his own lineage, and a devotee of Him,
one who knows the true family attains perfection through a woman born of that same noble family.
May she who dwells in the lineage (Kulavāsinī) always be a bestower of auspiciousness upon us. || 75 ||
Desire. || 176 ||

If you, O Viṣṇu, were not the one who creates, how indeed would the Creator create? And if Maheśa were not the one who protects, how would he protect? And if you were not the one who takes away, how would he take it away?
For you are the agent whose nature consists of manifestation and its opposite.
O auspicious one, you would be the will of the Mistress of all arts.
The Blessed Lady || 177 ||
How could he, who is himself naked and carries a skull-bowl, give anything to another, unless the Goddess, the Blessed One, were present in his home? (77)
Subtle, unmanifest, solitary, and devoid of qualities, yet even without any external apparatus, Śambhu— who is made to reel by joy through devotion to him— brings about this manifold creation.
Withdraw your power from attachment to the cycle of rebirth. || 78 ||
The wish-fulfilling cow. || 179 ||
You are renowned as the wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu), and it is well known that you grant every desire at will;
yet that title would truly be meaningful only if [you granted] my own [desire].
For from this, the accomplishment of all desires and pleasures shall be granted. || 79 ||
She is compassionate. || 180 ||
She who bestows compassion by slaying the asuras and by delivering the gods— she is that certain, indescribable one known as Kṛpāvatī.
Vajrāyudhā || 181 ||
May that very goddess, by whose power of affection the bone of Dadhīci attained world-renowned status as the essence of all things, be for the glory of this wielder of the thunderbolt.
Vajrahastā || 182 ||

To her devotees, the flower is a thunderbolt, and the thunderbolt is a wondrous flower; to those who are not her devotees, she is the supreme [power]. Victorious is she, whose hand holds the thunderbolt! (82)
Caṇḍī || 183 ||
Slow in her gait, with lotus-eyes rolling, gentle in speech and removing the heat of her own devotees,
I know her to be so through the destruction of ignorance that is difficult to overcome.
She who is sung of as Caṇḍī is the fortunate Bhavānī. || 83 ||
She of fierce prowess. || 184 ||
In former times, in that battle, the city— strewn with stars falling from all the clouds struck down by blow after blow— shone like a beautiful woman covered in flowers;
seeing which, she herself had fallen into a swoon, yet now you have brought her back to life.
That goddess, who fulfills her own purpose and possesses fierce prowess, triumphs without effort. (84)
Gaurī || 185 ||
May Gaurī, whose pair of feet is honored by the crowns of Śiva, Indra, and the other gods, and whose dignity is renowned by her very nature, grant the attainment of greatness. 85.
Golden-colored. || 186 ||

Because this gold has attained a state of excellence (*suvarṇatā*) in the world, it is praised by those who have acquired its qualities; thus, though her complexion is beyond description, she is sung of as "Suvarṇavarṇā" (Golden-hued), her beauty having been fully described.
She who effects maintenance and destruction. || 187 ||
At one time one [aspect] effects maintenance, while at another time the other effects withdrawal;
yet simultaneously, this independent [power] brings about both maintenance and withdrawal.
If two things, being mutually excessive, appear as if they have attained oneness, they are not to be described [as such];
however, this [oneness] is always and everywhere one.
How could she herself be worthy of description? || 88 ||
Not manifold. || 189 ||
What would the Creator have created, what could this possibly be,
and what would the Vedas say regarding this? What wonder is there in this, if the one stainless consciousness were not independent?
There might be some indescribable ground for dalliance. || 89 ||
The great sacrifice. || 190 ||

The Great Goddess Maheśvarī, who is the source of existence, yoga, austerity, action, knowledge, and sacrifice, and who is the Earth that brings forth all things—may this Mahejyā burn away our sin. 90.
Śatabāhu (The Hundred-Armed One). || 191 ||
For the protection of all devotees, this Great Goddess Śatabāhu—the many-armed one, who is both manifest and unmanifest—is victorious. 91.
Possessing great arms. || 192 ||

That mighty-armed hero among the Kurus crossed that ocean-like army, which had skin-whirlpools and blood for its waters, was teeming with arrows and other weapons for its fish, contained various creatures such as elephants and horses, and was surrounded on all sides by garments like great serpents.
Thus arose a perfect emergence of grace, born from the worship of the mighty-armed one with truth. || 92 ||
Adorned with serpents as ornaments. || 193 ||
Wearing this upon her hips, neck, and head, she removes the fear of serpents;
she who is adorned by serpents is the ornament of Śambhu, whose own ornaments are serpents.
Ornamentation || 194 ||

May this ornament, which bestows an unbroken, desirable, and supreme luster upon the limbs of lovely women with lotus-like faces, and which always provides nourishment to the eyes, remain forever. 94.
She who dwells in the sequence of the six chakras. || 195 ||
She who, possessing a desirable majesty within her own respective abodes, is worshipped and praised by Vighneśa, Janeśa, Keśava, Hara, Ātman,
and the true teachers of the inner self; she is the one, all-pervading, devoid of the discourse of coming and going, and merged in the Self— the Supreme.
May she who dwells in the sequence of the six chakras reside in my mind by her own radiance. 95.
She who pierces the six cakras. || 196 ||
Known by those skilled in the arts of the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya), she pierces the six chakras;
may she grant him the perfection that removes the notion of duality, even without forceful effort (haṭha).
Śyāmā || 197 ||

The night, like a radiant woman of pleasure intent on wandering, is Mahākālī; she, possessing the lovely hips of Rambhā, brings about the onset of dissolution through a fraction of feminine emotion that disregards even the intoxication of tasting nectar.
May she become Śyāmā, the destroyer of the ill-will toward you.
Residing in the body. || 198 ||
Illusion is illusion; it is the adversary of knowledge residing in the body, and its dissolution is difficult to achieve.
Even while situated in the body, this [knowledge] is not itself an illusion.
This consciousness is indeed wondrous and perfectly autonomous.
Devoid of a body. || 199 ||
May that Bhavānī, who is considered to be spread throughout and renowned even beyond the masses of cosmic eggs, and who is devoid of a physical body, bring about the prosperity of the virtuous. 99.
She of the beautiful smile. || 200 ||

She who, merely upon being seen, spreads wonder through her smile— she is not to be approached by those who rely on the doctrines of philosophical views; rather, she belongs to the devoted and passionate man when he has attained dispassion.
May she, with her beautiful smile, be a power for your benefit. || 100 ||
Śrī Kṛṣṇakaula, whose glory consists in the experience of Śrī Kṛṣṇa as both Self and Supreme, begot a son, Sāhibkaula, whose mother was the virtuous Buddhi, who is fully awakened; and this [work],
having attained a state of kinship with the jewel of contemplation on the conduct of the Guru, exists within that poem.
Devotion has reached its cessation in the seventh [chapter] titled "The Amorous Play of the Goddesses. || 101 ||
Thus ends the seventh devotion in the *Nāmavilāsa*, composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Sāhib Kaulānandanātha. || 7 ||
The eighth devotion is Sumukhī. || 201 ||
Since neither the sun nor the moon, nor the lotus nor fire has ever attained equality with her face,
may that fair-faced one, whose excellence is well-established by the prefix "su-", always abide in our mouths.
Emaciated. || 202 ||
Alas! May that certain Supreme Goddess—who, though her very sustenance consists of the constant presence and absence of worldly existence—remains ever emaciated, protect me in this perilous realm. 2.
The primordial nature. || 203 ||
That from which all entities arise, in which they dissolve,
and of which they consist— this wondrous Root Nature (mūlaprakṛti) is to be known through the Sāṃkhya system.
The Sovereign Goddess. || 204 ||
By means of desire, non-desire, and the reversal of desire,
this pure compassion bestows existence upon that which lacks it, and likewise bestows non-existence upon existence.
This goddess is proclaimed as Seśvarī. || 4 ||
The Unborn. || 205 ||
Just as the empty space situated within a jar does not become produced even when the jar is produced,
so too, although the Goddess resides both outside and inside that which is born, you are renowned as the Unborn (Ajā).
Multicolored. || 206 ||
May that auspicious one—who, though of a single color, is colorless, yet possesses many colors;
who is perfectly autonomous—grant us gold of manifold excellence.
It is that which sets in motion the goals of human endeavor. || 207 ||
O Goddess, may she who bestows the two-fold fruit of human endeavor according to each devotee’s own desire,
and who impels them toward the goals of human life, ever stand before me.
Her devotees— who have become detached from everything else and are devoted to meditation— are able to cast off the fear of time;
having abandoned all defects, they are superior to others.
The goddess is red, established in a red state of being. || 8 ||

May that Goddess Nīlā, who shines preeminently in the clouds, in water-bearing clouds, in the ocean, in trees with well-defined leaves, in blue lotuses, and especially in red and blue [garments], be for our welfare.

May she—white in the snow, white in the moon, white in the celestial river, white in the beloved of the clouds (the peacock), white in the elephant of Indra, white in prosperity, and preeminent among the pearls and other things belonging to Śiva—make my heart white. 10.
Śyāmā || 211 ||
The dark-complexioned one, whose side-glances are beautiful, caused the lovely women to whirl;
he who was born as a cowherd, the dark one, was not subject to desire,
yet in whom [the world] attained compassion through the mere entry of his own self.
May that dark-complexioned woman fulfill his desire for pleasure. || 11 ||
Kṛṣṇā || 212 ||

When the stars flicker at night, for the dull-witted man who considers the excellence of beautiful women to be paramount, may Tārā—who removes even the darkness of ignorance from the thirsty seeker and bestows the state of Kṛṣṇa upon her most excellent devotee—be ever present. 12.
Yellow. || 213 ||
Yellow in hue, with yellow matted locks and yellow garments, she who is sung of as the Mother—may she, the sister of the virtuous, abide in their hearts for their welfare. (13)
Variegated. || 214 ||
When the variegated [state] resides at the aperture of Brahmā, Śībhinī is seated upon a lotus;
may the goddess Karburā be the remover of the burden of worldly existence. 14.
Hunger. || 215 ||
Even the Creator and others, as well as the gods who consume nectar, were unable to restrain her;
victorious is this Goddess Hunger, the sole seed-source of all elements. 15.
Craving. || 216 ||
Victorious is that Thirst, by whom the sage born from a jar, Fire himself marked by the submarine mare’s mouth, was impelled as the sole cause for the drying up of the ocean. 16.
(147) Old through age. || 217 ||

It is a marvel that even one who consumes poison becomes a lord free from old age and death through her association; yet she herself is aged by old age—may she bring about my freedom from the decay of old age.
A young woman. || 218 ||
When Smara, whose mind is fixed on passion, is sometimes deprived of his limbs,
he conquers this entire universe with flowers;
yet he is conquered by her with a mere glance.
For a young woman, the highest favor consists merely of a smile. || 18 ||
The abode of compassion. || 219 ||
Since you keep even the terrible Hara— the bearer of the skull, surrounded by hosts of spirits—
at a distance, you are therefore sung of as the abode of compassion.
The art. || 220 ||
When one meditates upon even a single digit [of the moon] as being the digit that removes impurity, how could all the digits, which are equal to a rosary of hands, not come under one's control? (20)
The ultimate limit. || 221 ||
That wickedness which would not be destroyed even by great hardship shall perish in an instant for devotees through the grace of this [mantra] known as Kāṣṭhā. || 21 ||
The Muhūrtas || 222 ||
May those muhūrtas be for your welfare—those which, having divided day and night separately into sixteen parts, are established on earth as their own distinct forms. 22.
The moments (nimeṣas). || 223 ||

She who is the object of the eyes of the world of mortals shines forth, bestowing agitation; but she who is beyond the winks of the eyes belongs to the Supreme Lord, granting all specific and complete prosperity.
She who has the form of Time. || 224 ||

She who understands existence through its origin and other such factors—though no one knows her origin and so forth—and who is inferred from the planets, zodiac signs, and the celestial sphere, is indeed renowned as being the very form of Time. (24)
With beautiful ears and tongue. || 225 ||
In order to properly receive the excellent message offered by the virtuous man,
Queen Nirañjanā also became possessed of keen ears and a refined palate.
The nose. || 226 ||

That which bestows exquisite beauty upon amorous women, which shines with pearls and other gems, and which also imparts a wealth of fragrance to everyone—that something indescribable is inferred to exist here. (26)
The eye. || 227 ||
That which has reached the range of the eye and which Death is unable to see is the sole cause of joy; that is designated as "the eye. (27)
Possessing touch. || 228 ||
Touched by the dust of whose feet, this illusion—which is never considered to be real or tangible—never again touches the forehead anywhere or at any time. (28)
The aesthetic flavors (rasas). || 229 ||
That which plunges into the state of sixfoldness and eighteenfoldness, or is thoroughly consumed by the terrible fire of passion;
that which is perceived by the lords of yogis as being of the nature of nectar.
That tongue shall savor the full flavor for the person.
One who is fond of fragrance. || 230 ||
Although the nose is insentient by nature, it perceives fragrance on all sides;
may she, who is fond of fragrance and through whose grace that [perception] occurs, grant us glory. (30)
Sugandhā || 231 ||
Renowned for possessing various fragrances and the eightfold scent, she is yet devoid of smell;
she is sweetly perfumed when born from existence, removing the foul odor of illusion.
Of pleasant touch. || 232 ||
The devotee who has mastered the preliminary practice perceives worldly existence as if it were a mere spy;
may that touch of the dust of whose feet brings auspiciousness through its exquisite contact be for your welfare. 32.
The movement of the mind. || 233 ||
That which they were unable to obstruct through efforts such as various rituals, discourses, and yogic practices—
exhausted and driven by their own intellects, they then went for refuge to attain the knowledge of its course;
even Īśa, Aja, and the others, having attained a state of pure mind, [attained] that very mind...
May that goddess always dwell in my mind, as the splendor of day dwells in the sun.
Mṛganābhi (musk). || 234 ||
Since it was born as the conqueror of all fragrances, possessing a musk-scent superior to that of everything else,
and since it directs the mind toward the single path of the sense of smell, it is celebrated by the noble ones as *mṛganābhi* (the musk-deer’s navel).
The deer-eyed one. || 235 ||
May that certain deer-eyed woman—who, with a mere movement or a half-glance, makes my mind restless—always remain before my eyes. (35)
Possessing the fragrance of camphor. || 236 ||
May that [goddess] who bears the fragrance of camphor be for our auspiciousness—she, by inhaling whose scent even a defiled impression perishes in an instant. (36)
The lotus-born one. || 237 ||
Born from various wombs and yet born from no womb, he is proclaimed as the Lotus-born;
may he dispel the suffering of entering the womb, which is so difficult to enter. (37)
Sukeśī || 238 ||
If there were an infinite number of Sukeśas as a comparison,
or an infinite amount of pigment, and if there were an infinite number of tongues enriched by that [pigment], then they might be able to describe his virtues.
Those whose lords of hair—the excellent, great, and shining locks—were beautiful. || 38 ||
She has beautiful marks. || 239 ||

The power of Śambhu, beginning with Māyā (Ajā), has manifested as a certain well-known force in order to clearly reveal the entire phenomenal world, which is the very form of His own sovereignty. (p. 151)
May Guptā, possessing excellent marks, become my companion. || 39 ||
She who has the form of the female organ. || 240 ||
May that certain [goddess], who by her very nature is capable of creating, protecting, and even destroying this world of manifold limbs— though she herself is one—
be the eternal bestower of bliss upon the heroes.
She, whose form is the Bhaga, is to be served by the wise.
The Yoni-mudrā. || 241 ||
That which, even when its foundation has fallen into poverty,
properly bears fruit,
and is easily traversed by those devoted to the noble path.
That Yonimudrā, possessing a beautiful body, is for the sake of joy. || 41 ||
Mahāmudrā || 242 ||
When the ten bases, along with the sixteen, have dissolved into the dvādaśānta, the Great Mudrā is proclaimed by the Great Lords as the cause of the unification of the two. 42.
Khecarī || 243 ||
Having attained that [state], those who are true to their word, whose minds are focused solely on the seed of creation through compassion for others,
and who are free from craving, become capable of completely pacifying even the most intense and perverse desire;
likewise, the lords of sages, who have known the essence of reality, find the terrible time [of death] devoid of the taste for sense objects.
May she grant us the beautiful movement of the Khecarī mudrā within the consciousness-filled sky for a long time. || 43 ||
She who moves through the sky. || 244 ||

That [goddess] who moves through the sky is she by whose grace the sun, though possessing no wheels on his chariot and having no thighs for a charioteer, remains a traveler through the air, eternally unwearied. 44.
Madhuśrī (the beauty of spring). || 245 ||
Alas, the mountains serve her with showers of flowers, the winds with constant fanning, the birds with songs of sweet melody, and the rivers with their pure waters—
thus they all attend upon her, who is the source of every desirable object.
May the goddess Madhuśrī, who is esteemed by me, always exist for my prosperity. 45.
The Mādhavī creeper. || 246 ||
May the Mādhavī creeper, which does not cause even a bee to wander elsewhere when it is in bloom, render my mind free from wandering.
Intoxicated by honey. || 247 ||

Madhumattā has arisen when she arranges full gazes, speech, and movement for one who is devoted to her, even though his own amorous agitation was previously marked only by half-glances, whispers, and advances.
Arrogant with intoxication. || 248 ||

Noble-born, wealthy, handsome in conduct, generous, powerful, learned in the scriptures, and skilled in weapons—he was never devoted to that one who was arrogant with pride; yet this very arrogance toward him has become a marvel for the sake of prosperity. 48.
Mātaṅgī || 249 ||
This woman of the Mātaṅgas, who travels on an elephant in rut, brings about a state of intense passion that is a source of reproach for those who serve elephants;
she casts away all fear of affliction upon the lamp of her own soul. 49.
Śukahastā || 250 ||

Who would not quickly find happiness through that hand of Śuka, which—being pleased by the devotion of the sage’s son Śuka, whose state was detached from worldly existence and non-existence—became the cause of the destruction of pride? 50.
Puṣpabāṇā || 251 ||

May she who, though possessing only flower-arrows, swiftly conquered even the wielder of the discus with his arrows—conquering Rudra by her mere glance without the discharge of an arrow—grant us prosperity. 51.
She who holds a bow made of sugarcane. || 252 ||

Praised by the two archers who wield the Pināka and Śārṅga bows, may the Goddess, who holds a sugarcane bow, who sports about, and who always provides protection for us in every direction, [grant her grace]. 52.
Wearing red garments. || 253 ||
Those who wear red garments meditate upon her as being red in hue day and night;
they know her everywhere, like the twilight worshipped by the gods.
Intoxicated. || 254 ||
Someone else might at some time become intoxicated and immediately thereafter become sober by himself;
but this [ignorance] is always intoxicated in its own nature, and it intoxicates the living being, making even one who is free from greed intoxicated. (54)
She who has a red flower as her ear-ornament. || 255 ||
Thinking the moon to be spotted and the head of Hara upon it to be unmarked,
I know she became one adorned with a crest of red flowers.
Wearing white garments. || 256 ||
May she, who sports joyfully with Śubhrāṅga upon the White Mountain while wearing white garments,
bestow upon you today pure fame.
The wise ones. || 257 ||
May the Goddess— who herself is surrounded by the terrifying hosts of Bhīma and by serpents,
who is ever united with the limbs of Hara, who is full of bliss, steadfast, and the accomplisher of her own purpose— protect us.
Mahāśvetā || 258 ||
Once, while Śarva was suddenly engaged in play in his own assembly hall upon the Mahāśveta mountain,
the exceedingly clever Mahāśvetā became so completely absorbed in her sport that she could not, for all her skill, be perceived even by him as he laughed heartily.
From the wind [comes] the mother; from the black friend, the one who creates cyclic existence, comes the brother. || 58 ||
Vasupriyā || 259 ||
Perhaps another might at some time become fond of wealth out of fear of poverty;
but I do not know how the Goddess could ever be fond of wealth, even though she is the Blessed One.
Suveṇiḥ || 260 ||

May this Gaṅgā, who has joined with the braid that reached the region of the tresses of Giriśa—shining as she rests upon his head like a braid extending over half his body—be forever for our welfare. 60.
She who holds a lotus in her hand. || 261 ||
To the one born from the mud who stood in the water on a single foot, gazing upward at the Sun with contentment,
she granted a boon while he held her by the name "Padmahastā" (the Lotus-handed One).
Adorned with ornaments of pearl necklaces. || 262 ||
Adorned with ornaments of pearl necklaces, that goddess, possessing the beauty of pearl strings, laughs like the fickle Gaṅgā when she is covered in foam.
(255) Her breath is fragrant with the scent of camphor. || 263 ||
Even the bee is always attached to the directions where Śaṅkara resides;
this [goddess] is one whose breath is the fragrance of camphor and who is honored by the wind. 63.
The Padminī. || 264 ||

Since the sun rises only occasionally after a long time, or since it moves very slowly as if desiring to gaze upon her for a long duration at the moment of her blooming, this [lotus] is called "padminī" by the wise. (54)
Padmamandirā || 265 ||
That the treasury of digits (the moon) here possesses a mark, that the sun, the maker of light, causes heat,
and that there is a distinction between the lotus-dwelling one and the one seen by sight— I truly understand this to be a division produced by the difference between the unseen and the seen.
Khaḍginī || 266 ||

Seeing the sword held in her hand—or rather, their own reflections therein—the Daityas fled as if out of fear of Death; thus she became renowned throughout the three worlds as "Khaḍginī" (the Sword-wielder).
Holding a wheel in her hand. || 267 ||
And how could even a mere cowherd boy, though alone and devoid of effort, slay many rulers of the earth who are masters of all weapons? This is impossible.
She would not be gracious if she did not hold a discus in her hand.
Bhusuṇḍī || 268 ||
The compassionate Bhusuṇḍa crow, relying upon whose mercy, has his hopes deferred;
even at the destruction of the universe, he does not meet with destruction.
May this Bhusuṇḍī, which bestows the splendor of consciousness, grant [blessings]. || 68 ||
Armed with iron clubs. || 269 ||
But she who, being satisfied with this treasury of the true jewel of her own self, swiftly releases [the soul] from the bolt of delusion— she is celebrated as Parighāyudhā.
The bow-wielder. || 270 ||
That certain bow-wielder who once completely enveloped him with showers of arrows,
and whom Hari— having achieved his purpose— honored with showers of flowers;
she now becomes the cause of his lamentation.
O Compassionate One, destroy that which is produced by delusion.
Holding a noose in her hand. || 271 ||
Even the lord of the inert waters, the renowned Pracetas, restrains the multitude of arrogant beings;
may she, having obtained whose compassion, grant the destruction of the bonds of worldly existence with her noose in hand.
She who holds the excellent trident. || 272 ||
May the Goddess, who carries away death, who dwells in the realm of the departed spirits,
who bestows prosperity upon people, and who bears the excellent trident, be auspicious.
Excellent arrows. || 273 ||
Displaying a single arrow, she discharged it and struck again that which had become her target;
by means of that [arrow] which assumed countless forms for the sake of pleasing the gods, she is celebrated as Subāṇā (the "Excellent Arrow").
Holding a spear in her hand. || 274 ||
Having gratified that maiden, the prince also slew the Asura Tāraka;
and some say that this is a certain Power (Śakti) attached to the Three Powers (Triśakti).
May the auspicious Śakti, who holds the Śakti weapon in her hand, be for our welfare. || 74 ||
She whose excellent vehicle is a peacock. || 275 ||
Satisfied by the words "dear" and "beloved," she, becoming herself the one whose excellent vehicle is the peacock, seemed to grant a reward to Śikhin.
Wielding excellent weapons. || 276 ||
This Goddess, who removes the destruction caused by the blow of delusion and who is both supreme and non-supreme, is praised as the bearer of excellent weapons by those of superior intellect. (76)
The heroes. || 277 ||
Even the wise and heroic, meditating upon it, tremble at the thought of never being able to take up or discharge their weapons—
whether for the sake of fame, the embodiment of the gods, or the earth itself.
Having obtained [this], let those heroes be satisfied for the sake of Śivā. || 77 ||
Intoxicated by the pride of drinking the hero's draught. || 278 ||
A secret and manifest union, like a mass of clouds in the sky,
she is fierce with the intoxication of the heroes' drink from the downward cast of her sidelong glances.
The earth. || 279 ||

May that excellent earth, well-protected by a good king, always be for me like the finest nectar—she who, through her grace, becomes a "good king" (surāja) among those who partake in royal assemblies and shines with unrestrained splendor. 79.
Vasudhārā || 280 ||

How could his noble wives—whose breasts were worthy of pearl necklaces, and whose graceful movements were languid from the weight of their hips—not fall under his control, he in whose hand, alas, lay that stream of wealth, the earth itself? (80)
Victory! || 281 ||

Whether in battle or in the dense forest, among people or before the gaze of kings, during auspicious ceremonies or when one’s name is being uttered—may Jayā, the ocean of compassion, appear in that face for the sake of victory. (81)
Śākambharī || 282 ||
May the Supreme Goddess—the Khecarī, Gocarī, Svecchāgocarī, Varasundarī, and Śākambharī—ever be the bestower of boons. 82.
That from which this world of forms rises and into which it dissolves like a wave,
yet which remains forever free of waves— may that auspicious Śivā, ever new, be for our welfare.
Vijayā || 284 ||

May she who stands granting victory and fearlessness— she who is to be meditated upon by people of the four castes in sequence through the forms of excellent flowers of white and other colors, and who bestows the moon from the ocean of the nectar of supreme bliss— be victorious.
Jayantī || 285 ||

May she who is victorious and ever bestows victory upon the virtuous be ever-present—she by whose grace even a person dwelling among the common folk shines like the moon situated amidst the stars, destroying the dense darkness of the enemy hosts. 85.
Sustanī || 286 ||

Having previously been intoxicated by the pride of the splendor of their own frontal globes, the elephants now, upon beholding her breasts, cast dust upon their own heads, thinking, "This one indeed possesses beautiful breasts. (86)
The destroyer of enemies. || 287 ||
He shall have no enemies; even if two or three should exist, they will become his friends, for this [goddess], when worshipped, is the destroyer of foes. 87.
Pregnant. || 288 ||
Even that which appears as externalized from the nature of the Self shines only within it;
this Śivā, who is pregnant with the reflective awareness (vimarśana) within the conscious Self, is to be praised by the wise. 88.
The power of the Veda. || 289 ||
Just as this person understands his own spoken word, but that [word] never knows him;
in the same way, he who knows the Veda— [does not know the Veda].
Whether it is knowable or not, such is the power of the Veda.
Bestower of boons. || 290 ||
The other gods, though they grant boons, do so only by gesture and in their thousands;
but she alone is eternally renowned as the Bestower of Boons. Therefore, take refuge in her feet with compassion. (90)
The bearer of boons. || 291 ||
You are the giver of boons and the Great Sovereign, for you yourself hold that boon; therefore,
you enter into the hearts of those who are devoted.
You are celebrated as the bearer of boons. || 91 ||
Śītalā || 292 ||
May that renowned and beneficial coolness, which is ever present in the sacred sites of Kaśmīra, in the snow, in the moon, and in the heart of the virtuous, be for your welfare.
She is the destroyer of the heat of anger and the awakener of one's own innate awareness.
Suśīlā || 293 ||
Having made this entire universe so very ill-behaved, she—
though her own very self— does not abandon her own nature, which consists of the bliss of others.
May Suśīlā protect him by her own playful power. || 93 ||
The destroyer of infant-seizing spirits. || 294 ||
Since she herself has not been propitiated by me—that destroyer of infantile seizures—I know that even yogins desire to regain their childhood state because of her. 94.
The maiden. || 295 ||

That which is the arising of the object of thought (*cetya*), yet is itself devoid of objects of thought, whose nature is pure being and consciousness (*saccidrūpa*), and which, by its very nature as that which is to be manifested,
is the beginning of all things and is without beginning, middle, or end.
That Goddess Gītā is the ancient maiden. || 95 ||
Suparvā || 296 ||

Whether extracted and drawn forth within the channels (nāḍīs), months, days, or years, that which consists of the form of great merit in acts such as giving is known as the "Excellent Festival" (suparvā); may it lead to universal happiness. 96.
Kāmākhyā || 297 ||

May that indescribable Goddess protect me from calamity— She who extracts desire, who possesses desirable forms, who dwells in the form of desire, who is the sole seed of all desires, who is known as Kāmā, and who is to be understood through desireless action.
Worshipped by Kāma. || 298 ||
I am Madana here, my power destroyed by the Lord of Yogins, while she, with her own power manifesting,
is renowned as Śambhā among the lords of the gods.
Having considered this, you were indeed honored by Kāma. || 98 ||
The bearer of Jālandhara. || 299 ||
In this Kali age, when all the gods are powerless, she alone is renowned as the Queen; she, the bearer of Jālandhara, is the sole deity of deities. 99.
Infinite. || 300 ||
That which has an end, that which brings about an end, and that which is the final limit— all these have transcended that [Reality] which is not limited by anything;
therefore, all things are infinite within its own nature.
May she make my inner heart one of firm resolve. || 100 ||
(162) Śrī Kṛṣṇakaula, whose glory consists in the experience of himself as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, begot a son, Sāhibkaula, whose mother was the virtuous Buddhi Prabuddhi;
[this work is] a translation from his poem, the *Ṣaṣṭikā*, which contains such topics as spontaneous worship (*sahajārcana*).
In the eighth [chapter], titled "The Play of Names," the delightful devotion has passed away.
Thus ends the eighth devotion in the *Śrīnāmavilāsa*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Sāhib Kaulānandanātha. 8.
The ninth [form] is Bhakti, who dwells in Kāmarūpa. || 301 ||
She who terrifies all fearsome beings, she who punishes the wicked, she who is fully blossomed;
may she, who possesses a beautiful smile and dwells in Kāmarūpa, bestow nectar upon us. || 1 ||
Possessing the seed-syllable of desire. || 302 ||
How could one's own form, once the body has been burnt again by the enraged Rudra, be regained—
even if it were the seed of desire, desired by all?
Therefore, you would never have practiced the vow. || 2 ||
Truthfulness. || 303 ||
Having ascertained this truth of all the Vedas and Agamas, why do the supreme Śivās— the sovereigns of the entire host of Buddhas beginning with Brahmā— issue this command?
Or how could this [world], though real, spread forth as unreal? || 3 ||
Devoted to the true Dharma. || 304 ||
Considering this cycle of existence to be unreal, the wise practice it;
steadfast in the true dharma, she is thus devoted to the true dharma.
Abiding on the coarse path. || 305 ||
The path of ritual action (karmamārga) is gross, difficult, and well-known, whereas the path of knowledge (jñānamārga) is subtle and full bliss;
yet this Goddess, though situated on the gross path, [is present there as well].
This is the wonderful and diverse manifestation of the fullness of bliss. || 5 ||
Subtle. || 306 ||
From a single atom of whose radiance millions of universes arise effortlessly in an instant— how subtle is that auspicious Śivā!
It awakens subtle intelligence. || 307 ||
It is reached through scriptures that are difficult to traverse because of that difficult cycle of existence;
how could it be known if it were not a awakener of subtle intelligence? (7)
The hexagon. || 308 ||
She who abides in the sixfold paths of initiation— within the black circle of Vāyu, in the Śaiva mantra, in the *hṛllekhā*, and in the second sovereign wheel (*cakrarāja*).
May that six-cornered [yantra] grant firmness through the sixfold ritual action. || 8 ||
The triangle. || 309 ||
In the root-cakra, in the mandala of fire, in Jambudvīpa, or in the three eyes of Śambhu,
that which is the primordial power alone is the triangle.
By what measure is this Māyā called "Mātā"? || 9 ||
The three-eyed one. || 310 ||
To the Lord of the Eye, whose closing causes the universe to dissolve and whose opening causes it to arise from its cause— [to him] who has attained the highest station...
May she, who possesses three eyes, grant me beautiful eyes. || 10 ||
Tripurasundarī || 311 ||

She whose domain consists of the three seed-syllables, who is regulated in three ways, who is heard in the three Vedas, who is the mother of the three worlds, who is praised by the three words of the Lord of the Gods,
who is the ground of the majesty of the three abodes, and who is indivisible from the three times— she is the Supreme.
May Tripurasundarī, the beloved of the Three-eyed One and the benefactress, protect us. || 11 ||
The beloved of the bull. || 312 ||
Wherein the manifestation of Vṛṣākapi was false,
and even Vṛṣa became a bull upon reaching her;
she whom the Lord of Bulls (Śiva) propitiates with hymns— [that Goddess].
May she, who is dear to Vṛṣa, be the remover of intense suffering. || 12 ||
Mounted upon a bull. || 313 ||
May that auspicious Śivā, who dwells upon the peak of Kailāsa and shines like a golden creeper,
and who is mounted upon her bull, swiftly cause me to be mounted upon my bull.
The slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura. || 314 ||
For the satisfaction of her own vehicle, Hara, who was weary and hungry, she indeed protected all beings—she who is the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura. 14.
Since even Mahiṣa attained the state of the bull-born [Brahmā] by worshipping her, who would not revere this slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura? (14)
She who removes the pride of Sumbha. || 315 ||
Sumbha was brought to oneness by you at the end and slain by your own "I-ness" (ego); you are the remover of Sumbha’s pride, or rather, you are indeed the remover of Sumbha’s pride.
Blazing. || 316 ||

Just as the sun and other luminaries, having attained a portion of blazing light from meditation and the like, create the universe through their very appearance— this indeed is [the power of the yogin].
May Dīptā, who fulfills the purpose of her own name, be mine. || 16 ||
Resembling a blazing fire. || 317 ||
For one who resorts to her, even for a moment, the dense forest of delusion becomes brilliantly illuminated; she is like a blazing fire. (17)
Adorned with a skull. || 318 ||
May this auspicious goddess, who shines like a bank of clouds followed by cranes and is adorned with a skull-ornament, grant us every ornament. (18)
Providing light by her own loud laughter,
she cuts off the flesh of corpses and eats it,
holding both a severed head and a sword in her hand.
May Kālī remove this terrible affliction. || 19 ||
She who bears a skull as her sacrificial offering. || 320 ||
May the goddess Balā, who bears a skull as her ornament, shine forth like a mountain of black antimony with its slopes overrun by a flight of cranes.
Kapālakuṇḍalā. || 321 ||
When the cool-rayed moon rises and the sun reaches the western mountain at the end of the day,
the sky— gleaming with radiant beauty— is as pure white as a conch shell.
Let this Kapālakuṇḍalā be for our welfare. || 21 ||
This goddess has been long served by those who have practiced asceticism for a long time, and she is beloved by one who has performed sacrifices for a long duration;
she bestows a long-lasting intellect established in stainless certainty.
May she, who is long, renowned, and beneficial, grant you prosperity. || 22 ||
Śivā is the female messenger. || 323 ||
The Mother of Mantras, Sughoṣā, is the one who effects the invocation of the gods; may Śivā be auspicious, she who is worshipped through the pervasiveness of Śiva by the messenger of Śiva. 23.
A deep resonance. || 324 ||
The peacocks rejoice and dance at it,
and even the cranes conceive young;
having heard this perfected [news], living beings continue to live.
May that deep resonance, which removes intense suffering, be auspicious. || 24 ||
Bestowers of accomplishment. || 325 ||
That which is distinct from those [powers] itself is capable of accomplishing the negation for living beings;
it is the seed of the various forms of sovereignty, such as the *kalās*.
May she grant success to me, whose intellect has attained perfection. || 25 ||
Bestower of intelligence. || 326 ||
O servant of the intellect, if you indeed belong to me, then grant me that wisdom esteemed by the virtuous,
by which one may navigate this cycle of existence composed of both knowledge and ignorance.
Indeed, the manifestation of duality could never possibly exist. || 26 ||
Eternal. || 327 ||
In some philosophical systems, others are proclaimed to be eternal, yet they too possess non-eternality elsewhere; however,
this consciousness is eternal according to all schools of thought.
Established in the final doctrine, she is a certain destroyer of ignorance. || 27 ||
The awakener of the path of truth. || 328 ||
In this shoreless ocean of saṃsāra, where no true path exists, may you always be the awakener of the true path for those who wander astray. (28)
A neck like a conch shell. || 329 ||

May Śivā, who delights in bathing with conch-shells, who is dear to Śambhu, and who is the supreme deity among deities—she whose neck is like a conch and who is adorned with golden conch-ornaments—be for our welfare. 29.
Vasumatī || 330 ||
Even without her, there is a creation that bestows aesthetic flavor; yet it is when the donor is virtuous and possesses good intellect that he attains renown.
She, when fully honored with wealth, resides upon the seat of one's own heart.
May they, together with their parts, bestow well-being upon Vasumatī from all sides. || 30 ||
Her dwelling is formed by the shadow of her parasol.
May she who shines resplendent in the assembly of kings as the Queen of Queens, fearless and providing shelter under the shade of her parasol, protect us with compassion. 31.
The one who contains the world within her womb. || 332 ||
The Goddess, the womb of the universe, is supreme like the beauty of a mirror;
O Supreme Sovereign, repeatedly remove the latent impression of dwelling in a womb.
Kuṇḍalinī || 333 ||
Having entered the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, she unfolds the creation consisting of the three states;
from her, the entire Brahman of Sound (*śabdabrahman*) expands, both in its collective and individual aspects.
Having reached the interior of the *brahmanāḍī*, she awakens one to liberation.
Victorious is this Kuṇḍalinī, the auspicious one who is the sole life-force of the individual soul. 33.
She who reclines in the form of a serpent.
Taught by the Buddhas as the one who bestows exclusive pure bliss, you have entered the Great Path (Mahāpatha), lying in the form of a serpent. 34.
From which seven lotuses emerge. || 335 ||
This [central channel], which practitioners worship in succession with the seed-syllables of the fifty letters,
possesses seven radiant lotuses and extends through the region of the sixteen supports.
The lotus stalk with its navel-like base is like a lotus plant. || 336 ||
Since the all-pervading Brahmā was born from it and expanded the wondrous cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
may this lotus with its stalk and stem serve as the awakening of his nature as Brahmā.
The root support (mūlādhāra). || 337 ||
Flooded by the flow of the moon, it is to be traversed at will by yogis seeking their goals; it is a delightful ground of pleasure-groves,
the singular stream of the essence of knowledge regarding the near and the far shore.
May she be the support for my mūlādhāra. || 37 ||
It is formless. || 338 ||
Since she is never seen even by the ignorant, nor by those who have attained unity with her,
she is therefore called "formless" (nirākārā) by the wise, though she possesses all forms in the Gītā.
She has made her abode in the sacrificial fire-pit.
You shine with garlands of flames that are yellow, red, and white; you are she whose abode is established within the sacrificial fire-pit.
Seated comfortably in the Vāyukuṇḍa [cavity]. || 340 ||
Therefore, Vāyu is well-known here as Pavana and Sadāgati;
for you, who are compassionate toward the distressed, sit comfortably within the Vāyukuṇḍa.
Without support. || 341 ||
There is a certain supreme power which, like a stream of nectar, pacifies the multitude of calamities and afflictions; it is expert at removing all forms of transformation.
Beyond the edge of the sword-blade, like the sky, it exists within the lower lip and the dense thicket of ignorance.
May she, who is without support, take away the expansion of my worldly existence. || 41 ||
It is without support. || 342 ||
That which people resort to entirely and yet which depends on nothing at all, being established in the dissolution of the eternal intention (sadāśaya), exists as a twofold supportless state. (42)
The movement of inhalation and exhalation. || 343 ||
In whose hand shines the white sugar-candied wisdom regarding the past and the future of those who know the five paths that are difficult to traverse.
It has been grasped and expanded;
indeed, through practice and by means of the compassion obtained from a true guru, it has reached its own perfection.
May the movement of the inhalation and exhalation of the wise be esteemed by the virtuous. 43.
Living beings. || 344 ||
Neither the senses, nor the objects, nor the mind, nor the intellect, nor even the qualities, nor indeed the vital breaths— without the Supreme Maheśī—
are capable of sustaining anything at all.
May this living one restore me to life here, for I am currently lifeless.
...the grasping [consciousness]. || 345 ||
May that certain singular Goddess, who manifests her divine play in two ways,
always be our protector— she who removes the suffering caused by the seizing and non-seizing of the planets.
Residing in fire. || 346 ||
We bow to her who rests upon fire, who is the support of all yet herself has no support;
she upon whom even that which serves as a seat for others depends. 46.
Arising from the thread of fire. || 347 ||
O pure one, how wonderful is the Sovereign Goddess, who arises from a thread of fire and possesses a luster like ten million suns, moons, and fires! 47.
Lusting after the taste of the six flavors. || 348 ||
How else could even the consumers of nectar descend here, were it not for the Goddess who is beloved by the world of mortals and greedy for the taste of the six flavors? 48.
The ascetic woman. || 349 ||
By her, who had descended into the abode of the King of Mountains with an inconceivable splendor that transcends all lords,
that fierce one [Śiva] was rendered mild through her severe austerities.
May that ascetic woman be led for the sake of her welfare. || 49 ||
The perfection of asceticism. || 350 ||
Even the emaciated attain beauty,
and even the hungry are always satisfied,
having obtained that which ascetics have reached through firm resolve.
May that perfection of my asceticism be realized right here. || 50 ||
The female ascetic. || 351 ||
Even in the heat or at the time of cold, they are not distressed, nor are they overcome by anger or desire;
how could this be, if there were not supreme devotion?
O Pārvatī, you would become dear as an ascetic woman. || 51 ||
She who loves austerity. || 352 ||

You are capable of protecting from fear and bestowing fruit even without effort; nevertheless, for what reason do you not know [this]? I do not understand why you, who are fond of austerity, remain thus.
Devoted to austerity. || 353 ||
Though the perfection of austerity yields both seen and unseen fruits,
may this [perfection] grant us an innate devotion to our chosen deity.
Endowed with austerity. || 354 ||

Divided by means of reasoning, having become a flight of stairs for the ford of liberation, and capable of destroying the power of the end-maker (Death), this woman, endowed with austerity, is victorious. 54.
She is the bestower of perfection upon asceticism. || 355 ||
May the Goddess, who bestows the perfection of asceticism through many forms upon many, and who is the beauty of absolute bliss, protect us manifoldly. 55.
The form consists of the seven constituent elements. || 356 ||
May this form, composed of the seven elements, though itself both manifest and unmanifest,
swiftly bestow the full illumination of right inquiry.
It has as its basis the seven internal elements. || 357 ||
May this auspicious mineral, the crest-jewel of the lineage of the mountain-king, which rests within seven minerals, grant well-being;
for this mineral is worthy of worship as it is the substratum of the seven minerals. 57.
Nourishment of the body. || 358 ||
May that [wisdom] which, when applied, enables a person to perceive their own body— though momentary as it is— as if it were stable for an eon,
be here the fulfiller of the mind's desires.
That nourishment of the body is the singular joy of the innate nature. || 58 ||
Contentment of mind. || 359 ||
His vision becomes steady even without an object of sight, and his joy increases, being natural and unartificial;
moreover, his excellence is manifested here in this world.
Contentment is the satisfaction of the mind of one whose intellect is uncorrupted. || 59 ||
Nourishment by food. || 360 ||
How indeed do the elements attain stability when, though combined, they falter in an instant?
If it were not for the nourishment of food, O Goddess of Action and the rest, how could this be?
In this matter, she alone should be the sole essential companion.
Arrogant due to strength. || 361 ||
Gods, asuras, humans, and serpents attain renown within their respective classes because of her;
she is this mother, exalted by her power, through whose support this world becomes prosperous and beneficial. 61.
The medicinal herb. || 362 ||
Overcome by these, a person perceives the pleasure of his own sense-objects as suffering;
these defects are to be shunned immediately, for through devotion to them, they themselves arise from one's own [mind].
This entire host of afflictions, headed by anger, is a source of distress; therefore, it is for the sake of contentment that [one should abandon them].
May this medicine, through mere meditation, bring the disease to consumption at the appointed time.
Vaidyamātā || 363 ||
Having attended to the patient and, by means of their own discernment, having abandoned [the notion of] entering into the interior of another's body,
the skilled physicians understand the entire nature [of the disease].
Thus, you are considered by the virtuous to be the mother of physicians. || 63 ||
The potency of substances. || 364 ||
Renowned for her manifold virtues and whose power is manifested through her practice, she brings benefit to people;
like a mother, she is capable of destroying all diseases.
May that power of the substance take away [your] lack of power. 64.
The Radiant One. || 365 ||
In the faces, eyes, and hands of the fortunate,
it has become manifest everywhere;
it brings about the knowledge of the state of mind among people.
May Prabhāvinī adorn [the world] with her own splendors. || 65 ||
The physicians. || 366 ||
If you, the supreme deity and physician, do not show favor,
then even those who are themselves afflicted by the disease of worldly existence would become givers of grief to the sick.
The physician’s medical treatment. || 267 ||
By whose grace even a mere mortal attains great fame like that of Dhanvantari;
O physician, may this treatment remove the fever of doubt.
Supathyā || 368 ||
If diseases were never to afflict him at any time,
yet they should arise, then even without medicine, he would inevitably meet his destruction in that very instant.
She who is always well-seated in his heart is like wholesome medicine.
The destroyer of diseases. || 369 ||
Because she destroys the abyss of meditation and the like, wherein all the senses dissolve,
she is therefore effortlessly praised as Īśānī, the destroyer of disease.
Hunting || 370 ||
Forgetting their duties and disregarding the fragility of their bodies, those of noble courage, filled with intense pride and vigor, always worship her.
That [hunting] has been proclaimed by those who know the treatises on hunting. || 70 ||
Eaters of deer-flesh. || 371 ||

Today it has been determined whether attachment gives rise to a fault or a virtue, since the creatures who were eaters of deer’s flesh became [virtuous] through association with their own mount, the lion. (71)
Deer skin. || 372 ||
That which, bound with various shining locks by those whose nature is sacrifice, pure and extended,
spreads forth a certain luster that serves as the mark of initiation.
This is called the "Deer-skin" [metaphor], as described by those ignorant of the true teaching.
The deer-eyed one. || 373 ||
That deer-eyed woman was she who, greedy for the passion of his eyes, entered the midst of the cemetery and fell into the snare of the Lord, like a deer. (73)
A snare. || 374 ||
If birds that dwell on the ground were not to become subject to one's will, then how could a snare—though constructed with logic and made of strong materials—be considered a marvelous thing? (74)
It has the nature of a bond. || 375 ||

O Goddess, that by which even this person— who, though eternally liberated, considers himself bound and is shrouded in delusion— is so constrained; that very thing, though its nature is bondage, is the bond of liberation.
She completely shatters for us the bond of worldly attachment. || 75 ||
Having the form of slaughter. || 376 ||
If you are of the nature of death, O Sovereign, then ordain his death in such a way that this wretched man,
having cast off his bodily state, may enter into great bliss.
"Thus it comes to pass for you, O Endless One, through the marvelous. || 76 ||
Arrogant due to the slaughter. || 377 ||
For one's own self is always inviolable, whereas the body is easily destroyed;
O Goddess, what other person would be so mad as to be arrogant about killing it? 77.
The bard. || 378 ||
She who, when remembered, releases one from all bonds—
how could she herself be a captive?
I know that she is here indeed by her devotees.
She has been made a captive in the abode of the gods. || 78 ||
The form of praise and eulogy. || 379 ||
Even Vācaspati is not capable of praising her form;
oh, how wonderful that the power who is kind to her devotees has a form praised by bards! 79.
She who releases from imprisonment and bondage. || 380 ||
May a certain woman, radiant as Virocana and uniquely beautiful with the bliss of consciousness, release me from imprisonment at this difficult time. (80)
A chain. || 381 ||
Even when they dwell constantly in the forest, elephants are arrogant with rut;
that chain by which they are bound and brought under control, like a tethered animal, is considered the true fetter.
khalahā || 382 ||
Those wicked serpent-kings who do not attain peace through various applications of mantras or medicinal herbs,
[attain it] when they become virtuous and find their sole domain in forbearance through the mere remembrance of him.
And you, O destroyer of the wicked, lead even those people to that very state.
Lightning. || 383 ||
A certain goddess who shines with splendor within the clouds, she, the sister of the submarine fire, ever triumphs as lightning. (83)
She who liberates from firm bonds. || 384 ||
That which is impenetrable by the floods of missiles and weapons, and which, through mere remembrance, severs that very bond of worldly existence—she is the one who liberates from firm bondage. (84)
Ambikā || 385 ||
This mother of mine is such that, in the interval [between her breasts], people never experience affliction from hunger or thirst; she is a vessel for the fulfillment of every desire.
May she, free from anger, utterly destroy [all obstacles] with her glance.
Ambālikā || 386 ||
O Sovereign, how could this child— not being soft, nor capable of accomplishing anything, and though full of joy—
be otherwise when You are not present with Your mercies?
May Rambhālikā be your nourisher. || 86 ||
Mother. || 387 ||
Praised by Indra, possessing Rambhā’s hips, and destroying all deceit—may this Mother further take away rebirth in this difficult-to-navigate existence. (87)
Of good eyes. || 388 ||
Skilled in the play of concealing her own self,
she is a carpenter (takṣā) for constructing the house called creation;
she is the cause for the destruction of the ego-sense (ahantā) right before one's eyes.
May this well-guarded protectress be mine. || 88 ||
Worshipped by virtuous people. || 389 ||
This very [goddess], worshipped by virtuous people, gladdens all with her glance—that grace by which the holy, having attained the nature of Mādhava through fearlessness, rejoice. (89)
The Kaulikī. || 390 ||
The Goddess, luminous and pure, who—through *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*—leads the devotee, detached from worldly existence, to contentment, and even further to selfhood;
she who, for one who has attained detachment, is wondrous, and who, though transcending existence, yet abides within existence. (p. 182)
In this world, the Svacchanda is proclaimed by the virtuous as both worldly and Kaulika.
The family lore. || 391 ||

May that ancestral lore, whose essence is easily attained through its eloquent and languid speech by the power of a nature skilled in the various lineages of the Kula, and whose state is crowded with the cultivation of many branches, shine forth in the mind. 91.
Of noble lineage. || 392 ||
That from which the families of the people’s clans emerge as petals, and wherein they,
crowded with two petals, go to their dissolution.
She is of noble lineage, worshipped by Nakula, and may she be auspicious. || 92 ||
Worshipped by the family. || 393 ||
May she whose beautiful arms tremble with bracelets, whose girdle-bands move slightly, and whose stainless lotus-eyes are steady—she who is honored by her family and is unconquered—be victorious. 93.
The rotation of the wheel of time. || 394 ||
Bound by this [power] and rendered powerless, the lords of birds wander incessantly through their respective paths; indeed,
it is this very thing that is the Wheel of Time.
May she who brings peace to the grove of my delusion be mine. || 94 ||
Deluded. || 395 ||

How could the individual soul (jīva), though consisting of non-difference from Śiva, be afflicted by delusion and wander here and there, having utterly forgotten its own nature, were it not for You? (p. 183)
One who is deluded should establish stability within the mind. || 95 ||
Delusions || 396 ||
Without her, even those of noble vision do not shine with their full adornment, nor does the mind sport; they quickly lose their composure and fall into agitation.
O Hara, remove the delusions of coming and going. || 96 ||
The destroyer of delusion. || 397 ||
In this adverse time, when agitation has been aroused by passion, may she—who is the very essence of the *samaya*—be my compassionate destroyer of delusion. 97.
A row of whirlwinds. || 398 ||
Moving like a wheel-rim, she appears as if unreal; she plays with time itself, acting as a magician who steals away the very union of the sun and the eye.
That is called Vātyālī by those who know the [rules of] time. || 98 ||
Meghamālā || 399 ||
Arising from somewhere and dissolving into somewhere else,
she is the state desired by all;
she is the cause for the union with the supreme lover for the woman who is like a traveler.
That garland of clouds was fashioned by those skilled in the arts. || 99 ||
A good rain. || 400 ||
Having obtained this excellent rain, even the intermediate and main quarters become unsullied and beautiful;
for whom, indeed, does such a creation not bring satisfaction in this world?
It is the sole cause of nourishment for one whose vision is well-developed. || 100 ||

Śrī Kṛṣṇakaula, whose glory is the experience of the Self and others through Śrī Kṛṣṇa, begot a son, Sāhibkaula, whom his mother, the virtuous Buddhi, brought forth with awakened intellect. In his poem, which is born of the innate awakening of his own Self, the fame of Kashmir—
Even in this degenerate age, devotion to the Lord has spread extensively; thus, the number nine has arrived. || 101 ||
Thus ends the ninth devotion in the great poem *Nāmavilāsa*, composed by the eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Sāhibakaula. 9.
The tenth devotion is that which causes the grain to flourish. || 401 ||
The seed attains the state of a sprout, and that [sprout] likewise becomes the leaves and so forth;
that which is bound by compassion is the state of the seed—that Goddess is the one who causes the crop to grow. || 1 ||
The letter A. || 402 ||
Pervading the earth, having the form of Brahman, she is the source of the Veda known as the Ṛgveda, whose seat is the Gārhapatya fire;
possessing unyielding pride and being the foremost among all castes—she is praised in her embodied form by the lords of yogis. || 2 ||
The letter *i* || 403 ||
The half-measure is the form of Śambhu; having transcended the three worlds, she resides upon the seat of pure awakening.
Though called Kāmākhyā, she is free from desire and is to be approached through spiritual realization.
This very [city] is delightful, yet it is devoid of form. || 3 ||
The letter *u*. || 404 ||
She who pervades the sky, seated upon the sacrificial fire of the Dakṣiṇāgni, whose abode is Viṣṇu, the mother of the Yajurveda,
the support of all, whose essence is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
This is proclaimed as *śokārī* by those who know the forms. || 4 ||
She whose form is the letter Ai. || 405 ||
Even when recited without the *bindu*, she expands the majesty of the Vāgbhava syllable;
appearing in the form of the single letter *E* (Ekāra), she brings forth ever-new [attainments] for those who are worthy.
The one who utters the syllable *hrīṃ*. || 406 ||
This [goddess], whose sole life is the young Śākta, when chanted,
bestows upon practitioners— whether they be Padmā in the eyes or Vāṇī in the lotus-face— a state free from all obstacles.
May this syllable *hrīṃ*, residing in our hearts, be ever-present with us. || 6 ||
She is the form of the seed-syllable. || 407 ||

May the infinite tree of awakening— whose roots are the phonemes, whose petals are the letters, whose trunk is the quarters [of speech], whose branches are the aggregates, and whose many blossoms are the various states of being— grant us the fruit of enlightenment.
She is the seed-form of the tree of the Vedas.
The syllable *klīṃ*. || 408 ||
O Goddess, you who reside within the heart of him who utters the syllable *klīṃ*,
pierce Vīreśāna with the arrows of your Māra-nārāca shafts—
piercing goddesses, daughters of the *nāgas*, and mortal women alike.
Why do they not constantly remember him out of desire? || 8 ||
The one who dwells in the sky. || 409 ||
Having bestowed various objects upon her devotees, gods,
and others, I know that she herself has become devoid of objects and dwells in the sky.
The power consists of all syllables. || 410 ||
May that Power, which is always clearly manifest through the play of "this-ness" encapsulated within "I-ness," and which consists of all syllables, shine forth in my heart. (10)
The syllables. || 411 ||
What could this injunction say, and what indeed would the nature of this sacred revelation (śruti) be? How, then, could a person here possess the mode of existence (vṛtti) of a deity?
If it were not imperishable, it could not be the source of compassion. || 11 ||
Varṇamālinī || 412 ||
How is it that this mind is not supremely steady in recitation or meditation, by which the Śāṅkarī Varṇamālinī was learned from the true guru? (12)
Her face is crimson with vermilion. || 413 ||
Upon seeing whom the blinding darkness of delusion flees far away—who, with her face crimson as vermilion, would not be praised by any wise man? (13)
She who is fond of the tilaka mark made with vermilion. || 414 ||
Bearing a face adorned with a pearl necklace and fond of a vermilion tilaka mark,
she shines like the moon that has entered into conjunction with Venus.
p. 188) She is submissive. || 415 ||
Through his gait, his intellect, his vision, and even his speech, everyone fell into such a state of delusion that they understood nothing at all;
for by him, the Great Goddess was perfectly meditated upon.
The God and Goddess must certainly be served by those who seek mastery.
The seed-syllable for subjugation. || 416 ||
By her grace, devotees cast off the insurmountable illusion (māyā) and attain the state of masters of yoga;
thus she is celebrated as the "seed-syllable of subjugation" (vaśyabīja). 16.
She who manifests the subjugation of the world. || 417 ||
How could that wise man, who has not propitiated her who manifests the power to subjugate the world, play so carefree with only a few people, free from sorrow? (17)
She who brings kings under her control. || 418 ||
She who makes even a lord miserable by her mere speech—this Queen of the Great Throne conquers him, bringing him under the king's control. 18.
She is to be served by kings. || 419 ||
Whatever desired object a capable person does not obtain, it is because the Supreme Goddess—who is thus to be served by kings—is not pleased with him. (19)
It brings kings under one's control. || 420 ||
It is indeed beneficial for one who seeks to obtain even a single grain of dust from his feet, for it brings the king under control—
even though he has already attained the state of being desired by all.
The king of kings here becomes full of longing [for it]. || 20 ||
Beloved || 421 ||
The queen. || 422 ||
Just as the king appears externally through his various arts, so too does she, who possesses all arts at the end of the night;
may this Great Goddess, my queen, look upon me with her gaze.
Let her, who brings about contentment, bring [him] into the light. || 22 ||
Honored by the king. || 423 ||
That person shall possess immeasurable merit and skill and be generous—he with whom you, the Great Goddess honored by kings, are pleased. (23)
nṛmānyā || 424 ||
How could the exceedingly meritorious fame of that blessed man, born of his extraordinary goodness, not have reached both heaven and earth, he whose goddess [of fortune] [resides there]?
She who bestows honor upon men, she who is serene, she who is auspicious, and she who dwells within the heart. || 24 ||
The daughter of the king. || 425 ||
Whether it be a horse, a human, or even an elephant and so forth, when each applies its own skill within its respective domain,
it comes to delight that lord of the earth.
O daughter of a king, you have captivated my heart.
It consists of the dharma of kings. || 426 ||
Carried by various vehicles, characterized by parasols and chowries,
may the auspicious royal dharma, which is eternally composed of happiness, be victorious.
Blessed! || 427 ||
Blessed is his mother and blessed is his own lineage;
blessed are his companions and blessed is his country;
blessed is his form and blessed is his intellect.
By whom you, the Great Goddess, have been worshipped with offerings of grain, he is blessed. || 27 ||
The increaser of wealth and grain. || 428 ||
Indeed, wealth and grain come to him even without effort,
because he has served Sannidhi, who increases both wealth and grain.
The form consists of the four castes. || 429 ||
Mutually useful and characterized by their respective defining marks, whose form consisting of the four castes is not to be celebrated? (29)
And she is worshipped by the four castes. || 430 ||
May she always protect me through the study of the Vedas, alms-gathering, and other means of protection;
may she be worshipped by the four castes through their various activities and services.
The accomplishment consists of all phenomena. || 431 ||

May there be the attainment of success, which consists of all phenomena, acts in accordance with its name and purpose, and is the sole witness of the pure intellect abiding in the self-nature that is devoid of [dualistic] dharmas. || 31 ||
She dwells in the four stages of life. || 432 ||
Another dwells somehow in the duties of each individual stage of life;
yet the wondrous Goddess resides in all four stages of life simultaneously, even without following their sequential order.
The Brahmin woman. || 433 ||
The Great Goddess is the student of Brahman, seated upon the throne of the mouth of Brahmā;
through meditation on Brahman, she has abandoned the exhaustion of false delusions,
and her mind shines with the splendor of the knowledge of Brahman.
May the Brāhmaṇī woman, worthy of worship by all, be for your prosperity. || 33 ||
The Kṣatriya woman. || 434 ||
May she who shines through the lineages of the Sun and Moon, and who out of compassion here heals every wound that causes the emasculation of all beings, protect you.
May Kṣatriyā protect me from constant illness. || 34 ||
A Vaiśya woman. || 435 ||

May the Great Goddess, who is complete with the full range of activities such as business and the like, who nourishes all the castes, and who is the sovereign of the Vaiśyas, always remain under my control. (35)
p. 192) A Śūdra woman. || 436 ||

Śivā, who is fond of service, who belongs to the Śūdra class, and who stands at the soles of Brahmā’s feet—she who grants fearlessness and is naturally devoid of the pride of debate—is victorious. (36)
Born of a low caste. || 437 ||
With her mouth and eyes ablaze, with the clouds thundering as they were tossed by her leaping feet, with the mountains at her sides rattling as they were shaken by her moving steps,
with her clusters of eyebrows curling and the surface of her hips bending low—
May those women of low caste, whose curls are lovely with their playful movements, lead us to prosperity.
Devoted to the path of the Vedas. || 438 ||
From whose breath the Vedas were born with their clearly articulated sequences—oh, that supreme Goddess herself is devoted to the path of the Vedas! 38.
Sacrifices || 439 ||
Some worship her with material offerings, some with austerity, others with the practice of sacred study, and still others with knowledge and yoga.
May these sacrifices, which bestow auspiciousness, lead to the attainment of perfection.
The illuminator of the Vedas and the universe. || 440 ||
She by whom the universe was manifested for the dissemination of the Veda, and the Veda for the activity of the universe—she is this very one who manifests both the Veda and the universe. (40)
The science consisting of missiles and weapons. || 441 ||
How could they attain that sovereignty of a universal monarch which is so difficult to obtain, if the science consisting of missiles and weapons were not mastered by them? (41)
She who wields excellent weapons and missiles.
May she who sports upon the field of battle be the remover of fear regarding time;
may she be the source of bliss for Īśāna, bearing excellent weapons and missiles.
Sumedhāḥ || 443 ||

When, through the awareness of even a single part of her, one becomes possessed of great intelligence, she expands those infinite scriptures; for she is that [consciousness] of whom even a single spark is the illuminator.
May that wise one always be my companion. || 43 ||
Possessing true intelligence. || 444 ||
For any other person, even if endowed with great wisdom, surely becomes dull-witted upon encountering the dull;
yet this Goddess, in the midst of the inert universe—
For even though she has departed, her true intelligence indeed remains ever-present.
Bhadrakālī || 445 ||
The auspicious meditator expands his subtle ego or his body—
that which, though born of vain ignorance, creates a slight flaw;
yet she, the wonderful one, dwelling even on Rudra’s lap, avoids all fierce nature.
May that Bhadrakālī be for the welfare and prosperity of you all, those living beings who are her devotees. || 45 ||
Aparājitā || 446 ||
By whose grace Gopāla, Viṣṇu, and even Rudra the Lord, as well as Śakra and Jiṣṇu, always [protect] the world; may she, the unconquered one, be for our welfare. (46)
The Gāyatrī || 447 ||
He by whom [Śiva] is known understands all the Vedas; he by whom Ambikā is meditated upon is always meditated upon by the thirty gods;
he by whom [the Name] is glorified has his fame purify the entire world; or he by whom Śivā is worshipped [attains the same].
And who does not constantly recite the Gāyatrī? Or who indeed does not worship him? || 47 ||
Honoring. || 448 ||
If you, who are truly compassionate, do not take honor to heart, then one shall not obtain on earth a kingdom free from the fear of enemies;
nor shall anyone attain the status of a lord of gods in heaven or the nature of a horse.
The state of Rudra, the wondrous digit, the green one, or the self-nature. || 48 ||
The Twilight [Prayer] || 449 ||
That which the best of the twice-born meditate upon, which exists in the city of the mind— free from anxiety and filled with supreme joy— and which awakens them;
this is the inquiry into the nature of the Supreme Self.
She is called "Sandhyā" (the Twilight) because she is spoken of by those who possess singular vision as being beyond all duality.
Sāvitrī || 450 ||

Just as the great ocean produces the entire mass of waves— which, though appearing divided, is not actually distinct from it— and into which they finally dissolve, so too does [the Self] produce the universe and its state of differentiation, wherein all this ultimately merges.
She is proclaimed as Sāvitrī by those who know the essence. || 50 ||
It rests upon three feet. || 451 ||
The three worlds appear before him like three steps to be leaped over,
by whom this [world] has been ascertained and known as fearless, resting upon those three steps.
The three junctions of the day. || 452 ||
That certain [reality] wherein the three times, the three worlds, the three Vedas, the three gods,
the three fires, and the three vowels always attain unity by their very nature— [to that I bow].
May the Gītā, known as Trisandhyā, be for our welfare; may she be our mother. || 52 ||
Tripadī || 453 ||
If you are not that which you are, then you are that— thus the Lord instructs his most detached and excellent disciple;
she is the most subtle mother of the abode of bliss.
Victorious is the Goddess, the Great Mistress, the three-stepped one! 53.
The nurse. || 454 ||

May the Sovereign Mother, who bestows the stains of doubt, anxiety, and blemish as if they were mere blades of grass, and who is the nurse who nourishes the milk of awakening, protect us with her grace. (54)
Suparvā || 455 ||
Victorious is this Śivā, who is desirable to the followers of the Atharvaveda for the complete satisfaction of all their festivals; she possesses beautiful limbs and is the source of immense pride.
The female singer of the *sāman* hymns. || 456 ||

She who, having been uttered but once, necessarily deludes the entire collection of sounds—which are fragile through their lack of attachment—and who dwells within my heart as the singer of the Sāman hymns; she is that one of infinite forms. 56.
The Pāñcālī [style]. || 457 ||
May Pāñcālī, who though being one, manifests her fivefold self for the delight of the five [Pāṇḍavas], lead my flickering mind to steadfastness. 57.
The girl. || 458 ||
Like a young girl filled with natural joy from fondling dolls made of cloth, she who has herself come here as this very "I" plays; may that young girl grant me strength. 58.
The foolish ones. || 459 ||

She whose peacock’s plumage was made to seem like mere ruffianry by the threats of children; who reduced the sweet warbling of the myna bird to silence; and who surpassed the best of swans in her languid gait—she [is here].
May Bālā, the treasury of strength and weakness, grant complete happiness. || 59 ||
Child’s Play || 460 ||
Victorious is this stainless child’s play, which has attained a state that is free from agitation, free from agitation, and devoid of fear, as is well known here. 60.
The eternal one. || 461 ||
She who is the Great Goddess, endowed with knowledge beginning with the power of manifestation, is herself eternal and free from those [qualities] belonging to Brahmā and the others. 61.
The earth that supports the embryo. || 462 ||
How could the amnion, which is only four finger-breadths wide, sustain the expanded embryo, were it not for the earth that supports the womb providing compassion? (52)
When this triple world, variegated with manifold arrangements, was proclaimed as "void," how could that Great Goddess be said to be eternally full? (63)
Dwelling within the womb.
Neither hunger nor thirst afflicts her, for she is inwardly sustained by compassion;
