this is the state of the embryo dwelling in the womb during its tenth month.
The Kṛtyā who slays the enemies of the gods. || 465 ||
If the Goddess were not present, how could the immortals, the ageless gods, exist?
By her own compassion, she becomes the Kṛtyā who slays the enemies of the gods.
Pūtanā || 466 ||
Because he drank that breast milk along with his life-force (jīva), that cowherd became powerful and slew the Daityas; she, however, was powerless and became Pūtanā.
Tilottamā || 467 ||
Her face, with its lovely forelock hanging down to the middle of her forehead and surrounded on all sides by disheveled curls,
shines like a water drop or like a lotus adorned with bees.
She who is Śivā is indeed Tilottamā. || 67 ||
Since even noble women who are devoid of beauty become most beautiful when accompanied by you,
while those who possess beauty are shorn of it when they treat you with contempt—
what is that beauty of yours, or rather, what is their lack of beauty?
I do not know whether you are the Goddess Lajjā or the Supreme Sovereign. || 68 ||
The savory dish. || 469 ||
Existence is treacherous, pleasant at first sight yet bitter in its end;
it would become truly full of flavor only if compassion were its sole remaining essence. (69)
Nandā || 470 ||
How could all the people standing by his side not be delighted by his gaze and his speech, since Nandā has been so honored?
Bhavānī || 471 ||
Whether worshipping you as Bhavānī, the foremost goddess,
or regarding you as Bhava within the states of existence and non-existence,
one abandons that miserable state of becoming at that very moment and attains liberation.
May you become a most wonderful mass of fresh bliss.
The destroyer of evil. || 472 ||
By our compassion, even that evil which consists of non-evil is difficult to attain;
for it is by her power that this auspicious goddess is celebrated as the destroyer of sin.
Wearing fine silken garments. || 473 ||
Clad in an elephant hide and seated upon her lap, the auspicious Śivā, wearing silken garments,
shines like a lotus-lady (padminī) clinging to a blue water-lily.
A song (gīti). || 474 ||
Deer, birds, and the best of elephants, having utterly forgotten their own nature, become absorbed in meditative concentration upon hearing her; for that which she is...
To whom, indeed, does a song not bring delight? || 74 ||
A beautiful song. || 475 ||
She who, when raised up by the best of devotees according to the proper method,
leads [the soul] from fear and other states to the ultimate state of being,
and bestows upon the heart a certain play of bliss— [to her I bow].
May that well-sung hymn bestow the flourishing of wisdom.
Jñānalocanā || 476 ||
That Goddess, whose eye is knowledge, having robbed away all misfortunes, perceives even that which is remote in time or space as being exceedingly delightful. (76)
The lute-string consists of the seven notes. || 477 ||
May this lute, consisting of the seven notes, where each individual note contains seventy million variations,
proclaim its sovereign independence.
Ṣaḍja, madhyama, and dhaivata. || 478 ||
That which begins with one of the seven notes, has *dhaivata* pulsing in the middle, and is considered to have [the same] at the end but one, is this *ṣaḍjamadhyamadhaivatā*. (78)
The *mūrcchanās* are established within the *grāmas*. || 479 ||
That which is fixed, bound in three ways, and causes the seven extremely unstable notes to rest, being established within the scales (grāma), is considered a *mūrcchanā*. 79.
Established in one's own state. || 480 ||
May that Goddess, who is renowned as abiding eternally within [the self] and whose self resides in the beyond, being established in her own state, make my mind well-established. 80.
She who dwells in her own abode. || 481 ||
Even though they attain their own multiplicity, they do not abandon the white place manifested by themselves; therefore, consciousness (citi) dwells in its own abode.
Laughing with a loud, boisterous laugh. || 482 ||
May that goddess Aṭṭahāsinī, whose laughter causes agitation, dispel [all obstacles], she by whose smile the day shines like a night blossoming with the moon. 82.
Pretas || 483 ||
She who clearly passes through the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, yet does not depart; who, though having entered the stages beginning with childhood, blossoms as pure bliss alone;
and whom the virtuous certainly satisfy with their final rites—that Sovereign Goddess.
May this wondrous [teaching], which brings about the departure of hungry ghosts from the city of the dead, burn away their sorrow. 83.
She dwells upon the seat of the hungry ghosts. || 484 ||
The lords of the pretas stand like pillars supporting the lofty couch of Śiva;
she who carries them is a certain goddess dwelling upon the seat of the pretas.
She is fond of dance and song. || 485 ||
Horses, Gandharvas, celestial nymphs, and others,
taking up musical instruments, greatly delight that Goddess of Gods here with dance and song— her whom [they worship].
May she, beloved by Śrī, nourish us with her own splendor. || 85 ||
Without desire. || 486 ||
O Śāṅkarī, wherever and whenever the mind of anyone is immersed in their own particular beloved,
right there and then it belongs to that very person.
Since it shines forth through you alone, therefore it has no desire for anything else.
Bestower of contentment. || 487 ||
Just as a person bearing a burden carries his body with a compassionate mind,
so too does he abandon it in an instant by that same [mind].
May she, who bestows contentment, always remain cherished within my heart. || 87 ||
Bestower of nourishment. || 488 ||
By whom can that auspicious Goddess be measured here, even by one of keen intellect? In what form are you not present, and to whom have you not granted nourishment? || 88 ||
Inexhaustible. || 489 ||
Even when joined with effort, all things surely go to destruction in their own time;
you alone, however, are of the nature of reality, imperishable consciousness by your very essence. 89.
The conclusion. || 467 ||
Let many speak of awakening through the study of the Vedas and Vedānta, yet they do not know their own true nature;
nor do they know that ocean of supreme bliss.
This [compassion] does not reach its ultimate consummation until it has been fully established. || 90 ||
One who loves the truth. || 491 ||
Having propitiated her, the son of Satyavat slew his enemies— who were themselves untruthful— yet he,
whose singular fame was celebrated, never wavered from his own truthfulness.
May she, who loves the truth, spread what is dear. || 91 ||
Wisdom. || 492 ||
Whomever you, the supreme goddess Prajñā, favor, how could others not carry his command upon their heads? (92)
Lokeśī || 493 ||
She by whose mere glance all regions come under her control— regions that can be created, destroyed, or even protected— and who,
upon merely entering the same world as her devotee, [grants them her favor].
May Lokeśī make me free from sorrow. || 93 ||
The best of gods. || 494 ||
She who, as the Supreme Goddess, protects the eightfold creation of the gods in their respective realms,
makes this person— the best among the gods— attain the highest goal.
p. 203) Poisonous. || 495 ||
I know that she who produces the bliss of immortality for her devotees merely by being seen is [actually] poisonous by name alone, like the names Ḍittha and Ḍavittha. 95.
Jvālinī || 496 ||

The darkness of delusion by which his eyes are veiled prevents him from knowing the nature of the Supreme Self; yet that very darkness is destroyed in an instant by her, the treasury of compassion, as soon as she is seen.
That Jvālinī removes the fear of Time (Death). || 96 ||
May that single flame, which, though remaining as one, blazes forth by dividing its own nature tenfold within the three fires, grant us strength. 97.
She who destroys the affliction of poison and delusion. || 498 ||
Just as even a great poison, though lacking the letter 'a' and other consonants,
becomes the conqueror of death (Mṛtyujit) and the lord of creatures (Paśupa) through its association [with them], so too is this [mantra] the destroyer of the pain of delusion caused by poison.
The poison-spreader. || 499 ||
Just as if out of envy at the act of her husband Nīlakaṇṭha assuming a dark-blue hue, that Viśvasū (the progenitor of the universe) also became a consumer of poison, turning into a serpent. 99.
Nāgadamanī || 500 ||
Adorned with costly ornaments and herself joined with her own serpent-ornaments, that sovereign power, Nāgadamanī, remains as if full of modesty. 100.

p. 204) He who composes this hymn to the venerable Candramauli, containing *yāmaka* (rhyme) from the feet [of the verses] onwards, in that work renowned as "Sāhibkaula"— a title that necessarily arose through the power of his own sovereign experience of the Supreme— [this is the *Śrīcandramaulistava*].
Now that he has come here as a brother, my tenth stage of devotion has reached its culmination. || 101 ||
Thus ends the tenth devotion in the great poem *Nāmavilāsa*, composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Sāhibakaulānandanātha. 10.
Ekādaśī is Bhakti;
Kurukullā is [the goddess]. || 501 ||
Victorious is this Kurukullā, who, when meditated upon, brings people under her influence;
she whose rising is celebrated for her skill in discerning the *kula* and *akula*.
Born from the nectar of immortality. || 502 ||

May that goddess born from the nectar of immortality be victorious—she by whose compassion even this foremost of devotees, though still tasting the pleasures of worldly existence, has become liberated while living. || 2 ||
The protection that removes fear of spirits. || 503 ||
Truly, she exists as independent;
for even when she has entered the limbs of those beings, she is that Supreme Goddess herself, the protection who removes the fear of all beings.
She is the destroyer of possession by malevolent spirits. || 504 ||
May the Goddess—who destroys the possession by spirits of those who have accumulated merit in the past—be the bestower of prosperity and the warder-off of the egoism of elemental beings. 4.
The demon-slayer. || 505 ||
The mortal Rāma, supported by the lords of monkeys,
crossed the ocean and, through his grace, slew that Paulastya, the leader of the hosts of Rākṣasas.
Whose mother is she not to be honored, she who is the destroyer of demons?
The Rākṣasī. || 506 ||

She alone, the supreme goddess of the enemy, who— though weak— is born as those various forms endowed with many kinds of shapes, capable of conquering even the foremost gods and the *rakṣas* lords of strength.
May that Rākṣasī take away our fear born of Rākṣasas. || 6 ||
Ah, she who unites even the lords of yoga with the splendor of perfect concentration, and the possessors of wealth with their beloveds;
she who unites those skilled in poetry with the art of meaning, and the lovers of travelers with their own [wives].
May the night bring happiness through the most beloved ones encountered in dreams. || 7 ||
The long sleep. || 508 ||
Just as there might never again be a return to worldly existence after attaining the state of Brahmā,
even so is she who alone destroys the conditions of birth, pride, and the rest that arise in vain.
May this auspicious long sleep bestow supreme bliss. || 8 ||
The daytime movement. || 509 ||

When objects have been forgotten during the night, it is through compassion for the protection of the mind that people regain their respective course of action; from compassion, they obtain [their goals] once again.
May that path of the gods be our auspicious refuge. || 9 ||
Candrikā || 510 ||
Although he is subject to waning, though his mark is well-known, and though he is a pale spot here on earth, the moon is nevertheless beloved by those in existence;
yet even so, the moon is fickle.
For this quality indeed has its existence based upon moonlight. || 10 ||
The radiance of the moon. || 511 ||
At night, as he beholds the world— deprived of sleep by slumber and hastening toward the house of Death— as if weeping, and himself appearing as one whose nectar-like essence is dissolving;
Here, the moonlight has sealed its own voice.
The splendor of the sun. || 512 ||
"Even this wicked darkness, though it returns again and again,
has been forever destroyed by me at your command," as if the sun had spoken thus but once.
This solar radiance blazes forth on all sides.
The night-walker (niśācarī). || 513 ||
She who moves about in some inexplicable play, unattached and unperceived like one in a dream during the night of Māyā—
she is that wondrous one renowned as the Night-Walker (Niśācarī).
May she always awaken you with her own radiance. || 13 ||
Ḍākinī || 514 ||
Alas, this [mind], which is the cause of conceptual construction and imagination, steals away the hearts of the dull-witted;
though its activity is imperceptible, its course is irresistible.
"She is indeed difficult to perceive as a ḍākinī," they say. || 14 ||
Śākinī || 515 ||
The sky-clad ones, supreme in all directions, who, having incessantly worshipped her, attain the praiseworthy state of Śiva;
they are the abodes of all beings and the destroyers of performed karma.
May that Śākinī be the bestower of celestial abodes. || 15 ||
The disciples. || 516 ||
Since everyone, having studied everything, attains the status of a teacher—oh!
for what purpose has even Maheśvarī herself become a disciple to anyone? 16.
Hākinī || 517 ||
Even after learning the extensive procedures for various medicinal herbs and the like,
and even after completing the manual practice under a guru,
the wise man does not yet attain the accomplishment born of the elixir (*rasāyana*).
For as long as that Hākinī does not extend her compassion. || 17 ||
The female ruddy goose. || 518 ||
Since the night of illusion never touches this sovereign lady,
she therefore always shines upon her banks, accompanied by ruddy geese.
She who is fond of white and black. || 519 ||
If she were not dear to him who is white with ash, how could the Goddess of the Gods have accepted the Blue-throated Lord as her own? (19)
Svaṅgā || 520 ||
He made his enemy, who had resorted to the theater of love, experience the breaking of his own limbs;
oh, how truly beautiful is a great form when it beholds one whose every limb is well-nourished!
Complete || 521 ||
May she who is endowed with all parts protect us from the calamity born of fear of time— that [Goddess] by whose power all these arts manifest themselves at every appropriate moment.
The forest deity. || 522 ||

She who makes her dwelling in forest after forest, fully honored with abundant roots and fruits, and who destroys the sins of the wicked by those living in the wild—is she not celebrated as the Vanadevatā (the Forest Goddess)? || 22 ||
Assuming the form of the Guru. || 523 ||
All people would become like children, partaking in suffering, were it not for you who always assume the form of a teacher in all activities. (23)
p. 210) It is heavy. || 524 ||
How could those who possess devotion carry even that which is weightier than their own teachers and others, if there were no compassion for that very [devotion] itself? (24)
In what form does she exist, and for whom does she bring about the end?
May that Death, who is auspicious (Śivā), grant us death only when our bodies have reached their full measure. || 25 ||
How is it that the Lord Brahmā, by some means or other, produces this wondrous phenomenon— both simultaneously and non-simultaneously—
that very same thing which, though fashioned by the immortals, brings about death through union with the Uneven One?
May Mārīśvarī grant this supreme satisfaction. || 26 ||
Confident. || 527 ||
Even a man who is exalted by the heroic sentiment, though possessing a body, a home, and the resort of fortune,
and even one who has mastered the sciences— such a person is indeed but a deer for as long as...
As long as you are not confident, you will not be serene. || 27 ||
The great pestilence. || 528 ||

May the Great Goddess Mahāmārī, who is born not from the self but from the principle of Mahat and other such categories, and who is difficult to overcome due to various forms of ego-inflation, surely slay [the enemy] when she is propitiated. (28)
Sleepless. || 529 ||
That which is [meditated upon] by yogis during the final part of the night, and that which is [attained] even during the first part of the night through the yoga of enjoyment,
and that which is always solitary for those separated from their lovers— (p. 211) [that is this very state].
That beneficial one, free from sleepiness, is served by him. || 29 ||
Lassitude. || 530 ||
Those whose sins have been washed away by meditation on the Goddess Tandrā,
and who have surpassed even Indra and the other gods through their intense bliss,
[should chant] her pure name very softly, very softly.
Singing thus, those virtuous ones are victorious. || 30 ||
The destroyer of death. || 531 ||
May the Goddess, the destroyer of death, who removes all suffering in every place, at all times, for everyone, and in every way, be present for the virtuous who possess devotion. (31)
Resembling the orb of the moon. || 532 ||
May she who, though one, shines manifold like the lunar orb, appearing in various bodies as if upon waves—may that Śivā be for our auspiciousness. 32.
She who dwells within the lunar disc. || 533 ||
O Great Goddess, dwelling forever within the lunar orb, she alone—stainless, supremely full, and ineffable—is victorious. (33)
Endowed with the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest. || 534 ||
In the heart, in space, in air, in earth, and in the intellects of individual souls, she who is endowed with the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and is self-perfected—she is victorious! 34.
p. 212) free from longing || 534 ||
How could Brahman, which is pure and enlightened, evolve into the form of the world?
You would become the Supreme Sovereign, O Goddess, were it not for your willing assistance. (35)
Capable of assuming any form at will. || 536 ||
Indra, the lord of the immortals, possesses the conceit of sovereignty,
and Hari possesses the conceit of being its protector; by whom [the Lord], even these two— Brahmā and Śiva— are rendered devoid of pride through the loss of their power.
Even when employed [in ritual], she is able to assume any form at will. || 36 ||
The bestower of the eight siddhis. || 537 ||

O Great Goddess, bestower of the eight supernatural powers, may that which is difficult to accomplish always be granted to us—those who are single-mindedly devoted to pure intellect—even without the practice of *haṭha*. (37)
Mature woman. || 538 ||

May this mature [speech] of the Supreme Goddess—whose nature is profound, a treasure-house of various and wonderful arts, possessing a state of all-enduring tranquility, and which brings maturity to the mind—be mine. 38.
The slayer of wicked dānavas. || 539 ||
In the dense forest, on uneven paths, or when crossing a river, may she who is remembered be a source of happiness and the destroyer of wicked enemies. (39)
Nourishment is without beginning or end. || 540 ||

May the Sovereign Lady, whose nourishment is without beginning or end, who is the witness to the beginning and end of the world, and who removes the agitation of beginningless ignorance, be gracious unto me. (40)
He has four arms. || 541 ||
Holding a conch shell aloft in her lotus-like left hand, while bearing a discus and a lotus with a snake respectively in her right hands,
she who sports with a playful mastery in the art of weaponry;
May this four-armed goddess become the bestower of natural happiness. 41.
Four-faced. || 542 ||
The one transformed Brahman, assuming four forms, bears the nature of Brahman;
she who sings that which is supreme is praised by the knowers of reality as the Four-faced One.
She whose bed is the four oceans. || 543 ||
By whose compassion Hari indeed once lay upon a single ocean;
by whom can that auspicious one, who reclines upon the four oceans, be measured?
Bestowing the fruits of the fourfold aims of life. || 544 ||
Contented and beloved by those of perfected intellect through various rites, that one Goddess alone, who bestows the fruits of the four aims of life, is victorious. 44.
Resembling the kāśa flower. || 545 ||
May that Great Goddess, who shines forth resembling a kāśa flower,
be the expansion of the sky of consciousness, which effects the firmness of the state of desirelessness.
Her eyes are like autumn lotuses.
May she whose eyes are like autumn lotuses grant pure joy—she, by the mere glance from the corners of whose eyes this man has become beautiful in every limb. (46)
It has come to be. || 547 ||
She who knows every Veda, whom even the Veda does not know, and whom Brahmā likewise does not know as a knower—
this Supreme Goddess has been sung as "Bhūta."
May he, who is the reality, constantly grant his own awakening. || 47 ||
Capable. || 548 ||
For one who has been honored by this [teaching] here in the heart,
what else could there be for him to become worthy in birth after birth, other than that which is already worthy by its very nature, even though he may be wavering?
Or rather, a man is not capable of [experiencing] the essence of bliss. || 48 ||
I shall become. || 549 ||
Even Viṣṇu himself, though unborn, having descended again and again after studying all the Vedas,
was unable to play here with her.
She shall be beneficial for determining [the truth] regarding the future.
Śailajā || 550 ||
This very earth is praiseworthy as the soil for the seed of karma, and among its regions, the Himalayas are even more so; for there,
Śivā is present even upon the vast and perilous paths.
Śailajā is the source of joy for the stainless union. || 50 ||
The dweller on the mountain (Śailavāsinī). || 551 ||
Then all the gods each established themselves in their respective places among the mountains;
for the Goddess, the primordial deity of the gods, herself dwells firmly upon the mountain.
Delighting in the left-hand path. || 552 ||
Even those accomplishments that are very difficult to attain come under his control in an instant through yoga, provided he has cultivated them while devoted to the beneficial *vāmamārga*. 52.
Women with beautiful eyes, whose other desires were frustrated, being afflicted by passion and skilled in gentle conversation,
attend upon him, sing for him, and delight him.
She who is always the left-hand path (vāmā) and auspicious (śivā) for him is Vāmā. || 53 ||
She who dwells upon the left side of Śiva. || 554 ||
This goddess who is celebrated as Parā, dwelling on the left side of Śiva,
shines here always within all my limbs.
She who is fond of the left-hand path (vāmācāra). || 555 ||

All things reach their end, yet Śambhu, by whose grace he is the destroyer even of Death—how can she, who is dear to those of unconventional conduct (vāmācāra), be worshipped by the dull-witted in the Kali age? (55)
Satisfied. || 556 ||

Even having obtained a human body, which is difficult to attain yet easily lost, those who are not satisfied with the realization of their own Self are truly satisfied with nothing; they are devoid of compassion.
Lopāmudrā || 557 ||
Chanted with the ten seed-syllables and the five mixed together, she who is incomparable spreads throughout the clear sky-treasury of the hearts of those who know her;
she is served as a certain moonlight of the first wave of joy.
How is it that Lopāmudrā here has her heart sealed by mortals? || 57 ||
The Awakener. || 558 ||
Even the stability of the worlds beginning with Brahmā, which a mortal— even though possessing a body— regards as equal to a blade of grass,
that very thing is always devoid of desire for me.
The power arising from the meditation on Prabodhinī. || 58 ||
The self consisting of the elements. || 559 ||

Previously, no one was able to distinguish the twin [aspects] situated within her center; even more so than that, this multitude of beings, whose beautiful arrangement is both one and many and yet without interval, manifested from her of its own accord.
Nevertheless, she alone is Consciousness, whose bliss is truly unfailing.
May Śivā, whose nature is pure existence, certainly bestow her own incomparable sovereign power (vibhūti). || 59 ||
The Supreme Self. || 560 ||
Even after composing a multitude of most diverse and variegated treatises,
it is not possible for sages to discern that which cannot be understood without compassion.
She is proclaimed as Śivā, the Supreme Self.
It reveals what has been and what is yet to be. || 561 ||

Since you alone are devoid of beginning and end, manifesting all that has been and is yet to be, who else besides you—being yourself eternal with beginning and end—is capable of comprehending you? (61)
Maṅgalā || 562 ||
In this world, there is a certain [goddess] who is renowned, by worshipping whom during journeys, marriages, and other such occasions, noble-minded beings attain unsurpassed success.
May she always be his auspicious companion. || 62 ||
Suśīlā || 563 ||
How could you, though beloved, be the sovereign mistress of Paśupati, the agent of destruction, who possesses a terrifying form and is endowed with a portion of omniscience?
If you yourself had not been well-behaved. || 63 ||
It is that which awakens one to the ultimate truth. || 564 ||
May she who awakens one to the ultimate truth always abide within my mind,
by attaining whom I recognize all other delusive objects as mere blades of grass.
The sacrificial fee. || 565 ||
Since you grant the desired perfection even when worshipped with ease,
for that reason you are celebrated by those of refined wisdom as "Dakṣiṇā" (the Bestower).
Dakṣiṇāmūrti || 566 ||
From the midst of the ocean of Śiva,
she has emerged bringing forth infinite jewels of mantra,
which have descended through various scriptures and ritual purification.
She is renowned as Dakṣiṇāmūrti. || 66 ||
Sudakṣiṇā || 567 ||
By means of knowledge you delight some, by austerity some, by yoga some, and by ritual action some;
yet here, you also delight some through devotion.
Therefore, O Goddess, you are truly Sudakṣiṇā (the one of excellent conduct). || 67 ||
The beloved of Hari. || 568 ||
Devoted to the pleasure of a hundred women and renowned for his green complexion, Śauri is the one by whose grace the Goddess is celebrated as the beloved of Hari. 68.
Yoginī || 569 ||

May that supreme Yoginī—who is intent on the restraint of the vital breaths, who is unconquered by the objects of the senses, whose mind is turned away from disease and grief, and who bestows the auspicious yoga—be gracious. (69)
Engaged in yoga. || 570 ||

Therefore, those disciplined in yoga are spontaneously [liberated] because they always perceive even the entire universe, as well as its individual parts, as a superimposition upon the Self— which is eternally consciousness and bliss— by means of that very [Self].
The limbs of yoga. || 571 ||

Bhavānī, who bestows each and every power of perfect accomplishment through each individual limb, is the sole cause for ending the calamities of those in distress; she is celebrated as Yogāṅgī by the lords of yogins.
She who abounds in meditative concentration. || 572 ||

That which is distinguished and that which remains—what indeed is it? For you, whose majesty is perfectly manifest, are both everything that is to be meditated upon and she who is the one absorbed in meditation upon all.
Wearing the yogic belt. || 573 ||
I do not know what yoga she practiced, having performed which—though weary—she became a bearer of the yogic belt; wonderful indeed is she, the sovereign of the lords of yoga! (73)
Liberated. || 574 ||
Just as water never touches a lotus leaf, she— liberated from both desire and the absence of desire— conquers the three qualities (guṇas) which can never touch her.
The supreme goal of those who are liberated. || 575 ||
Of what nature is this Great Goddess, the supreme goal of the liberated, reaching which the wise attain [liberation] even without going anywhere else? (75)
The Nārasiṃhī [mantra]. || 576 ||

She who made one [man] full of death and the other full of fortune, having fulfilled their respective vows—the Śivā known as Nārasiṃhī, who [deals with] both the hostile and the worshipper when they are equally devoted—[is she]. (56)
One of noble birth. || 577 ||
Even Rāma and others, having attained birth here, have returned to the state of being ordinary beings; whereas you, though existing as the eternal reality, are always of the nature of innate bliss.
You are celebrated everywhere as such, O lady of noble birth.
Bestowing the fruits of the three aims of human life.
What wonder is there that you bestow the fruit of the three aims of life upon householders? But this is a great wonder indeed—that you do so even for those who are liberated.
The gift of the Dharma. || 579 ||
Whether it be a quality (*guṇa*), a duty (*dharma*), or even that which is considered the supreme duty (*dharma*), you alone are that which takes away or bestows these two;
therefore, O Goddess, you are Maheśvarī.
Indeed, Dharmadāsī is honored by everyone. || 79 ||
The giver of wealth. || 580 ||
O Giver of Wealth, if you are the mistress of such riches, O Sovereign Lady, bestow mercy and grant it to me,
so that I may have no fear from kings or others.
And that which is of an extremely painful nature at the beginning of creation and so forth. || 80 ||
The bestower of desires. || 581 ||
It is certain that where both the existent and the non-existent prevail, there victory resides;
for you, Śambhu, who are half his body, and you, the granter of desires, together triumph in two ways.
The giver of liberation. || 582 ||
"You are indeed the giver of liberation in the Śaiva teachings, and you are the giver of liberation in other teachings as well;
since you are so, you are approved by me in both ways."
Where then am I, who possess perpetual authority? || 82 ||
Splendor. || 583 ||
The goddesses have a longing for supreme enjoyment, as do the women of the Nāgas known as Bhayānakās; likewise,
there are women whose pride is fueled by their shifting youth.
If it is asked how [these] desires [are possible], it is because the splendor [of the Lord] is not devoid of compassion. || 83 ||
The witness. || 584 ||
She who perceives the unborn Lord as threefold— both as the whole and as the individual soul engaged in the play of created desires—
and who sees Him, though one, as if manifold;
Indeed, she is directly the witness who is beyond all description.
The night. || 585 ||
How could these people— who perceive the self as distinct from illusion and are always, or even for a single moment, attached to evil deeds—
ever attain rest?
May you be compassionate, not night-like, and auspicious. || 85 ||
Since even Dakṣa, the lord of progeny and son of Bahu, who showed him disrespect and was unaware of his power,
was deceived by her after performing the ritual;
What other [entity] besides that is capable? Does such a thing exist? || 86 ||
Born of Dakṣa. || 587 ||
As soon as you were born from Dakṣa, you brought about his status as a father of a daughter;
yet because of that [other reason], it is true that you, the mother of the world, are born of Dakṣa.
She who has the form of ten million. || 588 ||
Constantly meditating, meditating upon the Great Goddess as having ten million forms,
I have certainly attained the state of possessing ten million forms, even though I am but one today.
Sacrificial rite. || 589 ||
Having summoned her, Dakṣa was separated from her in an instant;
she became the very essence of the sacrificial requisites, yet she herself was the sacrifice of all sacrifices.
Kātyāyanī || 590 ||
By her gait she makes even an elephant appear heavy; by her intellect she is the sovereign who steals away the vital heat of living beings;
and by her fortitude, she surpasses even Hari due to his lack of steadfastness.
May Kātyāyanī protect [me] from the perfected one of Kṛtānta. || 90 ||
p. 223) It is translucent. || 591 ||
I know that while still living, my state has reached such a condition that it is distinct and distinct like milk; though I consume all kinds of food, I remain untainted— this indeed is [the state].
May she, who is pure, void, and the remover of the sense of "I," be yours. || 91 ||
Independent. || 592 ||
Whether unity or non-unity has been established through discourses,
at what sacred site, by whom, in what measure, or in what manner?
For if it were devoid of form and name, it would simply be "that" (cit).
She is autonomous and cannot be reached by the non-duality of the self. || 92 ||
Kavipriyā || 593 ||
They compose poetry profusely, as if longing for the momentary dance of the play of eloquent speech; yet,
his status as a poet here is self-evident.
For he who is well-known would indeed become both dear and undear to poets. || 93 ||
Truth and scripture. || 594 ||
The various Īśvaras have composed many scriptures for the sake of delusion, in order to manifest their own individual sovereignty; but you alone are eternally true.
You perform the coming and going without any delusion. || 94 ||
External. || 595 ||
How could you, who consist of the supreme form and whose distinctions are fashioned by differentiation,
be defined by those of limited intellect when you do not assume the form of articulated speech?
The outwardly situated [consciousness] is the flow of all the single streams.
The power of poetry. || 596 ||
Having daily studied the scriptures from the best of teachers, and having immediately understood the worldly conduct and flourishing ethics, and having integrated them with one's own intellect—
how indeed can that true essence residing in every word and syllable be known?
As long as this power of poetry does not shine within the sky of one's own mind. || 96 ||
Bestowing the power of poetry. || 597 ||

O Goddess of the Lord of Lords, if it is indeed said that you bestow the gift of poetry, then, having thoroughly set aside my study of the scriptures and other such works, grant me that very poetry which is so difficult to attain.
Upon hearing this, even a multitude of flowers would become dejected in mind. || 97 ||
The daughter of Menā. || 598 ||
When Menā saw that even after seeing her son Maināka depart to a distant place there was no sorrow,
she was indeed constantly satisfied, having obtained you.
Therefore, though you are celebrated as a daughter, you are unborn.
A mother who is virtuous. || 599 ||
How could that Hara endure the creation ordained by Brahmā, unless his mother Satī were to overwhelm him with her own playful charms so that he forgets it? 99.
The sister of Maināka. || 600 ||
May Śakti—the beloved of Śambhu, the commander-in-chief, and the leader of the Gaṇas;
the mother of the world and the sister of Maināka—be for our prosperity. 100.
He who, by the power of his own sovereign freedom and supreme experience, has necessarily arisen in the renowned position known as Sāhib Kaula and established his seat—
his own *Suprabhātastava* (Hymn of the Fair Dawn) is a *yamaka* (rhyme) that extends to the end of the verses within that poem.
Devotion, having reached the state of being marked by worldly existence, experiences detachment from it as if it were a sibling in the hereafter. 101.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter on Devotion in the *Nāmavilāsa*, composed by the illustrious and preeminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Sāhib Kaulānandanātha. 11.
The twelfth [letter] is *bhakti*, which is lightning. 601.
Beholding her unsurpassed beauty for a moment,
the cloud seems to rejoice; yet immediately thereafter, it seems to weep as she has departed elsewhere.
May this lightning-strike bring you firm happiness. || 1 ||
Saudāminī || 602 ||
Alas, this lightning, whose form consists of light, spreads forth darkness; how is it that she acts like the night?
For upon seeing her for even a moment, a loving woman separated from her lover becomes intensely distressed.
With her inner being more intensely heated by grief, she went to take refuge upon her bed. || 2 ||
Svadhāmā || 603 ||
The three gods, though struck by the impurity of the three *guṇas*,
have attained a radiance that illuminates the world;
yet even they do not reach their own true state in the presence of her.
She is devoid of qualities, she accomplishes her own purpose, and she is her own abode. || 3 ||
Sudhāmā || 604 ||
The sun and other luminaries, even when joined with their various rays, never attain such splendor as this [consciousness],
which always possesses all [qualities].
That [city], renowned as Sudhāmā, brings about splendor. || 4 ||
Possessing a majestic abode. || 605 ||
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, he who has this [goddess], radiant with splendor, pleased toward him out of compassion, always rejoices in happiness.
The bestower of good fortune. || 606 ||
"She truly bestows good fortune, but not upon one with corrupt senses;
for although he is handsome, he appears as if he were ill-favored. (6)
The sky. || 607 ||
That which is heard by others as the goddess Heaven appears to me, whose mind is devoid of desires,
as Brahman everywhere, through the clarity born of the realization of Brahman.
[This refers to] that which belongs to one who has resorted to such a body from childhood onwards. || 7 ||
The fortunate one. || 608 ||
Even Manmatha, together with Rati, was not able to steal the mind of her who had brought even him under her control; she is rightly called "the Fortunate One" (Subhagā).
p. 228) It increases splendor. || 609 ||
May that deity who increases splendor always be our companion, by whose reliance on even a single portion the entire world shines forth.
In the nectar-like essence of the words of the virtuous, in the graceful movements of the limbs of beautiful women, in all the arts of kings, and in the manifold unfolding of the course of time—
indeed, in all aesthetic sentiments (rasas), she is the wish-fulfilling gem of skill in the art of rasa.
May that Śrī bestow some splendor upon her whose noble mind and conduct are praiseworthy. 10.
Clad in a garment of animal hide.
May she, whom Indra and the other gods— resplendent in the beauty of costly garments— bow down to,
though she herself is clothed in rags, dwell within my mind.
Kaṅkālī || 612 ||
She shines, sporting loftily in the empty space nearby, having completely consumed her own limbs from every part with flames that have arisen like a garland of lamps and turned black by the fire.
May the Kaṅkālīya [mantra] make me fearless. || 12 ||
The destroyer of the Kali age. || 613 ||

In this Kali age, which is difficult to traverse, how could one dwell where the pursuit of innate disposition is not yet mastered, and where the beautiful stage of the stainless scriptures has been shattered? (p. 229)
If she, the destroyer of the Kali age, were not present here in this assembly. || 13 ||
Arrogant from having slain Raktabīja. || 614 ||

Having rendered difficult-to-perceive objects imperceptible, possessing excellent and diverse weapons, and exulting in the slaughter of Raktabīja—victorious is she alone, though appearing in two forms! 14.
The thread of the Sūtra. || 615 ||
In which [intellect], the world—strung together as is fitting and attaining a likeness to a string of jewels—shines forth as a marvel; O thread of the son, extend your understanding. 15.
The continuity of the seed. || 616 ||
She who, through her pervasive radiance, makes the seed-syllable— which is partless— possess a wondrous form;
she who is adorned by and has manifested every diversity.
May that lineage of my seed lead to prosperity for me. || 16 ||
The living beings of the world. || 617 ||
By which that which is empty suddenly becomes full, pervaded, partless yet possessed of parts,
a difficult-to-perceive light, stainless, unreal yet real, and devoid of pleasure; which shines with friction, perfectly transcends the world, and is difficult to comprehend— this [is it].
May the Soul of the world reveal to us the life pertaining to Brahman.
The seed of the world. || 618 ||
By her, the tree of the world was made manifest, with its own will as its sap, existence as its fruit, and the senses as its flowers;
it has the mind as its sprout and is agitated by the minute divisions of time. (p. 230) The world—
May she, whose seed is that, always grant me victory. || 18 ||
She who desires the welfare of the three worlds. || 619 ||
She who, by means of various offerings of objects to be grasped, satisfies the various subjects of perception here without succession—she is this one who desires the welfare of the three worlds. (19)
Possessing the luster of gold. || 620 ||
Strewn with flowers whose pure fragrance wafts from loosened knots of hair, she who has entered the pleasure-chamber shines most brilliantly—
like a Campaka creeper, its limbs radiant and swaying in the breeze, appearing as a benevolent goddess.
It is not capable of causing the mind to expand, nor does it possess the luster of gold. || 20 ||
The sixteenth digit of the moon is imperishable.
Even though Śaṅkara possesses all inauspicious traits,
he bears a splendor by means of this sixteenth digit of the moon, which is beneficial and imperishable.
That which is connected with that state.

Victorious here is that intellect which, following the path of its own words, shines like the embodiment of Brahman; it is understood through well-known, experienced, and natural meanings, and it is delightful in its elegance throughout all the scriptures. (22)
Yakṣiṇī || 623 ||
Trembling like a lotus in Lake Mānasa on Mount Kailāsa, which shines with the mingled rays of the morning sun,
she seems to have been fashioned out of envy for the comparison with her own lotus-face.
O Yakṣiṇī, you who remove the unabated afflictions caused by yakṣas and other spirits! || 23 ||
Worshipped by the Giver of Wealth (Kubera). || 624 ||
By whose grace even Kubera, the lord of Yakṣas and master of wealth, exists as a dear friend of the Three-eyed One; you alone are that giver of wealth who is worshipped by him.
Citriṇī || 625 ||
Having seen that wonderful, diverse, and pure dance, and having heard the song not sung [by others],
the world’s mental activity becomes wondrous.
May she who possesses a variegated garland be his friend here. || 25 ||
The variegated illusion. || 626 ||
Having repeatedly determined that this saṃsāra is momentary, appearing and then vanishing, it remains nonetheless a marvel that delusion causes one to treat a friend as no friend.
She by whom that was attained is indeed Citramāyā. || 26 ||
Diverse. || 627 ||
Although she abides in various forms within the absence of forms without confusion, she shines forth as non-dual; may she, in her manifold aspects, be for your welfare. 27.
Bhuvaneśvarī || 628 ||

She who, a treasure-house of compassion, employed the heart of the Tantras and Mantras to fashion the worlds through her wondrous activity—and who, though active in many ways, shines here as the Sovereign Goddess (Bhuvaneśvarī) alone—she is she. (28)
Cāmuṇḍā || 629 ||
Who would not experience wonder or amazement upon seeing the complete regrowth of that which is called speech from the site of a severed limb?
May that Cāmuṇḍā protect me from the flood of sins. || 29 ||
Holding a shaven head in her hand. || 630 ||

Distinguished by her practice with severed heads, her breasts adorned with a garland of skulls, may she—wearing earrings of skulls, holding a skull in her hand, and devouring the breasts [of her foes]—be present. (30)
Fierce in slaying Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.

May she who brings about the stability of the universe, who is resolute in the slaying of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, and who is perfectly served by Indra and the other gods with unbroken meditations, be victorious.
The eighth [chapter]. || 632 ||
Resplendent with the moon of eight digits, having attained the state of the jewel among the seventy-eight lunar days,
her form consisting of the eight powers, she who is the eighth [tithi] triumphs, worshipped by the eight planets.
The eleventh day [of the lunar fortnight]. || 633 ||
The ten powerful senses, though numbering one, abandon their state of tenfoldness when they offer themselves to meditation;
she alone is this certain Eleventh (Ekādaśī) to be worshipped by the lords of the ten directions.
The full [offering]. || 634 ||
Those clusters of flowers, which had been overwhelmed by the nectar-like radiance of the full moon,
were treated with utter disregard in even a mere twinkling of an eye.
Indeed, when full, it quickly brings about welfare. || 34 ||
The ninth [chapter]. || 635 ||
Whether hidden in both ways or manifest in both ways, she is not worthy of worship without the realization of non-duality;
she who, when satisfied even once, bestows my sovereign power.
May she, the ninth [digit], make it ever new and new. || 35 ||
The fourteenth [day]. || 636 ||
May that Caturdaśī, who shines resplendent, pervading the fourteen worlds,
grant the fourteenfold knowledge.
Born from the mind of Puruṣa, Soma returns again to dissolution within the minds of people; may that Supreme Deity, who brings about peace and delight, be mine. 37.
Holding a water-pot in her hand. || 638 ||
May she who satisfies the entire world with her own digits in an unceasing succession—this Kālī, holding a water-pot in her hand—grant me support from her hand in this time of distress. (38)
Holding a full water-pot. || 639 ||
This kalpa-tree of saṃsāra is supremely succulent and radiant; because she constantly fulfills it by pouring water upon it, she is called "the bearer of the full jar. (39)
The earth. || 640 ||
Sprinkled by the cloud that is so difficult to restrain,
and reddened by the reflection of the sun’s rays,
it is like a woman whose limbs are stained red with bathing-powder and unguents.
This [truth], when proclaimed, shines forth as "Dharā" (the Earth). || 40 ||
Fearless. || 641 ||
That which proceeds by abandoning the state of being a servant to the Vedas,
operating through the expansion of the Vedas bound by its own sovereignty,
swiftly bestows various and abundant fruits.
Alas, let that timid woman take away his timidity! || 41 ||
Bhairavī || 642 ||

Devoted to wandering at will, intoxicated with passion, her lips greedy for the essence of wine and meat, and bristling with the four faces of boisterous laughter—may Bhairavī remove the fear born of enemies. 42.
The Terrible One || 643 ||
Her head, with its braid mingled with white serpents bound at the parting,
now shines like the celestial river whose boundaries are divided by the son of Aryan, the Lord of Day.
Though Bhīmā is the beloved of Bhīma, she casts a gentle glance upon me. || 43 ||
Fearful. || 644 ||
She who is steadfast in bearing the burden of crossing over the profound and heroic, though intent on the playful arts of Keralī’s amorous sport,
is expert at destroying the fear of others through the glory of bliss.
Oh, how strange! That very one who is afraid herself has taken up the plough as her weapon.
Tripurabhairavī || 645 ||

May the goddess Tripurabhairavī be present here before us—she whose garment is as red as the rays of the rising sun, whose eyes are adorned with blue kairava lilies, and who shines with a chain of skulls. 45.
Mahāruṇḍā || 646 ||
Victorious is this great skeleton woman (Mahāruṇḍā), who, composed of the quality of darkness (tamas), having seized everything, plays [the instruments] and dances herself. 46.
Raudrī || 647 ||

How indeed can this supreme Goddess Gītā—who always grants everything desired by everyone, everywhere, and in every way—be called by the name "Raudrī" (the Fierce One), when her nature is supremely gentle? 47.
She is worshipped by Mahābhairava. || 648 ||
Intoxicated by the essence of human flesh and wine, possessing the luster of a great sapphire stone, may she who is worshipped by Mahābhairava become the bestower of great peace. 48.
Nirmuṇḍā || 649 ||
Beholding her dancing in the region of the battlefield,
some fall into a swoon, some ascend to heaven, and others, gasping for breath, meet with a premature death.
May she who is headless protect me, Vakratuṇḍa, as she has done. || 49 ||
The female elephant. || 650 ||

With a wisdom that knows the essence of all arts and which has utterly destroyed all ill-guided methods, she is intoxicated by the discernment of the various manifestations and distinctions of the objects of her desired goals;
distressed by the excessive enjoyment of the expanse of her breasts, which are as difficult to cross as scattered boulders.
May the female elephant Hastinī, whose forehead is shining with abundant musk, bestow well-being.
Caṇḍā || 651 ||
How indeed have you been sung as "Caṇḍā," the seed-syllable of the digit of supreme bliss? Or what [is the meaning]? Is it because of union with Rudra, or [the destruction of] Dakṣa’s sacrifice?
Or what is the point of this so-called "contradiction of purpose" by means of [alleging] destruction? || 51 ||
With a mouth possessing formidable fangs. || 652 ||
May she who dwells in the cremation ground, whose mouth has terrifying fangs, and who is greedy for the tasting and chewing of the flesh, blood, and bones of corpses, be victorious! 52.
Karālā || 653 ||
Beholding whom, Brahmā, as if terrified, concealed himself within his lotus,
and even Viṣṇu, whose birthplace is the ocean, took up residence in the sea; he too,
moving through the quarters of the world, remains utterly naked.
Victorious is that formidable Śūlinī here, who is exceedingly triumphant.
Vikarālā || 654 ||

O Hara, may the formidable one— who moves among the moving and unmoving through loud, intoxicating laughter arising from the flesh and blood of corpses, who is the cause of fear for all beings, yet who herself seeks dissolution— destroy the impurity born of the Kali age.
(237) Uttering a terrible, gurgling sound. || 655 ||
"This man is a lover of pleasure, while I am absorbed in meditation; how is he ignorant of the proper time?"—as if out of anger at this thought, the Goddess let out a terrible, growling roar.
Red teeth. || 656 ||
Beholding the crimson glow of youth throbbing through all her limbs,
she became possessed of red teeth, as if out of a competitive desire for that [youth].
One with upturned hair. || 657 ||
The braid on the half-body of Śiva, joined with the waves of the Gaṅgā flowing from his upward-turned head,
possesses such exquisite beauty that it cannot be equaled by the union of day and night.
She who bestows hair and ashes upon one another has upward-pointing hair. 57.
Reddish like the flower of the Bandhūka tree. || 658 ||
Praised by the youthful charioteer, she is adorned with highly precious red ornaments;
indeed, the night is as red as the bandhūka flower, appearing so due to the delusion of worldly existence.
Kādambarī || 659 ||

Like the Sarasvatī river with its internal flood of water, like the Sarasvatī with its internal form of passion—may that Kādambarī manifest her own joy residing within her heart regarding this matter. (59)
The cloth-robe. || 660 ||
That which is without appearance, yet by its radiance illuminates the three worlds—she who has made her dwelling in the noble mind, that slender one, burns away all evil. 60.
The Kashmiri [recension]. || 661 ||
Having propitiated her, the wise Kaśyapa— who brought prosperity under his control— made this region of the earth a unique stage for lofty holy sites, like a representative image [of the world],
possessing a perfect levelness renowned through its high and towering peaks.
May the lady of Kaśmīra bring me joy through the experience of her perfectly full garment. 61.
She who loves saffron. || 662 ||
Disregarding the other heaps of flowers,
and seeing the saffron powder situated outside, she [approached] in order to strike down the enemy of Madana, who was obstructed within.
Is that beloved of saffron perhaps [fond] of the blood from a wound? 62.
Patience. || 663 ||
Neither diligence, nor power, nor speech,
nor even the intellect serves as a cause for happiness here in such a manner as this [truth] has been so thoroughly revealed.
Patience is to be praised by those whose delusions have been destroyed. || 63 ||
Bahusuvarṇā. || 664 ||
It is true that you possess much gold, since you dwell in the home of a mendicant whose conduct is entirely inauspicious; yet for him, you are the source of all auspiciousness.
Delight. || 665 ||
She who has even the Lord of Beings as her subordinate— he who was never conquered even by Madana, though he is ever accompanied by Rati— she indeed is the delight of Rati.
Bahusuvarṇadā || 666 ||
Since she was sought by others for the sake of the gift of much gold, she became truly Aparṇā (Leafless); yet here, the Goddess herself has become Bhūtā (the Elemental). 66.
Mātaṅginī || 667 ||
Though deprived of his own head,
that Lord of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa), having obtained life through the compassion [of the Goddess], was indeed joined with the head of the king of elephants by her hand.
May Mātaṅginī, the remover of obstacles, be present in this world. || 67 ||
She of the beautiful hips. || 668 ||
Sovereignty over the earth, a body free from fear and devoid of all mental deficiencies, a healthy physique, most beautiful and far-reaching fame,
a wondrous eloquence of speech, or a multitude of virtues headed by fortitude and intelligence— [all these arise from that].
It does not merit even a hundredth part, nor even a fraction of a fraction, of the service rendered by hundreds upon hundreds of women of excellent gait.
She moves with the gait of an elephant in rut. || 669 ||
He by whom she of the lovely countenance, who moves with the gait of an elephant in rut, has been served, his mental state shall never incline toward another being. (69)
Violence || 670 ||
Having composed that which is desired by the command of the Veda, those who know it attain perfection in sacrifices;
and [they] have entered into the state of being the agent and the object in the ritual action.
Indeed, let there be violence for the sake of victory and for the sake of the inexhaustible welfare.
The gait of a swan. || 671 ||
In the heart of one by whom this "swan-like gait" (haṃsagati) has been practiced, that supreme swan-like gait itself shall become perfectly and always most firmly established.
The female swan. || 672 ||

Moving with the gait of a swan, bestowing the knowledge of the *haṃsa*, with a face like that of a victorious swan, consisting of the recitation of the *haṃsa*, may the Swan (Haṃsī) grant you the state of the *haṃsa*. 72.
Her hair is radiant like a swan.
Adorned with the true ornaments of the swan-emblem, possessing the beautiful warbling of a swan, may she shine in the Mānasa lake of her devotees, her hair radiant like a swan. 73.
Her face is like the full moon.
When the moon— restrained by the clouds of her hair, which are like lightning amidst the vermilion of the parting-line—
is released, may that full-moon-faced woman, who brings joy, ever remain before me.
Śyāmā || 675 ||
Does this night possess such power that it spreads an unprecedented white darkness, appearing as if it were dark?
For the mere sight of her suffices to overwhelm even a holy man.
O dark one, here there is blindness of the eyes due to having no other recourse.
With a smiling face. || 676 ||
The Goddess, who, as if desiring to swallow the single digit of the moon that is the head of Śiva, exists for the sake of completing the half-body of Śambhu.
She displays a smile; may she, whose face is smiling, be for our welfare.
Śyāmakuṇḍalā || 677 ||
Her face, adorned with earrings and graced by locks of hair, shone like a blue lotus upon the ground accompanied by two bees and encircled by palāśa petals—she was Śyāmakuṇḍalā. (77)
When you, Bhavānī, the Goddess of gods yourself,
become ink— eternally free from destruction— in the vessel of the ocean, you alone shall be the supreme one as you write.
Even now, your virtues remain boundless.
The pen. || 679 ||
By her command, the Āgamas and Nigamas were formerly adorned by the best of sages for the sake of the world's engagement [in dharma], even as she herself was born from the Self-existent One.
And may this pen grant liberation and bestow happiness. || 79 ||
It should be written down. || 680 ||
In what form and in what place are you seen by living beings, whether in painted or unpainted images upon various instructional tablets? (80)
Sulekhā || 681 ||
Upon seeing her, released by those who are dear to him, every person in this world becomes a partaker of a beautiful painting;
with a clear inner heart, face, and eyes, he knows her.
May that excellent letter, which accomplishes my own purpose, be directed toward me.
The beloved of the scribe. || 682 ||
Therefore, having beheld the letters here as they are depicted, people become adorned; for those who are pleased with him are dear to the scribe.
Śaṅkhinī || 683 ||
How indeed could this other supreme form, radiant with the splendor of a conch, be anything other than his own body, which he has here perfectly offered as an oblation in incalculable numbers?
For by him that Śaṅkhinī is indeed well-served.
Holding a conch shell in her hand. || 684 ||
That which spreads joy for the son of Vasudeva, Kṛṣṇa, with the Pāñcajanya conch, and likewise for Arjuna with the Devadatta.
She who holds a conch in her hand; O Kuru, extend your hand! 84.
Situated in water. || 685 ||
Water is fickle, flowing along a downward path, and it is utterly defiled by multitudes of living beings;
nevertheless, that which constitutes life here is situated within water.
Due to constant proximity, there is a certain manifestation of emotional intensity. || 85 ||
The water deity. || 686 ||

Even that which has sunk into the mud, even that which emerges from the midst of the waters, even that which remains perpetually shrouded in darkness throughout the nights— the sole abode of Fortune— [is yet sought].
That lotus was the favor of the deity of that water. || 86 ||
The land of Kurukṣetra. || 687 ||
May the earth of Kurukṣetra protect me from fear—that place where the two Kṛṣṇas effortlessly defeated the army of the Kauravas, which was filled with variegated warriors. 87.
In this place where Śiva, the illustrious Viśvanātha, expands the state of being a monk for those who dwell there;
where one who has died does not undergo rebirth, having attained an unprecedented state of existence;
which is the object of the sole witness at the end of creation and is self-luminous in every way—[in that place, I bow].
That Kāśī shines eternally and without obstruction within the space of my heart.
Mathurā || 689 ||
Though unborn, he was born to his parents who had reached the end of their lives;
though black, he removed the blackness from his own parents;
and though already moved, he immediately caused their hearts to tremble.
There is a certain sweetness of flavor that is enduring and exquisite. || 89 ||
Kāñcī || 690 ||
With their creeper-like eyebrows arching repeatedly upward and downward, these lovely women, whose voices were like the lute,
turned their ears slightly toward the stage of the corners of their eyes;
seeing this, she did not realize she was being deceived by the bliss of the nectar of aesthetic flavor, her gentle smile betraying her state.
May Kāñcī bestow her splendor upon whichever city has the golden mountain as its domain.
Avantikā || 691 ||

What is the vocative address for Acyuta? What is the seed-syllable (bīja) that indicates nectar? What is the first suffix (pratyaya) in the singular masculine number? What is [the form] for the non-reflexive (anātmanepada)?

And what is the form of the letter *ya*—consisting of a single *mātrā*—belonging to the class beginning with *sparśa*, which bestows liberation? **Answer:** *he hare*, *laṃ*, *ti*, *te*, *yam*. **Explanation:** 1. **he hare**: This is the vocative singular of *acyuta*. It is derived from *a-cyuta* + *he* (vocative particle). 2. **laṃ**: This is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) representing the nectar (*sudhā*). It is formed by the letter *la* (the first consonant of the labial class) combined with the nasal *m* (the fifth vowel, *anusvāra*). 3. **ti**: This is the third-person singular suffix (*tiṅ-pratyaya*) used in the present tense. 4. **te**: This is the second-person singular suffix (*te-pratyaya*) used in the non-reflexive (*parasmaipada*) voice. 5. **yam**: This is the form of the letter *ya* consisting of one *mātrā*. It is formed by the letter *ya* (the first consonant of the palatal class, *sparśa*) combined with the nasal *m* (one *mātrā*). This syllable is traditionally held to grant liberation (*mokṣa*).
Which city, situated in the region between the path of the sun and the Yamunā, shines as Avantikā? || 91 ||
(This is the inner apartment.
Ayodhyā. 692.
At the time of death, all of them were in a state of mutual rivalry to be the first to immerse themselves individually and with haste in the Sarayū for the sake of the descendant of Raghu.
There is Ayodhyā, and there is also some other Ayodhyā.
Dvārakā || 693 ||

For the sake of Śauri’s supreme joy, there arose through devotion a certain unprecedented seed, which for a time remained as if hidden by the beginning and end of its manifested objects, yet brought about fearlessness from worldly existence;
it was the very form of liberation for all the noble cities that are like groves of the gods and for the creepers of the path to release.
That which, even when seen, remains as if hidden from the mind due to its vibration—that is Dvārakā.
Illusion. || 694 ||
By what is that illusion (māyā) measured, such that the people dwelling within it, having abandoned it, become possessed of true awakening and themselves masters of Viṣṇu’s illusion? (94)
The sacred ford. || 695 ||

Those who are devoted to her—whether she is alive as a teacher or present in her teachings—and who have bathed and anointed themselves with [her] very name, attain the status of holy ford-sites (tīrthas). (p. 245) Some...
By what means does she not become a ford for the heretics? She is not a heretic. 95.
Beloved by the Tīrthakaras. || 696 ||
How can these people reach the further shore when obstructed by impassable and inaccessible terrains, by waters too difficult to cross, by forests, and by predatory beings?
If it were not beneficial, it would be dear to the Tīrthakaras. || 96 ||
Tripuṣkarā || 697 ||
May she whose mind is bestowed by the sound of the lotus, who has raised her hand from the lotus,
who is both supreme and non-supreme, who is seated upon the lotus-throne, and who possesses the three lotuses— may she shine here within my heart-lotus.
Immeasurable. || 698 ||
Know that the nature of reality is as follows: among the nihilists, it is the state of non-existence; in the Sugata’s doctrine, it is the nature of fluctuating consciousness;

in the Jaina system, it is the doctrine of the soul (*jīva*) and so forth; in the Sāṃkhya, it is the enumeration of principles (*tattva*) consisting of nine objects; in Mīmāṃsā, it is the nature of ritual action (*karman*); and in the philosophy of Kaṇabhuj (the Vaiśeṣika), it is the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*).
That which attains oneness with existence in the crest of the Vedas is the supreme, both knowable and unknowable. 98.
Abiding in the treasury. || 699 ||
Whether by Vaiśvānara, a thief, a king, or anyone else, that wealth is treated like a clod of earth by one who honors the treasure remaining in the treasury. 99.
The dweller in the treasury (Kośavāsinī). || 700 ||
"By whose grace even Kubera is empowered in the presence of Hara;
may he become the king of kings and lord of wealth, and may the Goddess of the Treasury dwell in my house. (100)
p. 246) He who has established his seat at the station renowned as Sāhib Kaula— a state that necessarily arises through the power of experiencing the supreme sovereignty of one's own freedom—
[now composes this] commentary on his brother’s poem, following the sequence of the *Gītā*.
Twelfth devotion has attained detachment from the play of names that exists through delusion. 101.
Thus ends the twelfth devotion in the *Nāmavilāsa*, composed by the illustrious and preeminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Sāhibakaulānandanātha. 12.
The thirteenth devotion is the Kauśikī. || 701 ||
This very Kauśikī is she who, having obtained his grace, created at her own will that wondrous river—the cause of fear for Kauśika and others—which was like a second sun of creation. || 1 ||
Kuśāvarta || 702 ||
This sovereign city of Kuśāvarta, with its vast and extensive mansions and the residences of courtesans, is both a bestower of happiness and a source of misery.
Kauśāmbī || 703 ||
Kuśa, who was emaciated and difficult for his enemies to behold, ruled at his own will;
may this city of Kauśāmbī, which bestowed prosperity upon him, flourish once again under his sovereignty. (3)
The increaser of the treasury. || 704 ||
That which another person covets for even a moment, this hoarding is indeed in vain;
for while it is always present, it is perishable, yet the greedy one constantly increases the treasury.
The giver of a treasury. || 705 ||
O Sovereign Lady, you always bestow that excellent treasure which is fit for enjoyment,
which grants freedom from sorrow, and which is devoid of defects;
for that which you manifest externally is superior even to that which is within.
That Jayantī bestows both a treasury and wrath. || 5 ||
Her eyes are like the calyx of a lotus. || 706 ||
May that Great Goddess, whose lotus-bud eyes are expert in relishing the essence of her sidelong glances and who causes Hara to tremble with joy, come within the range of my vision. (6)
Kusumā || 707 ||

May that *kusumā* (flower) be mine—she who, manifesting in various forms and pervading the quarters with the unfolding of fragrances, flourishes by resorting to the six seasons; she who is to be served by the presiding deities of the creepers and who bestows her own essential nature.
Kusumapriyā || 708 ||
In this world, flowers are not dear to anyone as much as they are to her;
for she herself, though beloved by all, is supremely fond of flowers.
The totality. || 709 ||
She who is the weighing-scale for noble and ignoble lineages, whose praise is offered by the stainless and composed Lord of the Scale (Dharma-rāja),
and whose lower lip trembles like a young sprout.
She is indeed that art which consists of all arts, beyond compare.
The tip of a balance-beam. || 710 ||
For here, even though the swans— subsisting on fragments of lotus stalks— have bathed in the lake as if for the purpose of training in meditation,
they have become pure beings, yet they are not at all seekers of sound.
May this Tulākoṭi bestow her own balance.
p. 249) Immutable. || 711 ||
Even after creating a manifold world-emanation through its own activity,
that certain [reality] which is eternally immutable and composed of consciousness is never at any time defiled by it.
Residing in a hollow.
O Goddess Koṭarā, who shines during the nights while concealing Your true form, and who has become known through the Vedas heard from no [external] source—
adorn the hollow of my heart!
By means of her own innate splendor, she is ever radiant upon her own throne.
The Self-Existent One. || 713 ||
Even Śambhu or Brahmā were not able to measure the radiance of his power, nature, and majesty,
which was cultivated by his virtues.
How can she, who is self-existent, be rightly conceived by the dull-witted?
Possessing beautiful form. || 714 ||
In whatever way and wherever she may be situated, she who forcibly captivates the minds of people is alone defined as truly beautiful. (14)
The essential nature. || 715 ||
Having himself performed the yoga of the division of creation and having entered even into its interior,
he never departs from his own supreme nature.
For she is always moving from this [state], yet she is indeed her own essential nature.
p. 250) Rūpavardhinī || 716 ||
How could a person created by Brahmā possess form at all,
as long as this formless goddess who increases beauty has not become pleased?
Radiant. || 717 ||
Who indeed, upon merely seeing his face endowed with such a complexion,
would not falter from their own fortitude, even if they have attained great power?
She whose splendor is always radiant and gracious. || 17 ||
There is an abundance of food. || 718 ||
If, when the time was unfavorable, you had abandoned your own offspring while he looked on and instead devoured him— had you not been well-fed—
you might have become some kind of constant companion to him.
Who then would be a knower of the power of the donor's portion? || 18 ||
Bestower of strength. || 719 ||
Since the wind blows even without seed through reliance on her compassion, may she who bestows strength everywhere always grant the power of independence. 19.
Bestower of strength. || 720 ||
Even those such as Indra, the horse-headed one (Ucchaiḥśravas), and the elephant-faced one (Gajāsya), who possess the play of powerful forces, he brings under his control;
for even a mortal who has attained true spiritual fortune [achieves this].
May she be forever the bestower of strength and the guide. || 20 ||
Mahākośī || 721 ||
In this world, Anyakośī bestows wealth that is already established;
but this goddess Mahākośī not only bestows it, she also brings it forth.
The great whirlpools. || 722 ||
Since this entire universe shines within even a single part of the navel,
may there be a great whirlpool at its end that bestows greatness, remaining entirely unconfined.
Intellect consists of both the existent and the non-existent. || 723 ||
I am that self-established intellect, whose nature is both being and non-being, by whom this wonderful world—fueled by the play of knowledge and ignorance—is illumined. 23.
The remover of great planetary afflictions. || 724 ||
Even one who grasps names is afflicted by the seizing planets that are so difficult to restrain;
but she for whom there is no grasping at all—that is the one who removes the great seizure.
Gentle. || 725 ||

I bow to that Umā, who is equal [to her name], whose name is not surpassed by any comparison, who is moistened by devotion manifested through her loud cries, and who is adorned by the moon shining upon her hand.
[She who is] the moon among women, adorned with the digit of the moon as her crest-ornament. || 25 ||
Free from sorrow. || 726 ||
The world's sorrow arises precisely from looking outward,
due to the loss of a second beloved object; it is not because that [sorrow] has transcended the self, for there is no light beyond it.
Therefore, she gazes upon this, being free from sorrow.
The destroyer of sorrow. || 727 ||
Satisfied by the joy of his own well-extended world,
how could he not be a companion while dwelling here in this treasury of the world, which is filled with constant sorrow?
For you are indeed the destroyer of his grief; listen to this. || 27 ||
It is of the nature of sattva. || 728 ||
Even though he has assumed the form of a child, he has attained the vast state of his father;
for one in whose mind the virtuous path, honored by all sages, flashes forth, [he attains that state]. 28.
The abiding of sentient beings. || 729 ||
The Creator fashioned this world most unevenly; may that Goddess, who abides in goodness, grant us that evenness which consists of compassion—the very essence of the Lord of the Sātvatas.
The rajasic [nature]. || 730 ||
May this Rājasī [Goddess], by the worship of whom the unborn and wise Lord creates this array of the universe, grant us the state of being worshipped even by the kings of kings. 30.
Covered with dust. || 731 ||
It is wonderful that by worshipping her for even a moment, a person becomes free from passion and always full of vitality,
while she herself remains perpetually enveloped in passion.
It is of the nature of darkness (tāmasī). || 732 ||
Those excellent Daityas were slain by that very same discus with its hard, sharp edge,
which fell upon the surface of the sun’s throat as if it were a mere remnant.
That is the secondary emotional state (*anubhāva*) arising from *tāmasa* meditation. || 32 ||
Endowed with darkness. || 733 ||
Sthāṇu, Paśupati, and Śūlin himself even destroys everything;
having seized his power, that Śivā is endowed with darkness (tamas).
She who manifests the three qualities. || 734 ||
Having observed these qualities, the Three Goddesses perceive the manifestation of those qualities within themselves;
though devoid of qualities, they manifest the three qualities for the sake of their own divine play.
The unmanifested. || 735 ||
Just as the eye, though seeing all, does not see its own form,
so too does this Unmanifest prevail— whether residing in the knower or residing in the ignorant.
Manifest in form. || 736 ||
May she, who through the power of her entire expansion of the creative impulse (unmeṣa) attains manifestation here as the world,
and who is characterized by the form called "the manifest" (vyaktarūpa), reveal the form that is delightful with the king of aesthetic flavors (rasarāja).
The knowledge of the Vedas. || 737 ||

She alone, who remains as the sole residue after all distinctions have vanished, shines forth as both the higher and the lower, being the cause for the establishment of both worldly activity and its opposite.
May the knowledge of the Vedas be perfected within the hearts of the virtuous. || 37 ||
Śāmbhavī || 738 ||
That which is inwardly visible yet always possesses an unwinking self-vision externally, weaves wondrous upon wondrous [forms] because its activity has destroyed the knots of mental fluctuations;
by practicing that which is repeatedly perceived as the "star," one attains that Savior (Tāraka).
May this [teaching] of Śambhu lead to the welfare of you all in the ocean of saṃsāra. || 38 ||
The Kalpa of Śaṅkarākalpinī is the seventh hundred and thirty-ninth.
How could he perceive an eon as a moment, and how could Hara not conceive it, unless Śaṅkara’s creative power were always present within his own body? (39)
The continuous succession of mental volitions. || 740 ||
In what form does it not appear, and to whom does it not shine?
Alas, the continuous stream of mental volitions is for the sake of constant rest! 40.
The power consisting of the entire world. || 741 ||
Having attained the state of illuminating both the mundane and the supramundane, the Power that consists of all worlds is beheld by those possessing the singular, extraordinary eye. (41)
Within the range of hearing of all beings. || 742 ||

Whatever cognition belongs to a person and falls within the range of all hearing, that very [cognition] moves through the moving and the unmoving, and it alone falls within the range of all hearing. 42.
The desire for omniscience. || 743 ||
When a desire endowed with all-knowledge shines in the sky of one's heart,
even while living, that person is liberated from the grasp of the emaciated noose of afflictions.
The awakener of all reality. || 744 ||
Having led all principles into the supreme, absolute reality of pure consciousness alone, that devotion which rejoices in that reality is the awakener of the knowledge of all principles. (44)
The waking state. || 745 ||

May that radiance of the Lord of Birds, which, while awake, perceives through Viśva and Vaiśvānara the most solid objects of the senses, remain ever vigilant within the heart in the sky of consciousness. 45.
Deep sleep. || 746 ||
That state by which even the wise Maheśvara, though empty of the radiance of the play of volitions and intentions, remains in full contentment— this is deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
Oh, how it shines even upon my field of worldly activity! || 46 ||
The state of dream. || 747 ||
Since everything attains its existence within its own creation through her glory, may she—who is worthy of extraordinary honor—be a bestower of happiness even in the state of dream. 47.
Turīyakā || 748 ||
From Brahmā down to the smallest ant, you abide as if woven through all, with unimpaired vision;
you are the common essence of the seed in the sprout and all that follows.
The state of being distressed by haste begins with the fourth stage. || 48 ||
May this very haste, by which a person of discerning vision seems to enter into a state where their inner being is purified of the winds [of passion], urge us toward the Infinite.
That which is desired is what is sought by embodied beings. || 49 ||
Slow-moving. || 750 ||
Having first adopted a swift pace, why does the Goddess now proceed elsewhere? Having reflected, she perceives once more her own self as all-pervading.
The Earth, the self-born, is our slow-moving refuge. || 50 ||
Slow-witted. || 751 ||
By her carriage, her smile, her well-spoken words,
and by each of her glances,
she brings joy through her gentle devotion.
And she was slow-moving, composed of gentle beauty.
Bearing the fragrance of wine. || 752 ||
How could Śiva, the king of the six-footed bees, though his very nature is to wander for alms, be attached to her, were it not for her bearing the fragrance of wine? (52)
A drinking hall. || 753 ||

Wherein, by means of the senses— which have become like vessels for the wine of objects— the thirst increased by the chewing of various objects of knowledge is tasted, free from even the slightest suspicion of the stain of delusion.
O devotees, the drinking hall here triumphs exceedingly! || 53 ||
Drinking vessels. || 754 ||

Where even two or three pure ones do not sufficiently dissolve into the nectar of the wine of true consciousness, those who are independent in compassion still take delight in that very state. (p. 257)
May she always be foremost in drinking from the vessel. || 54 ||
She was intent on bestowing the gift of drink. || 755 ||
May she, who is ever submissive through devotion and intent upon bestowing the drink upon practitioners who are free from worldly desires, be a giver of joy. (55)
Her reddish eyes were rolling. || 756 ||

How could she, whose reddish eyes are rolling, not be worshipped by those who worship? For by the mere glance of her eyes, one attains in an instant the sovereignty of yogis along with all prosperity. (56)
She spoke something in an indistinct manner.
Lest the Lord fall into a state of swoon due to her words tasting like nectar,
she spoke somewhat indistinctly while clinging to his body.
Fulfiller of hopes. || 758 ||
She who, pervading all this universe, both the manifest and the unmanifest, creates it from every side; she who,
though difficult to abandon even by me, yet exists on the path of the Universal Self— may that fulfillment of hope, whose essence has slackened the bond of this worthless saṃsāra, [grant me peace].
May he instantly bring affliction to exhaustion by the mere sight of his eyes. || 58 ||
Initiation. || 759 ||

Having attained this very [state] through the grace of the supreme Guru's feet, one who was exhausted by the delusions and afflictions of difficult-to-grasp [objects] suddenly obtains liberation through the realization of identity with the Self;
even while living, having reached the transcendence [of the body] via this sixfold path.
O compassionate one, through initiation, strengthen your discernment regarding what is real and what is unreal.
Though devoid of walls and lacking variegated colors, it spreads out the vast and diverse canvas of saṃsāra;
since it swiftly produces that which is composed of a multitude of colors merely by the glance of the eye, it is therefore skillful.
She is worshipped by those who have been initiated. || 761 ||
Residing in the form of a drop within the triangle, Ajitā, worshipped by the initiated,
who pierces through all distinctions such as worship and the like, may she grant him both worldly existence and liberation from becoming.
Betel vine. || 762 ||
Another creeper never goes forth,
yet this one does so with its blue leaves;
another is reddish, while others are dark or white.
Therefore, the wise call it *nāgavallī*. || 62 ||
Nāgakanyā || 763 ||
