O Goddess whose nature is Śiva, O friend of Śiva, O remover of the fear of worldly existence! || 80 ||
May that power, which is served in every world by those of virtuous deeds,
and by meditating upon which even Brahmā and the other gods— though contemplating incomparable prosperity little by little— experience wonder for a very long time, be [granted].
She is the supreme bestower of boons to her devotees, the embodiment of perfect auspiciousness. || 81 ||

From Śrī Kṛṣṇakaula— who possesses the glory of the experience of the self and others as Śrī Kṛṣṇa— there clearly emerged Sāhibkaula; for he attained that state of Śiva which is the source of both intellect and [the world],
and his devotion toward Him, being resplendent, has reached its excellent fruit and final consummation.
In the poem titled *Nāmavilāsa*, this is the sixteenth chapter, the graceful and fully manifest *Pūrṇaprathā*.
Having attained supreme perfection through the great worship of the feet of Śrī Jñāninātha, he who was a master of all accomplishments (Siddhis),
composed [this work] on the play of names, the Sāhib...
The Kaula [attains] the state of fullness of Maheśī. || 83 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth devotion in the *Nāmavilāsa*, composed by the illustrious and preeminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Sāhib Kaulānandanātha. 16.
O Lords, this effort does not shine for those whose intellects are shrouded by the veil of stinginess; who indeed here could make it appear in the stainless mire of the moon’s orb?
But certain fortunate ones, alas, who are ever-striving—may they be victorious!
In the rite of purifying the teeth, they are the extractors of nectar, like the powder from the *kataka* nut used by the *cakora* bird. || 1 ||
With his speech he says one thing, yet with the intellect he places another within his own mind; he determines something else entirely while looking around with his eyes,
or hears a conduct directed elsewhere— thus he is filled with a garland of fruitless egoism.
We do not know the otherness of the Supreme Being; in what state is He equal? || 2 ||
Does a cat, seeing from afar the meat fallen into the talons of a hawk, feel any distress?
This [meat] is obtainable only by flying up; its weapon is its claws.
The supreme state never comes into the hands of those who possess only words. || 3 ||

Let the deluded ones go forth together in their opulent attire; likewise, let even a single knower of that reality go forth in humble dress— just as a herd of deer is overcome by a single solitary hunter.
Are they gathered together—variegated and yet similar? Indeed! || 4 ||
Why is there no direct approach through eight forms? Why is the title "Mahādeva" not well-known by virtue of having three eyes? Why indeed is the possession of great power not to be surpassed?
Why is that state of being the self of all not present? And why is the status of being the Conqueror of Death not supreme?
But if they are deluded and remain unaware of it, it is because they have been deceived by a fragment of Śiva's power.

Those whose boat of intelligence would indeed be wrecked while searching for the jewels of great significance—they alone are struck by misfortune because of their own limited capacity; but is the ocean itself diminished thereby? (6)
The state of being a flower-producer, the manifestation of fragrance, the provision of space, and the exclusive authority over aesthetic flavor—
if one is afraid without having examined these qualities, [one should not fear].
Since one who delights in the Self is already unified [with it], what effort is required here? || 7 ||
Just as his intellect is extensively engaged in the systems of the Upanishads and other philosophical views,

so too is it found to be restless with the playful enjoyment of aesthetic flavor within literature; yet, although he is considered one who has extracted the awakening to liberation, his primary concern is the discourse on the bliss of the Supreme Brahman.
Nevertheless, the story of Rāmānanda was investigated for the sake of experiencing that very reality. || 8 ||
Although there are many stars known as luminaries, is it not true that the moon alone—the treasury of digits—is the light of lights? || 9 ||
It is true that even the moon and others dispel darkness;
nevertheless, he alone is the victorious one—the sun, who is renowned as the jewel in the sky.
Is this brilliance not found in crystal? Does it not shine in snow?
Or does it not exist even in the stars? Nor is it lacking even in the preeminence of water.
Why then is it celebrated here only in pearls—that for which there is great value?
Only someone whose intellect has been awakened by the higher knowledge of the jewels knows its true nature.
Though they are monkeys, those who, struck by dullness, depart upon beholding the world-transcending mountain of rubies;
nevertheless—
Do they know its value or its sufficient quality? || 12 ||
Upon seeing a young girl, even though she is adorned and her essence is extracted [in beauty], does sleep—
which is naturally easy to attain— depart from the sight of a child that brings no awakening? Blessed indeed is that youth who [beholds] the moon of her artistic skill.
He who, upon merely seeing it, causes the ocean of his mind to surge with intense rapture. || 13 ||
From the mountain of Kaśmīra’s rise, that sun of sacred pilgrimage sites emerged; for it was skilled in bestowing grace renowned by all eyes, yet it too was shrouded in evening gloom.
Alas, now wretched, it has gone to the blinding darkness at the end of its difficult course, having set!
Salutation to that Kāla, the bringer of the end of all, by whose power [this is accomplished]. || 14 ||

If he by whom even Ramā—who is devoted to perfect harmony yet fickle—was won over through his forbearance alone; if he by whom even the invincible Smara was brought under control; and if Viṣṇu himself, who created the universe and all its origins, descended into this world by his own will—if such a one were the ill-fated son of Diti...
They strive for their own humiliation; yet this brings him no harm whatsoever. || 15 ||
Even though situated near a lake of blooming lotuses, does a swarm of frogs attain fame for its qualities? But the bee, having perceived the fragrance, approaches it.
Let him drink the full essence; let him rejoice or let him censure. || 16 ||
From humility arises the accumulation of abundant virtues within the heart;
first making its belly vast, the ocean was made a mine of jewels.
[Thus end the verses of instruction for others:
In the Śaka year measured by fire, arms, mountains, and lotuses (1323) of King Vikrama, and in the month of Mādhava during the bright fortnight numbered by eyes and Vedas (42), in Kaśmīra...
In the year marked by two Vedas (42), on the day of Bhūta (the fourteenth lunar day) under the lord of the Gaṇas (Śiva),
he who rejoiced in the splendor of the title Sāhib Kaula brought his life to its end, following after the illustrious Śakti.
The excellent young girl of Tripura, the very youthful girl of Tripura, the auspicious young girl of Tripura, the time of the three puruṣas,
she whose time has dissolved, who has slain the time of Hara.
Possessing the entirety of the vast [world], possessing the entirety of the vast [world], the abode of the best of mountains; having established the supreme foundation,
having established the supreme foundation, having established the supreme foundation.
A garland of white jewels, a radiant garland, a garland consisting of auspiciousness, a garland of shimmering locks,
having conquered the darkness of ignorance, and a garland that destroys the poison of enemies.
She who rests upon the skull of Karaka, whose subjects are protected by her, who wields a white sword, who is beheld by the wise, who dwells in the assembly of Śiva,
and who is a swan gliding upon the lotuses that are her feet.
With hair disheveled and wide open, making the world appear formidable; having destroyed the net of worldly existence and removed the web of rebirth;
a balm for the pain of the heart, she who holds a sword in her hand—

The young women, whose fragrances have spread and whose many tresses are loosened, surpass the *sāla* trees with the form of their flower-fruits; they possess the essence of their own natural beauty, ever fresh. || 1 ||

Her supreme state is renowned; she is the sovereign power of Śiva; she possesses the majesty of the virtuous; she humbles the pride of others; her overwhelming splendor flows forth; and she has generated a beautiful nature.
Existence and non-existence, with states that cannot be grasped;
of great majesty, of great majesty—of no great majesty; the state of existence in the realm of Śikhin.
Possessing both dissimilar and non-dissimilar states, characterized by existence and non-existence, filled with clamorous sounds, holding vessels of honey,
trumpeting like victorious elephants, and having young lions as their seat.
O you who possess a mind free from all obstructions, O young one of unobstructed intellect;

O you who run against the enemy forces, O you who possess incomparable nectar; O you who wash away the filth of the elephant-like passions—O you who possess a most gentle smile, O you who possess a most gentle smile!
The one who brings the three libations, the giver of the three realms, the giver of the supreme station,
the giver of progeny,
the giver of a heartless [state], and the giver of a sympathetic heart.
Whether by one whose mind is struck down, or by one whose intellect is impaired, or by one whose own mind is deluded, [this] has been thoroughly understood. 2.
She who surpasses her own innate beauty with the beauty of others,
whose rest has ceased, who delights the best of gods,
who is embraced by the Supreme Lord, and who is supremely enchanting.
The lord of the abode of the three-eyed one, whose nectar is the light of the moon, the light of the three worlds,
who has fulfilled the desires of those longing for worship, and who is the new desire of the gods.
The beloved of the Lord of the Immortals,
whose youth is never-fading, who is beautiful with her gracefully arched brow, who wears a fine garland of flowers, who has bound her hair with a crest-jewel, and who has destroyed all ignorance.

He whose names are manifold and whose transformations are complete; he who is the name of the Vedas; he who is well-acquainted with the *sāman* chants; he who has made the *sāman* his own; he who consists of hymns of praise; he who is the restrainer of the sons of Diti.
Devoid of the watches of the night, with a perfectly regulated measure of time, possessing immeasurable splendor, her radiance unimpeded,
and her beauty enhanced by her companions.
She who is the supreme ornament of the golden crest-jewel, the ornament of the mountain range, the ornament of her own family, possessed of various arts, and who has attained auspiciousness. || 3 ||
She who surpasses the white water-lily and the stars, she whose radiance eclipses the stars,
she who is the star of the Victor’s teaching, she who is the star of supreme bliss,
she who is the Tara facing the countenances of the lords of the reflected stars.

With movements through the parts of the returned necklace, with shimmering offerings, with necklaces of sweet fragrance, with necklaces worn upon the throat, and with the radiance of the nectar from the hoods of serpents—
She who steals the hearts of the three [worlds], who transcends the Vedas yet is not excluded from them,
whose form consists of various transformations,
who has produced no humiliation, who is free from the injury of force, and who is adorned with a protective circle.
She who brings benefit to the world, she who performs prostrations at her feet, she who acts as a refuge for the best of men, she whose eyes remove the spreading darkness of saṃsāra.
With a supreme essence resulting from constant discernment,
with the essence of a mind whose delusions have dissolved, with the arrows of non-violence directed toward the divine,
she is the one who subdues the pride of those who attack the cities of others.
May the edge of the sword, which is the support of the three worlds and the foundation for those who bow down, grant auspiciousness. || 4 ||

May this work, titled *Daṇḍaka*, composed of one hundred and eighty-eight verses consisting of eight hundred syllables, shine forth for the purpose of the lustration rite (*nīrājana*) of the Illustrious Goddess.
Thus ends the *Śrīnāmavilāsa*.
This work is the composition of the venerable Śrī Mahāmāheśvara Ācāryavarya, the most worshipful lotus-feet of Sahib Kaulapāda, the foremost among all the excellent teachers and supreme lords.
